So are these codec updates 4 days ago Microsoft catches hackers exploiting Zimbra bug before disclosure 4 days ago Azure maintenance mess disrupted hybrid clouds, VPNs, cloudy VMware services 5 days ago Microsoft is very keen for Outlook users to ditch the classic version in favor of the new one, and a search bug isn't helping the old client's cause. Results can fail to update after mailbox items are moved or changed, with Microsoft's workaround sending affected users back to Windows Desktop Search. Microsoft has acknowledged the problem . When users move an item from the search results to another folder, it remains listed and produces an error when clicked. Changes to categories or read/unread status may also be affected. The issue affects Server Assisted Search for mailboxes in online mode. Microsoft's workaround involves a registry change to disable server-assisted searching and make Classic Outlook fall back to Windows Desktop Search. According to Microsoft, a fix is in progress, and the issue has been escalated as a hotfix to the Outlook team, but "there is no ETA yet." Classic Outlook is on the way out as far as Microsoft is concerned. Although existing installations will be supported until at least 2029 , the opt-out phase is due to kick off in 2027 , when affected enterprise users will be moved to New Outlook by default unless administrators block the migration. Users will still be able to switch back to Classic Outlook. The next stage, cutover, will remove the option to change back. Microsoft has, however, still managed to find time to load Classic Outlook with Copilot via a button beside the ribbon , along with the odd bug or two, like the borking of the Quick Steps function . Microsoft also acknowledged an issue that prevented some users from accessing voicemail audio attachments. The voicemail issue was fixed in build 16.0.20430.2000 and later, but the Server Assisted Search problem remains. Another update for Outlook on the Web and New Outlook to make the new tools look a bit like Classic Outlook began rolling out recently. Something to ease the transition. However, it's only skin deep. events.title: Leaving the US overnight felt like a 'bad dream'
events.summary: Ananya Joshi moved from India to the US in 2022 to pursue a master's degree in biotechnology at Northwestern University. She later joined a cultivated meat startup in Chicago as a scientist and planned to continue working in the US. Joshi had a promise of H-1B sponsorship, but her employer ultimately backed out. Her work option could not be renewed, and her F-1 visa was cut short. In September 2025, President Donald Trump set in motion a change that would throw the H-1B visa application process into disarray. His proposed $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions changed the immigration landscape for some employers, employees, and visa hopefuls like Joshi. Since last September, Business Insider has been interviewing people who have borne the brunt of the chaos , including those who have applied for visas and are debating whether to stay in the US. Others have opted to tap out of the system altogether. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
events.summary: Published 6 October 2026, 13:55 BST Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape. The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers. It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory. The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network. Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings and Mission: Impossible. The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover. Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry. "From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said. Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive. Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology. Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News. Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content. Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation". "While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned. Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you Published 1 hour ago While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning. Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away. Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide". US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead . As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS. Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount. Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained. Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons. Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours. The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick. The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement. To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films. As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.

events.title: 'We did it!': Read David Ellison's memo to employees after Paramount's WBD deal closed
events.summary: David Ellison is CEO of Skydance after Paramount merged with Warner Bros. Discovery. David Ellison is taking a victory lap after completing Paramount's merger with Warner Bros. Discovery , forming the new-look Skydance . "It has taken hard work, perseverance and commitment with many challenges along the way — but we did it!" Ellison said in a memo to employees on Tuesday morning, which was obtained by Business Insider. Ellison expressed thanks to staffers across Paramount and WBD for "your patience, your resilience and, above all, your belief in what we could accomplish together." Skydance will be "powered by creativity and technology," Ellison said, adding that the company has four top priorities: Win in storytelling. Become the most technologically capable media company. Lead in a crowded market. Earn Trust Every Day. "Audiences have more choices than ever, technology is reshaping how stories are created, distributed and experienced, and competition for people's time and attention has never been greater," Ellison said in his memo. "We don't just want to succeed in this environment — we want to win and help shape the future of the industry." events.title: Protesting pupils blockade French high schools again, testing a weekslong movement
events.summary: Tens of thousands of demonstrators have marched in cities across France in support of protests by school pupils demanding more education funding PARIS -- Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched in cities across France on Tuesday in support of protests by school pupils demanding more education funding, increasing pressure on the government of outgoing President Emmanuel Macron . As pupils again blockaded high schools, large crowds waving flags and placards gathered in Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The demonstrations showed how protests that began at a high school in the Paris region in mid-September have grown into a nationwide movement — the latest of many that have marked Macron’s nearly decadelong tenure. “We need to listen to them,” said Léa Monimart, a demonstrator in the northern city of Lille. “They are 17 years old; they are not completely clueless, and they know what they are talking about. It’s important to show that there are adults who support them.” The Interior Ministry estimated that 86,000 people took part in demonstrations outside Paris on Tuesday morning. Thousands more marched in the capital in the afternoon. More than two weeks of class boycotts and school blockades, and policing that has led to more than 6,100 arrests, mostly of minors, have become a flashpoint in the early days of the presidential election campaign . Felix Barney, a university student, described the police response as disproportionate, saying it doesn't make “any sense to hit minors.” “Riot police, batons, rubber bullets, tear gas,” said Aurélien Le Coq, a lawmaker with the far-left France Unbowed party. Its presidential candidate is strongly backing the protests. The violence is “absolutely unbearable,” Le Coq said. The teenage protesters have struck a chord amid widespread discontent in France. Frustrations extend beyond immediate difficulties , such as fuel prices that have soared because of the Iran war , to broader concerns about constraints on public spending, rising poverty and wealth inequality under Macron, who can't run for a third consecutive term. Against that backdrop, pupils’ complaints that education funding shortfalls are endangering their futures have found a sympathetic audience. “You say ‘young people are the future,’ so listen to them,” read a handwritten placard attached to a metal barrier outside a Paris school. At the Hélène Boucher lycée, or high school, in Paris' 20th district, protesters tipped over trash cans and bicycles onto their sides to create a makeshift barricade. Like hundreds of others around the country, the school was closed. Authorities began shutting schools last week to take some steam out of the demonstrations after widespread damage to schools and mounting injuries among staff, students and police. Classes were totally or partially suspended on Tuesday at 891 schools, according to the Education Ministry. Iran live updates: Trump says war will be over 'very soon,' but offers no details Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Facing accusations that it was ignoring protesters, the ministry launched an online portal inviting high school students to anonymously describe the difficulties they face at school and the changes they want to see. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on Tuesday defended policing methods used against high schoolers, despite a growing list of gruesome injuries blamed on officers' riot-control weapons. The latest was a 15-year-old boy who lost a hand on Monday in an incident involving a police stun grenade. Nuñez said that the police response has been proportionate in “almost all cases.” The widespread use of arrests, tear gas and riot-control weapons against teenagers is fueling defiance and angering some parents and teachers. Nuñez said that protests transformed at times into rioting, requiring police intervention. He said that 715 officers have been injured. At Hélène Boucher, parents and other adults positioned themselves on Tuesday between protesters and police keeping watch. “They are our children. Teachers, parents, federations, we all share the same goal: the protection of children’s rights, and it is a legitimate right to demonstrate and to make demands,” said Emilia Sichili Suriam, who is a member of an association of parents. Demonstrators have voiced a range of grievances, often centering on a lack of resources and opportunities for students in disadvantaged schools, despite the promise of France’s national motto : “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.” Students have drawn attention to rundown classrooms that lack basics such as desks and chairs, become sweltering in summer without air conditioning and, in some cases, are infested with rats. Other common complaints include staff shortages and exhausting workloads. French high school students’ compulsory classroom hours are among the highest in Europe.

Pinterest on Tuesday showed off a new feature that will leverage AI to take action on your saved inspiration from beauty-related Pins, like hair and nail ideas, and turn them into actionable plans you can take with you to the salon. “Beauty Guides,” which are powered by the company’s visual intelligence and generative AI technology, Pinterest Intelligence, will translate Pins into terms and phrases used by stylists and nail artists that everyday users may not know, like “balayage,” “root melt,” or “almond nails.” The feature is a small but practical way to introduce AI into users’ everyday lives, as it slots into something that people are already doing: bringing a photo of their inspiration to the salon. That’s useful to a large extent, but having the right terminology at hand while you discuss what parts of the look you want to edit or change can be useful as well. Plus, the guides offer the sort of information that can help users plan for their visit, like the time each part of the process may take and the cost. (Balayage goes into the hundreds of dollars, so that’s information you might like to have up front!) The action guides will show up when you tap on the “Get the Guide” button within the app, and will then offer details about what, specifically, you should ask for to achieve the same look, the time it takes, price range, and maintenance requirements, like how often you’ll need to trim, tone, or touch up, for instance. Uber is buying a catering company called ezCater, as it continues to grow the types of services available through its Uber Eats division. It’s an all-cash transaction valued at $2.3 billion. Billed as a “leading U.S. platform for catering and workplace meals,” ezCater is a marketplace for businesses that need large meals, like an Expedia for catering. The company was founded in 2007 and has become a business that generated over $2.5 billion in gross bookings over the last 12 months, according to Uber. It’s a huge exit for a company that was bootstrapped for seven years before raising its first $4 million round in 2014. Dara Khosrowshahi, Uber’s CEO, billed the acquisition as a way for restaurants to find new, larger customers. “Catering is a big business, and can be a huge revenue stream for restaurants,” he said in a statement. “With Uber’s reach, we can bring that experience to millions more customers and help restaurants win more of these valuable orders.” The acquisition is the latest in a run of moves by Uber to grow its food delivery business. The company is also in the process of buying Delivery Hero for $15 billion, and it’s investing in (and partnering with) drone delivery companies like Zipline and Flytrex . events.title: Google DeepMind's Lila Ibrahim, world's top AI 'readiness' officer, on preparing for what's to come
events.summary: Lila Ibrahim has been with DeepMind since 2018 and recently shifted from the role of chief operating officer to her new "AI readiness" C-suite title. The former Intel chip engineer and venture capitalist shared the ways she uses AI in her professional and personal life with CNBC's Julia Boorstin during the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast. Ibrahim says as AI changes in society accelerate, it will be critical for the next generation, including her own children, to learn responsible ways to use the technology so they can demand to "actually have a role in how that change happens." CNBC is now accepting nominations for the 2027 Changemakers List. Google DeepMind Chief AI Readiness Officer Lila Ibrahim may be the only person in the world with that title, and she says she would not have accepted it if she didn't believe that the AI scales will ultimately tip to the positive. "I don't think I could do this job if I didn't believe that the benefits will outweigh the risks," she told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in the latest episode of the "CNBC Changemakers" podcast. Ibrahim has spent almost a decade helping Google DeepMind build artificial intelligence and stay ahead of the thorny ethical, and downright existential , questions that surround the rapidly advancing technology. Now, she is focused on whether workers, schools and communities are prepared for what comes next. Ibrahim was named to the 2025 CNBC Changemakers list . Earlier this year, Ibrahim shifted into her new role from being Google DeepMind's chief operating officer. The job, she says, is not about DeepMind's own readiness for AI, but about helping the rest of the world understand and adapt as changes accelerate and as AI moves beyond the lab and into more parts of everyday life, from scientific research and weather forecasting to education and workplace productivity. For Ibrahim, the question is not whether AI will become more capable, or exactly how it will. The more important question, she says, is whether people have a say in how it is used. "While I might not know what it will do, I know that we still can – we have the agency to shape how we get there," she said. But she added, "You can't shape the right future unless you do so with the communities that it's going to impact." For workers confronting headlines about AI-driven layoffs and automation, her advice is simple: begin using the technology. "You have to start using AI yourself and create the time and space to do it," she said. "You don't have to be the smartest in the room." How DeepMind corporate teams use AI every day Ibrahim and her teams at DeepMind put this into practice daily. She says the "most transformational" AI use case for herself at work on a daily basis is with briefing documents. "I went into engineering partly because I didn't want to have to read and write a lot, and the ability to be able to synthesize in a way that I can absorb information very quickly has been transformational, not only for me but the team that has to prepare that," she said. "And given how much is going on right now and trying to move at pace, it's not necessarily where everyone adds the most value. Being able to be efficient in that and then free up everybody to do the work ... the big thinking ... way, way better use of their time," she said. Ibrahim breaks down her daily AI use case method into three questions that she asks all team members: That third question is the human talent element, and she said it is critical. "That's what we need to hire for; we need to reward. This is what we want to continue developing in our employees," she said. And she added that goes for herself as well. "AI can help automate all of my tasks, but it cannot automate my Tuesdays," Ibrahim said. With her two teenage daughters in mind, she says the AI learning process needs to start long before people enter the workforce . "They're going to inherit the technology we're developing, and yet they're not getting a voice in how this is being taught to them, how it's being integrated into their schools or into their life, so I think I would love us to see schools lean in a bit more to work with the teachers," Ibrahim said. "Teachers always have to be in the lead with the students to say how do we explore the boundaries for what makes sense with with AI," she said, but she added that students need to "grow up more literate in what the technology is and isn't, and also what are responsible use cases for it." Thinking back on her professional path from graduate student in electrical engineering to work on designing Intel's Pentium processor and now to Google DeepMind and AI, Ibrahim said "so much has already changed in our lifetime, and the same will be [true for] the generation that follows. So all we can do is teach a love of learning and curiosity, and the resilience to know that change is coming, and they can actually have a role in how that change happens.

events.title: 64% of Gen Z has tried manifestation, psychics or other mystical dating tactics: ‘People don't feel like they're in control,' says relationship coach
events.summary: Psychology and Relationships How to meet people without dating apps, according to a relationship coach Psychology and Relationships Social isolation can inhibit success: ‘You need to make time for people' Psychology and Relationships Dating tips from a relationship coach: 'You need to see character' The Next Dream The American Dream is missing a key ingredient, says expert: Without it, 'life is pretty grim' Psychology and Relationships Using AI chatbots mainly for companionship can lower feelings of wellbeing When it comes to their love lives, young people are leaning into the mystical. Manifestation, psychics, astrology, tarot cards, love spells — 64% of Gen Z and 51% of millennial adults have tried at least one, according to a new survey of 1,013 Americans ages 18 to 60 by DatingNews (with an estimated margin of error of ±3.1 percentage points at the 95% confidence level). That compares with 25% of Gen X and 12% of Boomers. Amy Chan, relationship coach and author of " Unsingle : How to Date Smarter and Create Love That Lasts," is seeing these trends now more than ever. "Especially the astrology thing," she says , adding that, "I can't escape the conversation about astrology and Mercury in retrograde." New York City-based psychologist Sabrina Romanoff has seen an uptick in this behavior among her clients as well. "In the past I've heard people bring it up as a joke," she says . Now they're embracing it. A tarot card reading can cost up to $162, according to Thumbtack . Love spells can go for as little as $2 on Etsy . Here's why Chan and Romanoff think young singles are getting witchy, and their advice to people trying these tactics as they look for love. The bottom line of why people try psychics and love spells is uncertainty. "When people don't feel like they're in control — and right now, dating is a dumpster fire," says Chan, "people become more vulnerable to magical thinking." It gives them the sense that they're taking the reins and even provides some hope. Gen Zers in particular are just starting their adult lives and face many unknowns. "There's just so much uncertainty," says Romanoff, "not just with love, but every single expectation that a lot of Gen Z had about their future has kind of just crumbled." That might make them more susceptible to leaning into the mystical than anyone, she says. Young people are also very online and could be more exposed to astrology and manifestation than other generations. "They're on TikTok, they're on Instagram, and they're being served" content about these activities, says Chan. They can be 'a springboard to actually get what they want' Neither Chan nor Romanoff would say it's inherently bad to try mystical love tactics. They both have clients who have. The point is to use these tools in the right way. If you "use the universe or magic or fate as a way of avoiding your own responsibilities and accountability" and do nothing else, then you're not moving your love life forward, says Chan. That's not a productive way to lean in. But if, instead, trying a love spell or a tarot card reading makes you feel more confident and hopeful, and you take that change of attitude and sign up for a new class or strike up a conversation with a stranger, then these activities are helpful, says Romanoff, adding that the practice becomes "a springboard to actually get what they want." Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Paramount announced on Tuesday that it has completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to create a combined company called Skydance. The deal, which is one of the biggest mergers of all time, brings together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with networks including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network. Skydance will also gain control of major franchises such as “The Lord of the Rings,” “Game of Thrones,” the DC Universe, and “Yellowstone.” The merger puts one of the world’s largest entertainment studios under the control of David Ellison. Just last year, Ellison completed his merger of Skydance Media with Paramount, and is rapidly increasing his influence in Hollywood. The Ellison family is Skydance’s largest shareholder, backed by the billions of Larry Ellison, David Ellison’s father and co-founder of Oracle. The completion of the deal comes after settlements with a coalition of U.S. states and a Hollywood writers’ union cleared the main legal hurdles facing the merger. Paramount announced in February that it would acquire Warner Bros. following a bidding battle with Netflix , which had previously reached an agreement to purchase Warner Bros.’ film and television studios and streaming business, excluding its cable networks. Paramount had sweetened its bid by promising shareholders additional cash if the deal failed to close by a specified deadline and agreeing to cover the breakup fee Warner Bros. would owe Netflix for ending its existing agreement. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry,” Ellison said in a statement. “From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Our focus now turns to the future: building a company that empowers creatives, entertains audiences and rewards shareholders. We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” The new combined Skydance corporation will have annual revenue of nearly $70 billion, the company says. events.title: Skydance has a debt problem. Meet new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, the man who's supposed to fix it.
events.summary: Ynon Kreiz's new job as co-CEO of Skydance makes him one of the most powerful men in media. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images David Ellison's new Skydance empire comes with $80 billion in debt. Ynon Kreiz, Ellison's newly hired co-CEO, is the man who has to figure out how to shave that number down. Kreiz is not a high-profile Hollywood figure. The cuts he's about to make may make him one. Hollywood has spent a couple of years trying to figure out Skydance CEO David Ellison, who now runs the companies formerly known as Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery . Now they have a new character to get to know: Ynon Kreiz , Ellison's newly appointed co-CEO. Kreiz, who is expected to co-host a press event with Ellison on Tuesday night, comes to Skydance from Mattel, where he is best-known for two things: engineering a deal with Warner Bros. and actress Margot Robbie to produce the colossally successful "Barbie" movie — and taking an ax to the toymaker's payroll, by laying off 22% of its workforce in one fell swoop. At Skydance, no one expects him to be making deals with studios and talent — that will be Ellison's purview. Instead, Kreiz will be expected to take on the grim task of finding a $6 billion in savings over 3 years — a job that will likely involve meaningful layoffs. It's a job that has drawn repeated comparisons to Gunnar Wiedenfels, the former CFO at WBD, who repeatedly hacked at that company's P&L via layoffs and other cost-saving measures, like mothballing TV shows and movies . "He's Gunnar," one of Kreiz's friends told me this week. But few people outside the company knew who Wiedenfels was. Instead, people in and out of Hollywood focused their attention and ire on David Zaslav , the spotlight-loving WBD CEO. This time around, it seems clear that Ellison will be the public face of Skydance, and the one who gets to do fun stuff like schmoozing with stars. Kreiz will be the one getting his hands very dirty. People who've worked with him in the past say he's cut out for the role. "He's very serious," says Candle Media co-CEO Kevin Mayer, who negotiated with Kreiz when Mayer was a top executive at Disney, and Kreiz was CEO of Maker Studios, a web video startup Disney ended up buying in 2014 . "He's unflappable, and is willing to take on the heaviest of heavy lifts." Kreiz, who declined to comment for this story, arrives at Skydance with a résumé stocked with media bona fides: He ran Endemol, the Dutch TV production company, back when it was a powerhouse; he helped Maker, founded by a group of young YouTubers-makers, scale up into something Disney was willing to buy for $500 million; and he led Mattel's move into IP licensing, which also gave us this year's " Masters of the Universe " movie. People who've worked with him describe him as an exceptionally high-energy executive. "Ynon will get on an airplane and fly across the country for a meeting if it's critical, and fly back the next morning," says Upfront Ventures' Mark Suster, whose VC firm was the primary investor in Maker. Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl, who has known Kreiz for decades, says Kreiz has a tough demeanor that's a little misleading. "Ynon's not a teddy bear. But he's a warm person," he says. Kyncl says Kreiz and his wife are the first people in Kyncl's emergency file — the people his kids are supposed to ask for help if anything happens to Kyncl and his wife. Kreiz has demerits on his record: Disney never figured out what to do with Maker , and Kreiz left Disney a couple of years after selling to them. And while Kreiz cut Mattel's costs, he struggled to grow the company — while Barbie sales shot up after the movie's blockbuster success in 2023, they fell again over the next two years, and eventually returned to pre-movie levels. Mattel's stock has been listing for some time. And while Kreiz is a veteran executive, he's never been in a position like this: While he's co-CEO of the giant media conglomerate, he's definitely not running the place. That person is David Ellison, who engineered acquisitions of Paramount and then WBD, backed by his father Larry Ellison's fortune. Tellingly, Ellison's title remains CEO, not co-CEO. And while Skydance won't have the same kind of pressure from shareholders that troubled Zaslav at WBD — the two Ellisons have effective control of the whole company — Kreiz will have to contend with the people who own the company's staggering $80 billion in debt. And those bondholders may already be worried about Skydance's prospects . Skydance didn't respond to my request for comment. Kreiz will be paid well for his troubles. His first-year pay package will total $47.5 million. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Russian lab worker's suspected plague death leaves experts puzzled
events.summary: A person has died in Russia after contracting a severe lung infection in a case of suspected plague. Experts say that key details remains unanswered, and call for transperency from Russian authorities. Based on currently available information, there are no reports of additional cases or sustained human-to-human transmission. The unexplained death of a lab technician at a Russian research institute handling plague bacteria has raised questions among infectious disease experts, who say the circumstances surrounding the case are unusual and key details remain unanswered. According to local reports, some 200 people have been put under medical observation , or quarantined, in the Siberian area of Irkutsk. Other reports say an incident in the lab dealing with the bacteria preceded the fatality. CNBC has not been able to independently verify these reports. Russia told the World Health Organization on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been recorded in Irkutsk, according to a WHO spokesperson. It wasn't immediately clear if that included the diseased lab worker. While the WHO and health authorities around the world say the risk of a wider outbreak appears low, experts told CNBC that the reported circumstances of the death are difficult to reconcile with the stringent safeguards normally used when working with the deadly pathogen. Javier Pizarro-Cerda, head of the Yersinia Research Unit at the Institut Pasteur in Paris, told CNBC he was "very surprised" by the report coming out of Russia, since people working with plague normally take serious protective measures because of the dangers of exposure. "You work with a full body suit. You work with masks. You work with gloves. So even if you break a tube, normally you should be protected," he said. In Russia, there's also a vaccine for plague. However, it doesn't meet the standards expected elsewhere and offers low, transient protection, Pizarro-Cerda added. Plague is an often fatal disease with very rapid progression. The fatality rate of pneumonic plague is nearly 100% if left untreated, and about 50% if treated. Several experts on the Yersinia pestis bacterium that causes plague told CNBC that isolation and monitoring of anyone who had been in contact with the diseased person is a normal and sensible strategy. As for the origin of the suspected case of pneumonic plague, Yersinia pestis exists naturally in animal reservoirs, especially among rodents, but it is highly unlikely the employee would have contracted the disease elsewhere, according to Pizarro-Cerda. The person would have had to visit a very specific place, been in contact with contaminated people or a sick animal in a wild environment, said Pizarro-Cerda. Reservoirs of Yersinia pestis exist on every continent except Oceania, however, that does not mean human cases occur everywhere those reservoirs exist. Russia's public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor , said the situation is under control and that measures have been implemented in response to the case. It also said that "based on the results of extensive testing, no microorganisms associated with the patient's professional activities were detected in the patient's sample." The WHO said in a statement to CNBC on Monday that the cause of death is still unconfirmed and testing is reportedly underway. All of the patient's contacts have reportedly been identified and are being monitored for illness, and none to date have shown symptoms of illness, the WHO added. It's not clear why dozens of people would be put under medical observation in the region if there weren't suspicions of plague exposure. According to Pizarro-Cerda, testing for plague is straightforward and quick. "If you perform an autopsy, it should be extremely easy because if it's pulmonary plague, then the lungs of the person should be filled with the bacteria," he said. Given that the death occurred on October 2, if testing had been done, authorities would have already been able to find evidence of plague if it existed. The Russian Health Ministry and Russia's public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor didn't respond to CNBC's request for further information. A European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control spokesperson said they were aware of the case of pneumonia of unknown origin in eastern Russia that is suspected to be the plague, but cautioned that "that suspicion is not yet confirmed." "The case is in Irkutsk, Siberia, close to the Russian border with Mongolia. There is little travel between Irkutsk and the EU/EEA, particularly at present due to Russia's war against Ukraine," they added. As opposed to the more widely known form of plague, which affects the lymphatic system and is associated with the Black Death in the 14th century, pneumonic plague can spread from person to person. While less transmissible than, for example, the flu or Covid-19, it's still more of a concern from a disease outbreak perspective.

events.title: Anduril lands $2.9 billion Navy submarine shipyard contract days after Luckey joins Pentagon weapons group
events.summary: Anduril landed a $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy to support submarine production. The company said it will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Co-founder Palmer Luckey, Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were named to the Pentagon's Anduril won an up to $2.9 billion contract with the U.S. Navy on Tuesday to boost submarine production, days after co-founder Palmer Luckey was named to a Pentagon future weapons task force. The company is also investing $3.7 billion to scale a new shipyard at Sparrows Point, outside Baltimore, Maryland, slated to start operations in 2030 and create about 3,100 jobs. Anduril said the 2 million-square-foot facility will build components for the Virginia-class submarine. Some parts, including torpedo tubes, will be manufactured at a 160,000-square-foot facility in Orange County, California. "This is about putting more food on the table and being able to meet the requirements that our country has to produce more submarines," said Anduril President and Chief Strategy Officer Chris Brose in a press briefing. The deal comes days after the Department of Defense tapped Luckey to join a new initiative called Project Meridian to identify and develop capabilities for future U.S. conflicts, raising questions over defense tech's growing sway in Washington as the companies compete for government contracts. Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk are also part of the project. Both SpaceX and Anduril are actively working with the U.S. government. Defense tech companies and their leaders have seen their influence grow in Washington in recent months as President Donald Trump seeks to bolster U.S. military capabilities, including shipbuilding. Marc Andreessen , whose venture firm Andreessen Horowitz pours billions into defense tech firms, including Anduril, was named to the Pentagon's defense policy board this summer, alongside Thiel Capital's Blake Masters. Anduril is widely known for building autonomous drones and crafts. Over the summer, the Wall Street Journal reported that the company was reportedly in talks to build drone boats on the site. Brose said the facility will focus on the Virginia-class submarine program, illustrating a push into conventional shipbuilding by the growing defense contractor. "Our goal here is to be a critical, and hopefully, over time, much larger and growing part of the supply chain for our lead shipbuilders," He said. "And over time, we hope that'll grow up to very large sections of the ship." The massive vessels are built by General Dynamics Electric Boat and Huntington Ingalls Industries. This summer, General Dynamics won a $76.6 billion Navy award to build submarines. "This is an opportunity to really reimagine how a shipyard is built and how this work is done, and that's just not something that our current industrial base has the luxury of doing," Brose said. events.title: Asos investigating after thousands of customers get notification saying retailer has been hacked – business live
events.summary: Asos investigating after thousands of customers get notification saying retailer has been hacked Asos is investigating after users of its phone app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the online fashion retailer’s data. The value of Asos’s shares on the London stock exchange dived almost 12%, after thousands of customers received a mobile app notification titled “Asos hacked” which sent them to a message on the Telegram messaging service. However, the website and app appeared to be continuing to operate on Tuesday morning and it is understood that Asos is still investigating whether any hack has taken place. The message was sent out to customers said “Dear ASOS DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.” Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data collected by Simon AI including transactions and demographic information, such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to clients’ phones. Dray Agha , senior manager of security operations at Huntress , an online security firm, said: Snowflake is a massive cloud database where retailers typically store sensitive customer information, a real worry if cyber criminals have indeed accessed it as they claim. The push notification suggests attackers have breached the systems controlling the ASOS mobile app also. This is clear public extortion. Sending a ransom demand directly to consumer devices is an aggressive extortion tactic designed to force the business into a quick negotiation. I strongly advise shoppers to watch out for targeted phishing attempts while we wait for official confirmation of a data breach. The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers including Marks & Spencer , the Co-op and Harrods suffered major hacking events last year. events.title: House China committee chair urges Fed to review Hong Kong’s access to dollar lifeline
events.summary: House China committee Chairman John Moolenaar is urging the Fed to review Hong Kong’s access to the FIMA repo facility, which provides short-term dollar liquidity to foreign monetary authorities, CNBC has learned. The request comes as China promotes the yuan more aggressively in global finance and expands Hong Kong’s role in that effort. Hong Kong has barely used the Fed facility since 2020, making the immediate financial impact of any restriction relatively small. Economists warn that restricting access could also reduce one of the mechanisms that reinforces demand for dollars and U.S. Treasurys. The chairman of an influential congressional committee is urging the Federal Reserve to consider cutting off a potential financial lifeline extended to Hong Kong during Covid-era market turbulence. The Fed should review the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's access to the Foreign and International Monetary Authorities Repo Facility, Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said in a letter sent to the U.S. central bank last week and exclusively obtained by CNBC. Moolenaar chairs the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party. The FIMA facility allows central banks to effectively borrow dollars from the Fed with those countries' Treasury holdings as collateral. It was conceived as a means to ensure governments could get access to dollars in a crisis without having to sell Treasurys, which could create a downward spiral for prices. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' Supreme Court Justice Alito said he's 'thought about' retirement as Senate control hangs in balance Trump taps Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as AI czar The push to potentially limit Hong Kong's access to a source of dollar liquidity comes as China is making efforts to promote its currency, the yuan, as an alternative to the dollar as the bedrock of the global financial system. The U.S.-China relationship remains fraught despite the cheerful tone of President Donald Trump 's recent meeting in Washington with Chinese leader Xi Jinping . The Fed is in receipt of Moolenaar's letter and plans to respond, a spokesperson said. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority declined to comment. A 'very tenuous truce' between the U.S. and China Still, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh is unlikely to take a step that could be seen as interfering with China policy at a sensitive moment, said Shehzad Qazi, managing director of China Beige Book, a research firm. "That said, this is an example of the novel ways Congress could begin asserting its role in China policy," Qazi said. The "very tenuous truce" between the two countries remains highly vulnerable, he said. FIMA has been used only sparingly since its creation in 2020 , though in August Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged Japan to utilize it to support the yen . The dollar remains secure in its status as the premier global reserve currency. It makes up 56.7% of global central banks' official foreign reserves, according to the International Monetary Fund , and is widely used to settle global trade. Investors treat short-term U.S. Treasurys as equivalent to cash. Those attributes give Americans major advantages by lowering the cost of financing the outsized U.S. debt and allowing them to conduct business abroad in their own currency. China has ambitions to edge out the U.S. dollar, though it is starting from a major disadvantage. The yuan makes up 2.1% of reserve holdings, according to the IMF. Still, Beijing is taking steps to change that, and is making Hong Kong its laboratory for the creation of an alternative global financial architecture. As a longtime British territory, Hong Kong developed its own financial and legal systems in parallel to China. But China now has firm control over Hong Kong, a factor Moolenaar cited in his letter. The Fed needs to take into account "the complete dismantling of the legal and institutional autonomy that has historically distinguished Hong Kong from mainland China and justified its preferential treatment under U.S. law," he said. The Fed should consider that shift in combination with China's recent efforts to boost its currency as an alternative to the dollar, Moolenaar said. The People's Bank of China in June launched its own version of the Fed's FIMA facility, to allow central banks to make short-term loans of Chinese government bonds. Hong Kong was its first user, PBOC Governor Pan Gongsheng said in July. The PBOC is China's central bank. "The Federal Reserve's own facilities should not be a passive participant in that process, nor should the Chinese Communist Party be allowed to copy and paste the U.S. system for its use," Moolenaar said. But removing Hong Kong's access to a source of dollar liquidity could create its own risks, said Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University.

events.title: IMF warns cost-of-living shocks cause ‘lasting deterioration’ in affordability
events.summary: The Iran war has led to a spike in oil prices and has pushed up global inflation. The IMF warns that price rises for essentials like food and energy, driven by wars in Iran and Ukraine, are more persistent, causing lasting affordability issues worldwide. Global inflation is elevated, with forecasts rising to 4.7% in 2026, as supply shocks and conflicts disrupt markets and strain household budgets. The IMF urges targeted, temporary aid over broad subsidies to support vulnerable groups, but notes many low-income countries lack fiscal capacity amid ongoing global debt and shocks. WASHINGTON – The International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned on Oct 6 that price increases for necessities like food and energy , fuelled by the wars in Iran and Ukraine, are more persistent than previously expected. Global prices for many commodities have remained elevated for several years, fuelled first by pandemic supply chain shortages and then by the wars in Ukraine and Iran. The war in Ukraine snarled supply chains for many food-related goods as well as energy, and the US-Israel war on Iran has seen energy and fertilizer prices skyrocket due to the closure of a key Gulf supply route. “We find that the prices of necessities relative to other goods continue rising for more than a year after the start of a typical episode, and remain persistently elevated,” the IMF said in a blog post accompanying its new report. “As a result, people face not only a temporary spike in food and energy costs, but a lasting deterioration in the affordability of essentials relative to other items,” it said. Households worldwide have struggled with cost-of-living increases due to the wars and the pandemic, with wages struggling to keep up with persistent price pressures. The Iran war, launched in February 2026 , has pushed global inflation and saw the IMF upgrade its forecast for the metric to 4.7% worldwide in 2026, compared to 4.1% the year before. The IMF is due to release the main portion of its World Economic Outlook update next week, with new figures for global growth and inflation forecasts. The latest report is part of that release, focusing on lessons learned from the cost-of-living crises of the last five years. The IMF warned that the consequences of so-called supply shocks extended far beyond “a few months of higher inflation”. Central banks across the world have begun raising interest rates to combat inflation. Raising the key rate of an economy can help fight higher prices, but also tends to slow economic activity, a difficult balancing act in developing countries that may not be able to afford the slowdown. The report said the persistent inflationary pressures were a threat to macroeconomic stability for many countries. “Inflation remains elevated long after the initial surge in food and energy prices,” it said. “Inflation expectations also rise and stay above pre-crisis levels for years, suggesting that these episodes may complicate efforts by central banks to control inflation.” The burden of those price increases falls disproportionately on working-class families, for whom spending on necessities is both non-negotiable and forms a larger share of their monthly spending. As a result, such inflation has a “substantial” impact on increasing poverty and income inequality. The IMF called on countries to avoid broad-based subsidies to combat such crises, and to instead issue “targeted and temporary transfers” to those who need them most. With global debt levels at elevated levels, however, many low-income and developing countries lack the fiscal space to do so, especially given the repeated shocks since the pandemic. AFP

events.title: UK police arrest British national linked to airbase incident
events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections 22-year old British national arrested on suspicion of terrorism. British police have arrested a 22-year old British national on suspicion of a terror offence linked to the security incident near a UK airbase hosting US warplanes on September 27. Counter Terrorism Police say the individual is connected with “activity that took place close to RAF Fairford.” In a statement, police said the arrest had been made “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts”. Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing said detectives, “continue to pursue multiple lines of enquiry” and “remain committed to investigating all possible angles.” It is the seventh arrest connected to the incident, which remains largely unexplained, over the past two weeks. Six people arrested on suspicion of terrorism over an alleged plot against the base have all been released on bail. The US moved its B-52 and B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford on Sunday, though it’s unclear whether the move is connected to the arrests. On Monday, US President Trump said his administration withdrew B-1 bombers from the site because of what he described as “some threats”. “We had a threat, and if we’re going to be threatened, we would just move them, and that sort of alleviates that,” he told reporters, adding the people who made the threat “would be linked to Iran,” without elaborating. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK sees, “strong indications” that Iran played a part in the incident, without providing details. Iran has denied involvement, but it has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

events.title: AI turns Wall Street into a herd
events.summary: Liz’s view The keys to succeeding on Wall Street are to a) make money and b) make money differently than others. Performance is table stakes; outperformance gets you the glory. AI is messing with that logic. Nvidia’s $500 billion consortium includes the four largest alternative-asset managers in the world and six of the top eight. Blackstone and Apollo are jointly providing billions of dollars for Anthropic to buy compute. Anthropic’s AI-for-the-real-world consultancy offshoot raised $1.5 billion from Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, Goldman Sachs, General Atlantic, Leonard Green, and Apollo. Nearly every big private-equity firm not on that list is backing OpenAI’s competing version. (Goldman, being Goldman, is in both.) Here is a handy chart. This is not how things usually work on Wall Street, where the goal is to snake investments away from rivals, not share them. The last time private equity clubbed up on deals too big for any one of them to handle solo, we got some of the worst buyouts in history . Some of the crowding can be explained by the sheer amount of money needed. “Why can you get five or six of the leading players at one table? Because there’s enough to go around, ” Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey told me last week. He thinks there will still be winners and losers in the AI trade as investors stake out corners within it; Brookfield has made bets on sovereign AI in Europe, Blue Owl is an AI landlord, Apollo is a lender willing to take on chip risk. But whether those are different bets or marketing gloss for the same big bet is less clear to me. AI is starting to look like an “IBGYBG” trade, a Wall Street phrase that made it into the US government’s postmortem report on the 2008 subprime crash: “I’ll be gone, you’ll be gone.” Everyone wins if it works, even if nobody looks like a standout genius. Everyone loses if it doesn’t, but nobody looks like a standout moron. The irony is that the investing world wasjust returning to a place where outperformance seemed possible again when AI arrived. Two decades of easy money had made everyone look like undifferentiated geniuses. A more fractured, risky, and dynamic world of wars, inflation, and tariffs might have encouraged investors to zig where others zagged. “I think we’ll start to see the pull of groupthink become a little weaker, and contrarianism start to pay off,” I wrote in early 2024 . Oops. Notable A recent PwC study estimates global spending on data centers alone could top $30 trillion through 2050, a buildout the firm says would surpass infrastructure booms such as railroads, the internet and electrification.

events.title: Mary Chia to issue $1m in discounted shares including to founder to strengthen finances
events.summary: The new shares will be subscribed for by company founder Mary Chia Ah Tow and three other businesswomen, Ng Yen Ying, Lin Yan and Maggie Lim Min Er. SINGAPORE – Mary Chia Holdings has proposed issuing 100 million new shares at one cent each to four investors, which would allow it to raise $1 million to strengthen its financial position and fund overseas expansion plans. The move, announced on Oct 6 after the market closed, will bring in new investors but siginificantly dilute the shareholdings of Mary Chia’s existing investors. The subscription price represents a discount of about 27 per cent to the volume-weighted average price of 1.37 cents between Sept 30 and Oct 5, the day the company called a trading halt. It is also about 35.1 per cent and 36.3 per cent below the volume-weighted average prices of its shares over the preceding one-month and three-month periods respectively. The beauty and wellness group said the proposed share issue is necessary to strengthen the group’s capital base and liquidity and give it greater financial flexibility to meet its operating and business development requirements. The company’s net current liabilities stood at about $12.58 million on March 31, while net liabilities were about $11.82 million. Its cash and bank balances stood at about $310,000. Net current liabilities measure the shortfall between assets and obligations due within a year, while net liabilities mean the group’s total liabilities exceeded its total assets. For the financial year ended March 31, the group recorded a net loss of about $2.64 million and net operating cash outflows of approximately $2.97 million. Its independent auditors had also said they could not obtain enough reliable evidence to form an opinion on whether the financial statements were accurate. Mary Chia expects to receive net proceeds of about $946,570 from the proposed share issue, after estimated expenses of about $53,430. Of the amount raised, $750,000, or 79.2 per cent, will be used for working capital, including manpower costs, professional fees, compliance and continuing listing expenses, and administrative and head-office costs, the company said. The remaining $196,570, or 20.8 per cent, will fund the expansion of its operations in China and Thailand, including the establishment of offices and other operating expenses. Chia and Ng will each subscribe for 20 million shares for $200,0 00 , while Lin and Lim will each invest $300,000 for 30 million shares. The company said Ng, Lin and Lim were identified through business networking and are independent of the company, its directors, chief executive, controlling shareholders and their associates. They are investing for their own accounts and are not acting in concert with other parties, according to the announcement. Upon completion, Mary Chia’s issued share capital will increase from about 333.84 million shares to 433.84 million shares. The 100 million subscription shares represent about 29.95% of its existing share capital and 23.05% of the enlarged share base. Chia, who is 76, currently owns about 4.23% of the company, and will hold about 7.86% after the transaction, making her a substantial shareholder of the company. She is the mother of Ho Yeow Ping, Mary Chia’s executive chairman, chief executive, director and controlling shareholder. Ho’s husband Lee Boon Leng is a controlling shareholder of the company. According to its announcement, Chia had approached the company on Sept 21 to express her interest in subscribing for new shares to demonstrate her support for the group. However, as she is an associate and immediate family member of a director and controlling shareholder, Chia’s subscription requires specific shareholder approval. Ng will own about 4.61% of the enlarged company, while Lin and Lim will each hold about 6.91%. After the share issue, the family behind Mary Chia – comprising Ho, Lee, Chia and Suki Sushi, an investment vehicle owned by Ho – will own a combined stake of about 61.5% in the company, compared with 73.93% currently. Mary Chia said it will seek confirmation from the Securities Industry Council that the allotment of shares to Chia will not require her or the family concert-party group to make a mandatory offer for the company. The transaction is also subject to shareholder approval at an extraordinary general meeting. Kang Wan Chern is deputy business editor at The Straits Times.

events.title: Paramount and Warner Bros are now one Hollywood giant: Skydance
events.summary: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros CHICAGO -- It’s official: Skydance-owned Paramount has closed its $81 billion takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery. The companies completed the deal on Tuesday, ushering in a new Hollywood giant with the now shorter “Skydance” nametag. The merger brings two of America’s oldest moviemaking studios together. And HBO Max, titles ranging from “Harry Potter” to “Sinners” and even networks like CNN find themselves under the same roof as Paramount+, CBS and the likes of “Top Gun” and “The Godfather.” All of them will come under the helm of billionaire David Ellison, and his new co-CEO Ynon Kreiz . That further concentrates power in an industry already run by just a handful of major players. Ellison’s Skydance bought out Paramount for $8 billion just last year , and set its sights on Warner — an even bigger fish — very soon after. What followed erupted into a tumultuous, roughly year-long fight over Warner’s fate. Skydance Corp. emerges from one of the biggest tie-ups ever in the media and entertainment industry. Including billions of dollars in debt, the Warner acquisition amounted to nearly $111 billion. “Today is a historic day, not just for Skydance but for our entire industry," Ellison said in a statement Tuesday. "We couldn’t be more excited to get to work.” Here’s a look at some of the key moments that got us here. The early days of Paramount's quest for Warner turned into a messy bidding war. Months after disclosing it was open to selling parts or even all of its business, Warner initially struck a studio and streaming deal with Netflix back in December. But Skydance-owned Paramount, which claimed Warner management “never engaged meaningfully” with its previous proposals, soon launched a hostile counterbid aimed at taking over the entire company — including networks like CNN and Discovery. The Hollywood giants spent much of early 2026 in a heated back-and-forth over who had a stronger offer on the table, with Warner leadership repeatedly backing Netflix as its preferred suitor. But Paramount eventually upped its offer to buy all of Warner for $31 per share, and Netflix opted to bow out of the race . Warner and Paramount inked a mutual merger agreement by late February. Hollywood was closely watching the fight over Warner's future. And from awards shows to online petitions, A-list celebrities and other creatives made their voices known. In April, thousands of movie stars, writers, directors and other professionals announced their “unequivocal opposition” to the Paramount-Warner merger. The open letter — which was signed by long-outspoken critics of the deal like Jane Fonda and Mark Ruffalo, as well as Hollywood heavyweights from Denis Villeneuve to J.J. Abrams — warned of fewer jobs and “less choice for audiences in the United States and around the world.” Meanwhile, some other stars lined up to back Paramount as Ellison reiterated his commitments to the movies. At CinemaCon this past spring , the company debuted a glossy mini movie about the studio directed by Jon M. Chu and narrated by Tom Cruise — who ended the spot atop the iconic Paramount water tower, with the words “the future is paramount and the future looks pretty great from here." Director James Cameron also doubled down on his support of Ellison. The prospect of a new Warner owner also loomed over awards season this year, from #BlockTheMerger pins to more subtle nods in acceptance speeches. When accepting her Emmy last month, “Remarkably Bright Creatures” actor Sally Field — who also signed the open letter in opposition to the Paramount-Warner deal — stressed that “unique storytelling matters” and “we can’t let those voices be silenced, or compromised or merged.” Many industry critics were also outspoken when Netflix's studio and streaming deal was on the table, with particular focus on the future of movies staying in theaters. Trump has regularly attacked reporting he deems unfavorable at CNN (most recently attempting to bar the outlet from the White House altogether). And over the course of the Warner buyout, his administration wasn't afraid to chime in about hopes for a new owner. Iran live updates: Trump says war will be over 'very soon,' but offers no details Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' In December — days after Paramount launched its hostile bid for Warner — the president said that CNN spread “poison and lies,” adding that “I think the people who have run CNN for the last long period of time are a disgrace" and "it’s imperative that CNN be sold.” The White House took aim again at CNN in March, over the network's coverage of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran. At the time, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told reporters that “the sooner David Ellison takes over that network, the better.

events.title: The 14 most innovative influencer marketers of 2026
events.summary: Julian Wass; NFL; ALSAC; Alyssa Powell/BI Creators can hype up a brand or  ruin its week  in a single social media post. For marketers, figuring out how to tap into that influence is a balancing act. It requires experimentation, choosing the right influencer partners, handing over enough creative control, and reacting quickly when lightning strikes and your brand's name is suddenly all over the internet. Business Insider's 2026 list of the most innovative influencer marketers inside brands highlights the executives figuring out how to make their companies look good on social media. This year's 14 marketers were nominated by peers and other industry insiders who shared dozens of examples of how the marketers are working smartly with creators or making original content for social. Some, like PepsiCo's Charlie Crideford and Walmart's Sarah Henry, work with curated networks of influencers who make content or help advise on their social strategies. Others, like the National Football League's Ian Trombetta, work with large teams of in-house producers to make original content tailored to social feeds. Breaking through the noise means finding new audiences in different corners of the internet. Footwear brand Rothy's turned to Substack , for instance, to hire tastemaker writers who could help drive attention to its shoes. "We don't really care about follower count necessarily," Rothy's vice president Anna Doré said. "We really look for great partners and creators who have pull in their own circles, and that can be anyone these days." Our roster of innovative creator marketers faces challenges. Though the creator economy is booming, engagement is harder than ever to come by as social feeds become more saturated and algorithms surface content selectively to different users. "The creative bar is going up in order for us to drive that organic reach and engagement," the NFL's Trombetta said. "No one can predict exactly where the algorithms are going to go one day to the next." Here are Business Insider's 2026 most innovative influencer marketers, listed in alphabetical order by last name. Lindsay Burstein, Keurig Dr Pepper's senior director of integrated social and communications Lindsay Burstein Lindsay Burstein jumps into action when marketing opportunities show up unexpectedly, like when TikTok creator Romeo Bingham posted an impromptu Dr Pepper jingle that went viral and gathered over 100 million views. Burstein oversees a social team that works on creator partnerships, social listening, and digital community building at Keurig Dr Pepper, which has a portfolio of beverage brands like 7UP, Dr Pepper, and Snapple. "We're always looking for ways to do it faster and in a way that feels more real-time so that we're keeping up with the pace and the culture of the internet," Burstein said. In the case of the Bingham Dr Pepper jingle, the company reached out to the creator to license the song for a Dr Pepper commercial that aired during the College Football Playoff national championship. Other recent projects Burstein worked on included a 7UP LuluLime creator campaign tied to the US Open and a Snapple-sponsored comedy night with Pete Davidson and Colin Jost on their decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. Burstein works with celebrities and top influencers, as well as creators with smaller audiences who have posted positively about the company's brands. "We like to reward our fans," Burstein said. "An example could be letting them taste test a new flavor first. They're a big fan. Maybe we send them something that's going to be on the shelves in two weeks, like, 'Hey, we know you're a huge fan. Why don't you try this first?'" Charlie Crideford, PepsiCo's media strategy and deployment director for international beverages Charlie Crideford Charlie Crideford has turned Pepsi Max's creator efforts from an experiment into a pillar of its marketing since taking over the zero-sugar soda's UK work with creators in 2022. Working with the NewGen agency, Crideford grew Pepsi Pioneers, a program that uses creators to advise and shape campaigns for Pepsi, from 15 to 80 people across music, sports, food, and lifestyle. Over the past year, content created by Pioneers creators has more than tripled its reach, while the cost to reach those audiences has fallen by 61%. Under Crideford, Pioneers previously helped spark two highly impactful earned-media campaigns — Pepsi's Iconic Corner Shop and Cherry Ring Popper — and a Christmas TV spot. Crideford has more planned. She's aiming to make Pioneers a permanent part of PepsiCo's marketing approach. She's also extending the program to Ireland and the Nordics and building creator rosters for each market's culture. Anna Doré, Rothy's vice president of brand and communications Anna Doré Word of mouth is how Rothy's, the shoe brand best known for its comfortable flats, got on the map. Influencers are the next evolution of that, and Anna Doré knows it. Doré is turning to Substack to find the next generation of creators spreading the gospel about Rothy's shoes. "People follow these Substack writers because they are in the know," Doré said. "They are arbiters of taste." While Rothy's is still working with creators on Instagram and TikTok content, Substack has been a spot to experiment with its marketing. For example, as part of Rothy's 10-year anniversary marketing campaign, the brand partnered with five Substack creators to write essays about their own personal growth. Rothy's has seen an 18% year-over-year increase in mentions on the newsletter and blogging platform. Doré is also pushing for more in-real-life (IRL) marketing experiences with creators. Creators, especially Substackers, "want to take their communities out of the inbox and into the world," Doré said. Rothy's has been helping creators do just that, sponsoring niche events like a vintage pop-up or a pizza party. Events have real business impact, too. Rothy's worked with Substacker Erika Veurink on an in-store activation at one of the brand's New York locations, where Veurink hosted a vintage sale. The event brought in more than 200 people and increased store foot traffic by 75%, according to Rothy's. The brand also worked with Substacker and travel writer Denna Nazem after Doré spotted that the creator was organically talking about Rothy's shoes in her newsletter. It resulted in a travel-themed event promoting the launch of Rothy's at Nordstrom and a new collection of its shoes, boosting orders for its Cruiser collection and doubling product saves on the affiliate platform ShopMy. Substackers have "really rabid fans and followers who care deeply about what the writers are putting out there and want to connect in person," Doré said. events.title: David Ellison has finally bought Warner Bros. Discovery, remaking Hollywood
events.summary: David Ellison has created Skydance by bringing together Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Mario Tama/Getty Images; David Becker/Getty Images for CinemaCon; Mario Tama/Getty Images Paramount has bought Warner Bros. Discovery, forming a new media giant: Skydance. David Ellison has become a media mogul overseeing two major movie studios, HBO, CNN, and CBS News. Skydance will be run by Ellison and co-CEO Ynon Kreiz, who will oversee the merger integration. David Ellison and his partners have completed their purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery for $110 billion in a mega-deal that promises to reshape Hollywood. Paramount Skydance, now known as Skydance , closed its acquisition of WBD on Tuesday. The combined company now controls Paramount Pictures and the Warner Bros. studio; streaming services HBO Max, Paramount+, Pluto TV, and Discovery+; and TV networks HBO, CBS, CNN, TNT, HGTV, and The Food Network. It also has iconic IP like DC Comics, Harry Potter, and SpongeBob Squarepants. Skydance has the potential to be an entertainment behemoth that can rival Disney and Netflix in size and cultural influence. Controlling this treasure trove of assets cements Ellison as a media mogul . Skydance Media, the production company Ellison started in 2006 that was behind films like "Top Gun: Maverick," merged with Paramount last August. Ellison was backed by the fortune of his billionaire father — Larry, who cofounded Oracle — and financial partners like RedBird Capital, plus a trio of Middle East wealth funds from Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi. The new Skydance will be led by David Ellison and former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz . Ellison will be in charge of Skydance's creative and tech strategies while Kreiz, who's joining as a co-CEO , will handle the merger integration and day-to-day operations. Casey Bloys, the head of HBO, will head up the combined company's streaming strategy after Paramount streaming chief Cindy Holland stepped down . CNN CEO Mark Thompson is staying on, while Bari Weiss is heading up CBS News. The new-look Skydance faces many challenges, including a massive debt load and stiff competition in streaming. Even when combined, Paramount+ and HBO Max lack the viewership of Disney or Netflix, let alone YouTube. "It's a war for time spent, you're chasing the juggernaut in the space, which is YouTube," media analyst Rich Greenfield of Lightshed Partners said about Ellison's streaming mission . This deal's completion ends a monthslong saga that's worthy of an HBO drama. Ellison's company agreed to buy WBD in late February for $31 per share and planned to close the deal in mid-July. Paramount had outbid Netflix , which had previously agreed to pay $27.75 per share for WBD's studio and streaming division. The merger got held up by lawsuits brought by 12 US states and the Writers Guild of America. Paramount settled those lawsuits in September and pledged to make concessions, including increasing its US production spending, releasing a minimum number of movies in theaters, and not selling either of the movie lots. Ellison told Paramount employees in a memo that its deal will lead to "more opportunity for our creatives, production crews and employees across the business, and more great entertainment for audiences everywhere." Critics of the deal said that putting Paramount and WBD under one roof could harm competition in the entertainment industry, leading to fewer jobs for creatives and higher prices for consumers. Thousands of Hollywood creatives, including stars like JJ Abrams and Ben Stiller, signed an open letter opposing the deal in April. Paramount had rushed to finalize its WBD takeover since it would have owed $650 million per quarter, or roughly $7 million per day, if the deal wasn't done, starting on October 1. Inside Paramount and WBD, employees are on edge and are preparing for internal competition as the two media giants integrate. Ellison has promised to deliver $6 billion in savings from this deal, though the company has said layoffs won't account for most of the cost reductions. As for which teams and staffers will stay at the new-look Skydance, Ellison said in September after settling the lawsuits holding up the deal that he and his colleagues "don't have all the answers yet" and that he "won't pretend otherwise."
