events.title: Walmart moves to grab a bigger chunk of the TV ad business
events.summary: Walmart ads are coming to a TV near you. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Walmart is making a bigger play for TV ad dollars. It's struck a partnership with Warner Bros. Discovery. The deal means advertisers can reach Walmart shoppers on linear TV networks like TBS. Walmart is taking its ad business to the TV screen. On Tuesday, Walmart exclusively told CMO Insider that advertisers can now use its shopper targeting and measurement data on linear TV through a new partnership with Warner Bros. Discovery, which is merging with Paramount to form Skydance. The move positions Walmart more favorably in its pursuit of the big brand budgets traditionally spent on TV, and beyond the performance marketing spend that typically accounts for the largest share of its Walmart Connect ad business . It's also the latest sign of retail media giants further expanding into new media beyond their own stores, sites, and apps. Walmart's pitch to advertisers is that they can reach its millions of shoppers and measure whether those ads drove purchases through its sales data. Those properties naturally have a finite amount of advertising inventory, so the company has been ramping up efforts to help advertisers target Walmart shoppers elsewhere. Walmart acquired the TV-maker Vizio in 2024, helping it tap into connected-TV ad budgets. This year, it scooped up the adtech firm Vibe.co , which also focuses on streaming TV, as part of a plan to pursue small- and medium-sized advertisers. Walmart's ad revenue reached $6.4 billion in 2025. Khurrum Malik, Walmart Connect VP of business and product marketing, told CMO Insider the WBD deal came about because advertisers and agencies had asked for the capability. Advertisers' audiences are split across CTV and linear, but advertisers want consistent targeting and measurement across both, he said. Walmart advertisers can access this linear inventory via a private marketplace deal on its demand-side platform. It includes WBD networks such as TBS, TLC, and TruTV, and can include live sports when those networks carry them. Walmart has experimented with linear TV before: In 2024, it partnered with NBCUniversal to make "shoppable" ads available on its live Thanksgiving sports programming via Walmart's DSP. Malik said he envisioned Walmart expanding into more non-digital channels. "We want to start slow and then go fast," Malik said. "I could see us scaling as the solution works for advertisers." Walmart isn't alone in chasing TV ad budgets in the fast-growing retail media space. Arch-rival Amazon — whose ad business reached $68 billion in 2025 — has spent years extending its trove of shopping data into streaming TV on Prime Video and through partnerships with Netflix , Disney, and Roku. Walmart is trying to differentiate itself by making its data available through competitor ad-buying tools, too. Also on Tuesday, Walmart announced that Yahoo DSP advertisers can target its audiences on Vizio and other CTV publishers through a partnership with the supply-side platform Magnite. Additionally, it announced a partnership between the Walmart DSP and Spotify across audio, video, and display ads. "We want to make it easier for them to buy how they buy today, instead of forcing somebody into one DSP that really conquers them all," Malik said. "I think about us as a friendly garden," he added. That's in contrast to "walled gardens" — like Meta or YouTube — that require advertisers to use the platform's own buying tools to access its ad inventory. Kevin Dunn, chief revenue officer of Experian Marketing Services, said he expects more retail media to move "offsite" into CTV and other web properties. "I expect the conversation to shift from 'which networks should we be in?' to 'how do we make them work together?'" Dunn said. The retail media space is growing rapidly, with spending set to top $203 billion this year, per Business Insider sister company EMARKETER. However, with more than 200 retail media networks worldwide, the space is becoming increasingly crowded, and some advertising pros have been calling for more consistent standards and language for measuring their effectiveness. A recent ISBA and MediaSense audit of five UK retail media networks found inconsistent metrics across them, including five different definitions of an "attributed sale." Malik said Walmart works with third-party measurement firms alongside offering its own first-party data. "As commerce media moves into a broader media mix, its accountability has to go with it," Malik said. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Mistral unveils new AI model it says rivals best open systems from China
events.summary: Mistral unveiled a new flagship AI model on Tuesday, which it said was the most capable open model outside of China. Access to open AI models, the most capable of which have been Chinese, has become a key flashpoint in the intensifying race for technological supremacy between the U.S. and China. Western developers are racing to compete with Chinese companies in open-weight and open-source AI. Mistral on Tuesday unveiled a new AI model it said ranked among the best open models in the world, as Western companies race to close the capability gap with Chinese developers in the market. Mistral Large 4 (ML4), also known as le Chonk, is a 1-trillion-parameter model that is particularly effective at tasks related to cyber, coding, manufacturing, finance and multimodal, the French company said. Long considered Europe's only answer to OpenAI and Anthropic, Mistral raised a 3 billion euros ($3.4 billion) Series D in September at a 21 billion euro valuation. The round cemented the company's status as one of the best-funded and most valuable AI startups in the region. Access to so-called open AI models — the most capable of which have been Chinese — has become a key flashpoint in the intensifying race for technological supremacy between the U.S. and China. Open AI models can be modified and self-hosted, in contrast to leading closed systems produced by OpenAI and Anthropic. Chinese open models are increasingly being adopted around the world. Mistral Large 4 is being launched in preview to developers and "cybersecurity leaders," alongside state authorities, before it is released more widely later this month, the company said. ML4 was trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months that were deployed in Mistral's own data centers in Europe. When its core parameters are released, ML4 will rank among the top open-weight models globally on aggregate benchmark performance, Mistral said in a statement. The company added that ML4 was the strongest open-weight model developed outside China by a "substantial margin." The new model still lags behind the frontier in areas such as coding. "The model capabilities will further improve as we scale up our training capacity, following our Series D fundraise," said Guillaume Lample, co-founder and chief scientist of Mistral. "Further, the cyber defense capabilities will enable enterprises and governments to defend themselves against threat actors that are jailbreaking closed models to perform cyber attacks," he added. Open models were thrust into the spotlight earlier this year when it emerged that startup Hugging Face turned to Chinese-based Z.ai's GLM 5.2 to defend against a breach from rogue OpenAI agents. Hugging Face initially turned to leading U.S. closed systems to defend itself, but was blocked by guardrails that mistook its actions for an attack. Nvidia-backed American startup Reflection AI unveiled its first open model on Monday, which it claimed matched the capability of GLM 5.2, which was surpassed by GLM 5.3 in August.

events.title: A $443 million memecoin frenzy dissolves into nothing—Robinhood and Circle are latest to taste the memecoin boom-and-bust cycle
events.summary: Memecoin trading is roaring back —but on a new blockchain with a different twist. In September, Robinhood Chain, launched by the fintech giant this summer, saw a surge in trading activity that involved not only tokens inspired by cats and other internet memes, but also stock tokens: digital assets designed to track individual companies’ share prices and backed by the underlying stock. The burst of trading, however, was short-lived. Daily trading volume in memecoin-stock-token pairs jumped from virtually zero in July, when Robinhood Chain launched, to $443 million in early September, according to CryptoQuant. Since then, though, trading activity has fallen 96%. The frenzy also brought a wave of token creation: About 26,000 new tokens were launched on the chain each day in September, according to Dune data, with the daily total reaching nearly 45,000 on Sept. 8. Most of these tokens achieved little or no volume after launch, and are today worth almost nothing at all, which is the fate of the vast majority of cryptocurrencies. Robinhood Chain hasn’t been the only platform to see a recent surge in trading activity. In mid-September, Circle, the issuer of the USDC stablecoin, launched Arc , a blockchain built for Wall Street banks and other large institutions to move money and trade digital assets. On its first day open to public trading, memecoin launchpads generated more than $336 million in trading volumes on Arc. These launches echo a familiar crypto pattern in which new blockchains and decentralized exchanges see memecoin speculation drive attention, retail interest, and early trading volumes. Solana offered one of the clearest examples in 2024 with Pump.fun , a platform that lets users create and trade tokens within minutes. At the height of that craze, TRON, the blockchain founded by Chinese entrepreneur Justin Sun, rolled out SunPump, a rival launchpad. Inevitably, though, the flurry of activity quickly subsided to almost nothing. According to experts interviewed by Fortune , these newer blockchains are experiencing their own memecoin boom—and the outcome may not be much different. “It’s a way for blockchains and/or new apps to attract money/activity into them, but it is not sustainable. Most of these assets/memecoins will trend to zero,” Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, told Fortune in a written statement.  Jim Thorne, chief market strategist at wealth management firm Wellington-Altus, agreed, comparing the memecoin frenzy to “trading Pokémon cards.” But he drew a distinction between the speculative trade and the technology underneath it, arguing that tokenization—turning assets into digital tokens that can be traded on a blockchain—is here to stay. “Memecoin trading is an unfortunate distraction [from] the power of tokenization,” he said. Thorne also noted that the September boom-and-bust cycle played out as the U.S. government was weighing major new rules for crypto. On Sept. 15, the Senate failed to advance the CLARITY Act , a bill that would have set nationwide rules for crypto markets. Over the course of the next few days, memecoin trading on Robinhood Chain and Arc surged.  “[It] was a short period where folks thought that we were going to go back to the wild, wild west after the Clarity Act failed,” Thorne said.  But when the Securities and Exchange Commission issued a five-year exemption allowing certain platforms to test blockchain-based trading of tokenized stocks under specific rules, the frenzy began to fade. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Flai’s AI dealership software is booking 50,000 appointments per month
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. When Flai was raising its seed round last year, it was just a team of three people pounding the pavement to get car dealerships to use the startup’s software to manage phone calls, emails, and texts. But CEO Ari Polakof was already looking to a more agentic future, where Flai’s AI would handle far more. One year later, that future has arrived. The startup is working with more than 10 of the top 50 dealer groups in the country, and its AI is being used to answer and engage with customers, run outbound campaigns, and schedule appointments — 50,000 per month — across both sales and service. This has led to a 20x increase in revenue, Polakof told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. Flai says this deep integration is helping the startup set itself apart from others trying to get car dealers hooked on AI. The growth is attracting investors, too. On Tuesday, Flai said it had raised a $27 million Series A funding round led by automation-focused firm Base10 Partners. The round included funding from dealers (Friedkin Group and Findlay Automotive), Toyota’s venture arm, Y Combinator, and First Round Capital. Polakof said Flai’s growth is coming from customers who see the bigger vision of what is essentially an AI-powered customer relationship management software built from the ground up and tailored to the specific need of each dealer. “Sure, we do answer the phone calls, but we’re following up with customers, we’re alerting the leadership whenever they need to take a look at something, maybe because the customer’s mad, or because you forgot to respond, or promised them something next week,” Polakof said. “We’ve grown quite a bit from just a phone solution to more of a platform. There are plenty of AI companies coming in, but I think that really speaks about the opportunity.” Flai claims its software is also flexible. Earlier this year it launched with a luxury dealer in Puerto Rico where customers “switch between Spanish and English mid-conversation,” Flai co-founder Juan Alzugaray wrote in a LinkedIn post. “We started where we always do: inbound service calls. It went well enough that they added sales. And now the group is rolling Flai out across all 8 of their stores,” he wrote. The result of all this is that dealerships are selling more cars, making more money, and “customers are getting answers faster,” according to one of the groups Flai works with . Perhaps unsurprisingly, Polakof said much of Flai’s customer growth has come from the dealers talking up the product to their peers. “If you really do great by them, they also do great by you, and they recommend you, and talk about you,” he said. This has led to Flai generating half of its revenue from new customers, according to Polakof. Customers are making these referrals because they like Flai’s software, Polakof said, but also because they get up and running quickly. Flai’s software can be live in a dealership 10 days after a contract is signed, and he tells his team — which is now up to around 40 people — that they need to respond to customers within 20 minutes “at most.” “The common experience, especially around automotive [software] vendors, is — and many are almost traumatized by this — is that they sign the contract and then the company disappears,” he said. “I’m fully focused on making sure that we treat every customer as if they’re our only customer, especially because I know how hard it was to get the first one.” That speed and customer experience, combined with the knowledge Flai has developed on how dealerships work and what they need, is what Polakof said protects the startup from products like Muse, which Meta has pitched as a one-shot solution for small businesses. “You get a group of really smart people, and you spend all your days, all your time thinking very deeply about this one space — it’s just so hard to envision that any other platform outside of the space can come in and start going after your customers,” he said. For all this momentum, there is still one customer Polakof hasn’t been able to land: his own local dealership. “I’m actually trying much harder than I should to make them a customer,” he laughed. “I’m sure we will get them by next year.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Run the CLI in autopilot mode and take your chances Asos app delivers a data leak threat instead of fast fashion 2 hours ago Denmark's ID register spills more people's details than the country has residents 2 hours ago Legacy sign-on service comes back to bite school software provider Bromcom 4 hours ago Atlassian warns of critical file access flaw in its datacenter products 9 hours ago Security researcher claims they found KVM guest-host escape flaw 12 hours ago GitHub Copilot CLI may reveal developer secrets if it comes across instructions that tell it to do so, depending on the underlying model. The coding agent tool was flagged earlier this year for being susceptible to indirect prompt injection . That's when a model ingests text from a source other than the user that directs it to take some action outside the scope of its intended function. This is more of the same, with a twist. According to security researchers at Adversa AI, GitHub Copilot CLI suffers from the same vulnerability identified in Grok two months ago : Cryptographic Context Injection (CCI). Imagine a GitHub Copilot CLI user is working on a project and running the agent in autopilot mode . In other agentic coding tools like Anthropic's Claude , that's the default, but it remains optional for GitHub Copilot CLI. Given that condition, the next requirement is for the CLI tool to read a web page with a malicious set of instructions that have been encrypted with a private key published on the same site. "Static guardrails read text; they do not run it," explained Rony Utevsky in a blog post provided to The Register . "CCI ships malicious instructions as strong ciphertext, along with the key material and an instruction to decrypt, and induces the agent to run that decryption in its own code execution runtime." Active content classifiers that might be reading ingested text as a model defense would miss the encrypted code, unlike encodings like base64 or substitution ciphers that can be undone because the model learned how to decode in training. The attack chain goes like this: The user runs Copilot CLI and asks it to fetch a specific URL. The page contains encrypted content, decryption instructions calling for use of Python, and two possible decryption keys. The first key is fake. It's a template that the agent tries to build by reading targeted files from disk (e.g., the user's .env file). Those secrets then get added to the key string. The initial decryption is attempted with this phony key but fails. So the second key is tried, the decryption works, and the agent is presented with instructions to fetch another URL for more context – but that URL contains the harvested secrets and the network request transmits them to the attacker. This doesn't work all the time, however. It depends on the model, which isn't always obvious to the user. GitHub Copilot CLI currently uses either Microsoft's own model, mai-code-1.1-flash, which executed the full attack chain on 50 percent of attempts, or one of two OpenAI GPT-5.6 models, both of which refused the attack payload. Utevsky describes the situation as a model lottery. "On the paid account we tested, the vulnerable model was not the default and had to be selected by hand," said Utevsky. "But on an account with model selection left on Auto, the router assigned the vulnerable model on some sessions and a safe one on others, with no action by the user away from defaults. The user does not choose, and does not see, which model handled the session." Adversa says it reported the vulnerability through GitHub's bug bounty program on September 17, 2026, and GitHub's triage team validated the finding but declined to treat it as a vulnerability. A GitHub spokesperson said as much to The Register , arguing that the user's actions amounted to consent for what followed: "GitHub values the contributions of our security research community and is committed to investigating reported security issues.

events.title: DeepSeek considers doubling latest funding round to up to $15 billion, sources say
events.summary: DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan, twice its earlier target, sources told CNBC. State-backed funds and corporate investors have shown heavy interest, while DeepSeek is restricting participation by individual investors, people familiar with the talks said. The fundraising comes as DeepSeek faces rising AI capital needs and prepares for a possible Shanghai listing next year. China's DeepSeek is considering expanding its latest funding round to as much as 100 billion yuan ($14.9 billion), double its earlier target, with state-backed funds and corporate investors jostling for stakes, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The AI startup has fielded strong interest from state-backed funds, investment arms of listed Chinese companies and venture capital firms, according to the two people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the private talks. But DeepSeek is vetting prospective investors closely, turning away private investment funds raised from individual investors and limiting the pool largely to government and corporate funds, the people said. The company, which began taking outside capital for the first time this year, initially set a 50 billion yuan target for the current round. The fundraising process remains fluid, and the amount could still change before talks conclude, the people said. Bloomberg reported earlier Tuesday that DeepSeek is close to securing at least 80 billion yuan, with Tencent and battery maker CATL among the largest backers, and is eyeing an IPO in early 2027. CATL, Geely Auto and investment managers Monolith Management and Loyal Valley Capital have committed capital in the latest round, one of the people told CNBC. DeepSeek, CATL, Geely Auto, Monolith Management and Loyal Valley Capital did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. The round, initially expected to close by the end of August, has taken longer than planned as some prospective investors waver over the price, one of the people said, though talks are nearing the end. DeepSeek is seeking a valuation of about 500 billion yuan, or $75 billion, the people said. Its first external funding round, which closed in June, raised about 50 billion yuan. An investor filing related to the round implied a valuation of roughly 350 billion yuan. The AI startup triggered a sell-off in U.S. tech stocks in January 2025 after releasing AI models that rivaled American peers at far lower cost. Its latest model, V4.1 Flash , released in September, is designed for greater capability and faster inference, the company said. DeepSeek's decision to open up to external funding was seen as a sign of AI's ballooning capital demand and mounting pressure to retain talent amid intensifying competition . Founder Liang Wenfeng told investors at a private meeting in July that he prioritizes pushing the technology toward artificial general intelligence over maximizing profit. Talks on the current round were briefly suspended after Liang reportedly said in a private investor meeting that Chinese AI companies still lagged far behind their U.S. counterparts and relied heavily on Nvidia chips. DeepSeek has tapped CITIC Securities to prepare for a possible IPO on Shanghai's STAR Market, Reuters reported in September. Its domestic rival Moonshot AI is also reportedly targeting an early-2027 IPO after raising at a $50 billion valuation, Bloomberg reported Tuesday.

events.title: Former German spy chief arrested on suspicion of treason and espionage
events.summary: August Hanning’s former chief of staff was also arrested on suspicion of ‘aiding and abetting attempted treason’. Germany’s former foreign spy chief has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason, prosecutors have said. August Hanning, 80, is under investigation for attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service, the Office of the Federal Public Prosecutor General confirmed on Tuesday. Hanning was president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service between 1998 and 2005. He was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. His former chief of staff, partially identified as Manfred D, was arrested in Steinfurt in western Germany on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”. The prosecutor’s office said, “On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.” Prosecutors said Manfred D also served as the chief of staff for Hanning’s successors between 2012 and 2026, and used his role to gain access to confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning “in exchange for remuneration”. Hanning then used the information in his private consulting work, prosecutors added. “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said. The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for or which country the foreign agent worked for, adding that “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient”. German MP Marc Henrichmann told the AFP news agency that Germany “will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets”. Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said, “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.” The premises of Manfred D and Hanning were being searched in several locations, including in the capital, Berlin.

events.title: Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two
events.summary: Russia says 290 drones targeted Moscow and nearby regions in the overnight Ukrainian assault. Ukraine has launched a major drone attack on Moscow, killing two people and setting fire to a warehouse in the capital city, Russian officials say. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that the overnight assault involved 650 drones heading towards the city, most of which were shot down, as both sides intensify long-range strikes on infrastructure before winter. list 1 of 3 Russia’s ‘new doctrine’ targets civilian sites in Ukraine, Zelenskyy says list 2 of 3 Russia hits Kyiv bridge as Germany’s Merz visits Ukraine’s capital list 3 of 3 Ukraine ready for US-backed talks with Russia: Zelenskyy Regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said one person was killed in Radumlya and another was killed in Barbybino. He said seven people had been injured and that 47 houses, four apartments and three cars had been damaged. He said 185 drones were “destroyed or neutralised” over the wider region. Prominent war blogger Yuri Podolyaka said an oil storage tank was hit at the Volodarskaya oil storage and distribution facility, the biggest in the Moscow region. The facility stores diesel, petrol and jet fuel. There was no official confirmation that it had been hit. Volodarskaya is one of the major hubs in the distribution system of Transneft and is linked to Moscow’s main oil refinery. It supplies fuel to all three of the capital’s large airports. Ukraine has increasingly targeted oil refineries, depots and export terminals in ⁠an effort to deprive Moscow of the revenues it needs to ⁠finance the war that Russia began in February 2022. Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvenko said the attack ended a relative lull in large Ukrainian strikes on Moscow since September 20. Separately on Tuesday, a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus in the Russian-occupied part of the Ukrainian Zaporizhia region killed three people, Moscow-installed authorities said. Russia has recently intensified ⁠attacks on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, sending waves of missiles and drones by night and day. Its latest targets have included bridges across the Dnipro River. Kremlin-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said on Telegram that a Ukrainian drone hit the minibus close to a village near the front line, killing “three people, including the driver” and wounding three passengers. Both Russia and Ukraine have increased strikes in the fifth year of the war, with diplomacy so far failing to end fighting and the United Nations warning of a significant rise in civilian deaths.

events.title: The midterms are an energy election — and here are five places to look
events.summary: Scratch the surface of the year's biggest stories — the Iran war and AI — and both are bound up in the costs of energy . Why it matters: Prices for gasoline, diesel and power are playing a prominent role in some of the tightest races for control of Congress. The war has kept gasoline prices way above $4 per gallon for months, and helped push diesel to record highs. Fairly or unfairly, data centers are getting blamed for rising electricity prices . It's all unfolding as affordability more broadly tops the agenda in races nationwide. Here's a look at how energy politics are playing out in five critical contests... Senate Michigan. Power prices climbed faster than the national average over the past year in the Wolverine state, and data centers surfaced early in the Democratic primary and stayed prominent in the tight general election race. Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers' campaign shows how Republican hopefuls are willing to split with President Trump on energy and AI — or at least get ahead of him. Rogers called for a one-year moratorium on data centers in August. And he called for a temporary ban on diesel exports in September, an idea Trump then flirted with but backed off. On the Democratic side, if Abdul El-Sayed's January "terms of engagement" for data centers looks familiar, it's because it reflects an increasingly common Democratic view around community buy-in and clean energy. Ohio. AI's voracious appetite for electricity is fueling the clash between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown. Husted has made the case that data centers — not households — should pay for the new power plants and grid infrastructure needed to serve them. A bill he sponsored aimed at doing that fell short in the Senate after passing the House overwhelmingly. Brown is attacking Husted for previously championing data centers and tax incentives to attract them to Ohio. The fight encapsulates a broader question surrounding the AI boom: Who should pay for the massive buildout needed to power it? Alaska. The Iran war is turning energy prices into a potent issue in the race between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. In rural communities, fuel already costs far more than in the Lower 48, with gasoline reaching $10 a gallon in some places. Peltola is tying rising fuel costs directly to Sullivan's support for the war, arguing higher diesel prices are hammering fishermen and families. Sullivan has called for temporarily halting U.S. diesel exports and argues Alaska should produce more of its own energy. Looming over it all is Trump's push for a massive Alaska project to export liquefied natural gas. House Colorado 8th. This is a contest where energy could be the tipping point. Both general elections in the district's young history have been decided by less than 1%, and energy is prominent this time around. One thing to watch is how much political cover a recent data center vote gives incumbent Republican Gabe Evans. Evans' bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3 last month. It urges states — but doesn't force them — to set rules ensuring data center developers cover generation and grid upgrade costs Don't sleep on gasoline either. New Democratic ads supporting challenger Manny Rutinel tie Evans to Trump's war with Iran and higher gasoline prices. Pennsylvania 8th. Data centers have become a central issue in the House race between Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti. Northeastern Pennsylvania is fielding proposals for the energy-hungry facilities. Cognetti is campaigning explicitly against projects that raise electric bills, threaten water supplies or receive tax breaks. Bresnahan, who has previously supported data center development, has introduced legislation aimed at protecting local governments that reject projects from corporate lawsuits. The fight captures the emerging politics around AI infrastructure: Communities may want the investment and jobs, but they also want control over the costs. events.title: Chevron CFO Eimear Bonner built a 20-plus-year career at the company. Now she’ll run its core business
events.summary: Good morning. Chevron is moving its CFO from the finance chair to the center of its operating business. Eimear Bonner, Chevron’s CFO, will become president of oil, products and gas on Jan. 1, taking charge of the company’s core business across the value chain. Jeff Gustavson, currently president of new energies, will succeed her as CFO, the company announced on Monday. Bonner’s career at Chevron has followed a unique sequence: engineer, technology chief, CFO, and now operating president. That combination could make her a particularly well-rounded candidate to lead an oil major, although Chevron is not saying whether CEO succession is part of the plan. She joined Chevron in 1998 as an offshore petroleum engineer in the United Kingdom. Over more than two decades, Bonner held engineering, operating, and strategy positions, including general director of Tengizchevroil LLP in Kazakhstan. In 2021, she became Chevron’s first female chief technology officer. Three years later, she made the transition from CTO to CFO . In her new role as president, Chevron said Bonner will be responsible for safe and reliable operations, disciplined capital allocation, asset-class excellence, and value-chain optimization. The assignment is more than an operating role. It puts her in a position to apply the financial and strategic perspective she gained as CFO to some of Chevron’s biggest operational challenges. I asked Chevron whether Bonner and Gustavson are considered potential internal successors to Chairman and CEO Mike Wirth, who has led the company for nearly a decade. “Chevron maintains a robust succession planning process overseen by the board,” a spokesperson said in an email. “We have strong leadership across the company and a deep bench of experienced executives prepared to lead the business. Our strategy, priorities and commitment to disciplined execution remain unchanged, and we are well positioned for continued success.” For recruiting experts, Bonner’s sequence of assignments is notable. Scott W. Simmons, co-managing partner at executive-search firm Crist Kolder Associates, described her progression as a “perfect script” for CEO development. Her technology and finance assignments gave her “in-the-weeds training” in two critical areas, he said. “The CFO role provides an incredibly unique vantage point that allows an executive to see across the entire enterprise,” Simmons said. He expects boards to continue using rotations through the CFO job as part of CEO-development plans. “A variety of experience is most important for growing future CEOs, and Bonner’s background is an excellent blueprint,” he said. Turning scale into returns The CFO transition comes at a consequential moment for Chevron ( No. 21 on the Fortune 500). In the second quarter, Chevron reported $12.1 billion in earnings and a 21% return on capital employed, along with record U.S. production and a 20% year-over-year increase in worldwide production, driven in part by legacy Hess assets and growth in the Permian Basin and Gulf of America. The challenge now is to turn that scale into higher returns. Morningstar analyst Allen Good wrote Oct. 1 that Chevron is targeting higher returns and greater free cash flow through 2030, supported by volume growth, margin expansion, cost reductions, and operational improvements. Those are precisely the objectives that put an operating executive’s judgment to the test: where to invest, which assets to prioritize, where to cut costs, and how aggressively to pursue growth. Bonner has seen Chevron from the engineering floor, the technology organization, and the CFO’s office. Now, she will have to run the business itself. Sheryl   Estrada Sheryl.Estrada@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Facebook tests going Reels-first in India
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Meta has started testing a new Facebook UX in India that sends some users directly into full-screen video when they open the app, putting Reels front and center. First outlined in July by Facebook head Tom Alison, the test is designed to offer a more immersive, video-forward user experience. Alison said at the time that Meta planned to begin testing it later in the year in “video-heavy countries” outside the U.S., though he didn’t specify where. The company will explore bringing the user experience to the U.S. next year, he said. Users included in the test can opt out and return to a Feed-first experience, Meta said. The classic feed will remain available as a second tab on the Facebook app. The test comes as Meta moves to make video more central to Facebook. Last year, the company said all new videos posted to Facebook would be shared as Reels , regardless of their length or format, and it even renamed the app’s Video tab to “Reels.” Meta has previously said young adults spend about 60% of their time on Facebook watching videos. India has long been a testing ground for Meta’s video efforts, particularly its push into short-form video. In 2020, Instagram began testing a dedicated Reels tab in the country, months after India banned TikTok . The company also tested a Reels-first experience for some Instagram users in India and South Korea last year that similarly sent them directly into the video UX when they opened the app. The new test comes as video consumption rises across Meta’s apps in India. At least 97% of users surveyed in Meta-commissioned studies said they watch video on its platforms daily, and 89% of Gen Z respondents said they use Reels every day, per the figures the company released in June. Meta has described Reels as increasingly becoming India’s “personal and primary screen.” India is Facebook’s largest market by users, with Meta’s advertising tools indicating an audience of more than 400 million people in the country. events.title: Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for work on ‘ghost particles’
events.summary: Belgian physicist worked to build Antarctic observatory that tracks neutrinos from deep space. Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating a giant detector in Antarctica that captures neutrinos, the so-called “ghost particles” from space that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prestigious award in Stockholm on Tuesday, crediting Halzen with a central role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. list 1 of 3 Is there life on another planet? Scientists find the strongest evidence yet list 2 of 3 Have scientists discovered a dark matter particle? list 3 of 3 Nobel medicine prize honours US and German scientists for optogenetics work The neutrino interactions collected by the observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said. “It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner. The 82-year-old said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize, but the announcement still made him feel “strange”. “I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience. Neutrinos have nearly no mass and carry no electric charge, so they can cross between planets, stars and human bodies without being altered, making them rare and hard to catch. There are roughly 100 trillion solar and cosmic neutrinos that pass through our bodies every second. Halzen first proposed the IceCube project in 1988, realising that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector, so on the rare occurrence a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light that buried sensors can record. Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, said although hundreds of people built the observatory, it “all started with one person”, noting that the physics prize has rarely gone to one sole winner in recent years. “People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars.” Eva Lindroth, a researcher in Stockholm and a member of the Nobel Committee, told Al Jazeera that Halzen’s observatory has helped scientists understand high-energy particles. “The nice thing with neutrinos is that they come straight at us,” she said. “That way we can ultimately understand these sources of high-energy particles and understand more about how things in the universe, like how galaxies are formed and the roles of the black holes in that process. “It gives a new way to study the universe,” Lindroth added. “They give us information which we cannot get in any other way.” Last year’s award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments on quantum physics. On Monday, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to two American scientists for discoveries that helped explain how the brain works. The next award will be the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which will be announced on Wednesday in Stockholm. Nobel laureates will receive their awards in a ceremony on December 10, marking the anniversary of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who established the award; members of the royal families of Sweden and Norway will be in attendance.

events.title: Mapping where US bombers are based globally
events.summary: The US has pulled its B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford amid Iran fears. Here’s where else they can fly from. Over the course of Sunday, a dozen B-1B bombers took off from Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in western England and flew home to the United States. Their departure abruptly ended the base’s role as a launchpad for US strikes on Iran, which began on February 28. The base, roughly 160km (100 miles) west of London, is the US Air Force’s only European airfield for heavy bombers and a key forward operating location for deployed bombers. Over the past two weeks, six people were arrested on suspicion of “terrorism”. They were all released on bail. US President Donald Trump said on Monday the bombers were moved because “there were some threats”, which he believed were linked to Iran. “So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” he told reporters at the White House. Hours earlier, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio played down any link to the alleged plot, saying it was “not unusual to see rotations happen” and that he had confidence in the security of US bases. On September 27, police arrested five men on suspicion of plotting to plant explosives near Fairford in the United Kingdom. They were released on bail a day later. Investigators found petrol but no explosive devices in their vans, though UK officials say the men remain under investigation . On Thursday, police arrested a 25-year-old UK-Iranian dual national in London on suspicion of plotting an attack on the airbase. He was also released on bail on October 3. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham suggested that “Iran played a part” in the alleged plot but declined to give details. Iran has denied any such scheme and summoned the UK ambassador in Tehran in protest at the arrests. The US Air Force flies three types of bombers, with a fourth on the way. The B-52 Stratofortress is the oldest. The B-52H model currently in service was built in the early 1960s. With a wingspan of 56 metres (185 feet), it is the largest US bomber and can carry about 31 tonnes of weapons, including nuclear bombs and cruise missiles. The B-1B Lancer , which entered service in the mid-1980s, is the fastest of the three. It can reach 1.2 times the speed of sound and has a swing-wing that sweeps back for high-speed flight. It carries the largest conventional payload, about 34 tonnes, but no longer carries nuclear weapons. These were the aircraft that left Fairford. The B-2 Spirit is a flying-wing stealth bomber designed to slip past air defences. Only 20 were built, of which 19 remain in service. It can carry both nuclear and conventional weapons, including the 13,600kg (30,000lb) “bunker buster” bomb used in US strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites in June 2025. The B-21 Raider , a smaller stealth bomber, is still in flight testing, and it remains on track for delivery in 2027. Over the next decade and a half, the air force plans to replace the B-1B and B-2, leaving a future fleet of B-21s and upgraded B-52s. All US bombers are permanently based in the US, at five main airbases: B-52H: Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana and Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota B-1B: Dyess Air Force Base in Texas and Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota B-2: Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri B-21: Due to arrive at Ellsworth in South Dakota in 2027 All of these bases have long, wide runways, typically exceeding 10,000 feet (3,048 metres). That makes bomber runways about as long as those at a big international airport. What limits where bombers can operate is not tarmac but security, weapons storage and support. For missions abroad, the US rotates bombers through a handful of forward bases. Other important overseas operating locations include Andersen Air Force Base in Guam and Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean. Beyond these, the air force sends small groups of bombers to allied airbases for a few weeks at a time, in what it calls Bomber Task Force deployments. Recent rotations have included B-52s at Moron in Spain, B-1Bs at Orland in Norway and Misawa in Japan, and B-52s at Tindal in northern Australia, which arrived in September. The bombers can also go on a strike mission from the US with the help of aerial refuelling. Bomber missions during the US-Israel war on Iran lasted more than 30 hours there and back. Each group of three bombers needed six to nine tanker aircraft to refuel them along the way.

events.title: Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi deterrence against Houthis: What that means
events.summary: Islamabad says its role is defensive, but Riyadh's offensive in Yemen tests how long it can stay out of the fight. Islamabad, Pakistan — For the first time since it was signed in August, the Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkiye is now in force. At an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, the pact’s top committee agreed to deploy Pakistani and Turkish forces to the kingdom, which is backing an offensive against Yemen’s Houthis. list 1 of 4 Turkiye, Pakistan agree Saudi Arabia military deployment under Mecca pact list 2 of 4 Turkiye, Pakistan agree to military deployment to Saudi Arabia list 3 of 4 Can Yemen retake territory seized by Houthis? list 4 of 4 Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest? “The Committee decided to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom, in accordance with the approved arrangements and the national legislation of the Parties,” said a joint statement shared by Pakistan’s Foreign Office. The statement did not specify the size or role of the forces. Saudi-led coalition spokesperson Major General Turki al-Malki said 100 fighter jets were supporting a Yemeni government counteroffensive to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month. Hours after the meeting, Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said Pakistani forces were already playing a part. “The forces of Turkiye and Pakistan are playing a supporting role. We are definitely involved in reconnaissance and such things, but the combat is practically being conducted by Saudi Arabia’s own forces, and they are the ones retaking those areas,” Asif told Geo News, speaking from Riyadh on Monday night. That leaves Pakistan in a defensive role alongside a Saudi offensive. Analysts told Al Jazeera that it raises a question Islamabad has yet to answer publicly: How long can it stay out of the actual fighting? Pakistan already had a military presence in Saudi Arabia. It has trained Saudi military personnel since 1967, with a 1982 agreement formalising the deputation of troops to the kingdom. A declassified CIA assessment from June 1985 estimated that 13,000 to 14,000 Pakistanis were serving in the Saudi army, including an armoured brigade at Tabuk. During the 1990-91 Gulf War, Pakistan also sent a large contingent to the kingdom for defensive duties. Pakistan also signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement with Saudi Arabia in September 2025 , which treats aggression against either country as aggression against both. In April, Riyadh confirmed that a Pakistani force , including fighter and support aircraft, had arrived at King Abdulaziz Air Base in the Eastern Province. Pakistan has never disclosed how many of its troops are in Saudi Arabia. In September, Lieutenant-General Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry, director general of the military’s media wing, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), told the Saudi outlet Arab News that Pakistani forces were already deployed to protect the kingdom and its holy sites. “I would like to underscore here the word ‘physically’,” Chaudhry said. “We will go to any extent.” ISPR did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the deployment agreed upon in Riyadh. On Tuesday, Pakistan’s Ministry of Information said in a post on X that the country’s commitment to the security of the holy sites and the kingdom was not negotiable. “The operational details of the actualisation of the collective deterrence are a matter of operational confidentiality and may not be made subject of media speculation,” the ministry said. Asif said Turkish forces were also present, but Ankara has not publicly confirmed any deployment. “There is no publicly acknowledged standing Turkish deployment in Saudi Arabia,” Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera. Ereli noted that under Article 92 of Turkiye’s constitution, the authority to send troops abroad rests with the parliament, which has yet to ratify the Mecca pact. Dania Thafer, executive director of the Gulf International Forum, said Riyadh wants the pact to carry real weight . “Saudi Arabia is trying to turn the Mecca Pact from a political declaration into a deterrent,” she told Al Jazeera. For now, she said, Riyadh mainly wants Pakistan and Turkiye to help defend Saudi territory and reinforce its air and missile defences, showing that another attack is no longer only a Saudi-Houthi matter. The Houthis have attacked multiple Saudi cities and facilities, including the East West Pipeline that Riyadh has been using to export oil amid Iranian restrictions on transit through the Strait of Hormuz during the ongoing war waged by the US. Saudi authorities said two of its airports had been hit on Monday evening, injuring at least three people.

events.title: New app Mazal targets luxury license plate resale market
events.summary: Dubai’s priciest license plate, P7, sold for $15 million in 2023. Yet the resale market has run largely on Instagram and independent brokers. A new app, Mazal, aims to change that by holding buyers’ funds in escrow until ownership is transferred, for a 5% fee. Its founders say plates worth $463 million have changed hands in three years, and that the market is growing by about 20% a year. License plates command huge sums in the Gulf, where every opportunity to signal status is welcomed — but proceeds from the government-run sales go to charity. Mazal grades plates like gold — 18, 21, or 24 karat — with a top tier called mithali, Arabic for perfect. “The only question is whether you are a millionaire or a billionaire,” said Chairman Abdulla AlMeer in an interview with The National. AlMeer’s green Range Rover sports a $245,000 plate. His Lamborghini, tragically, has to make do with a $136,000 one. — Ed Clowes

events.title: Saudi’s expat workforce shrinks for the first time in more than two years
events.summary: Saudi Arabia’s expatriate workforce shrank for the first time in more than two years , amid layoffs, the Iran war, and a backlash against hiring foreigners at state-controlled companies. Foreigners employed in the country, excluding domestic workers, fell by 16,000 in the three months to June, driven by a drop in construction jobs, according to the government’s quarterly report. Medical insurance policies for expats didn’t grow at all in the first six months of 2026, another indicator that fewer foreigners are coming to the kingdom. State-controlled firms have been trimming workforces or not renewing contracts as budgets were cut for some projects, while others, like NEOM, have scaled back significantly . The Iran war has also dented the region’s reputation for safety. The unemployment rate for Saudi citizens hasn’t budged and the economy is creating new jobs, albeit at a slower pace. Forward-looking data from the Purchasing Managers’ Index suggests hiring will bounce back. — Matthew Martin

events.title: Qatar and India among seven countries bidding for 2036 Olympics, IOC says
events.summary: South Africa, Turkiye, Germany, Hungary and South Korea are in the list of countries revealed by the IOC. Qatar’s bid to host the 2036 Summer Olympics has been confirmed by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), which said India was also among the seven countries in the running. South Africa, Germany, Hungary, Turkiye and South Korea make up the rest of the current list issued by the IOC on Tuesday. Other countries have until October 31 to declare an interest. Qatar hosted the 2022 football World Cup and was home to the 2006 Asian Games, which it will host again in 2030. In March 2027, the IOC Executive Board will draw up a shortlist of the interested parties, who will then enter dialogue with the Olympic body. The IOC said the 2036 hosts would be assessed on factors such as funding and political and public support. “Wherever the Games take place, one thing must never change: Athletes have to be at the heart of everything we do,” IOC President Kirsty Coventry said in a statement. “That is why, for every future host, delivering the best possible experience for the athletes must always be the starting point,” the Zimbabwean former swimmer added. India has stated its intention to host an Olympics for the first time, centred on Ahmedabad, the key city in Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s home state of Gujarat. Ahmedabad will host the 2030 multisport Commonwealth Games, seen as a major rehearsal for an Olympics. The city is also home to the world’s largest cricket stadium. South Africa hosted the 2010 football World Cup and the 1995 Rugby World Cup but has never played host to an Olympics. An Olympics in the Gulf would have to be moved to later than its traditional July-August slot due to the heat. The German National Olympic Committee voted last month to select Munich as its candidate city for a Games that will take place a century after the infamous 1936 Berlin Olympics, which were overseen by the Nazi regime. The Turkish Olympic authorities hope to do one better than in the bidding for the 2020 Summer Olympics, when Istanbul came second to Tokyo. The 2028 Summer Olympics will take place in Los Angeles, while Brisbane has been awarded the 2032 edition. Preferred hosts ⁠⁠will be named in ⁠⁠2028, and a final decision is expected in mid-2029, the IOC said.

events.title: Meta Muse gives AMD a boost as AI momentum shifts to personal agents
events.summary: The personal agent boom is lifting the fortunes of AMD and Intel, which have outperformed their megacap tech peers this year and over the past month. As leading developers of central processing units, the longtime rivals are finding a major role in the AI market, which had been dominated by Nvidia. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65. The personal AI agent boom is giving Advanced Micro Devices and Intel new life after the companies spent years watching Nvidia and its GPUs dominate the artificial intelligence market. The central processing unit, or CPU, was once the primary workhorse of a computer server before Nvidia's graphics processing units took center stage with the launch of ChatGPT and the start of the generative AI era. Now CPUs are back, lifting the fortunes of market leaders AMD and Intel, whose chips specialize in powering long-running agents that can work for hours on their own. Last week OpenAI released its AI agent Dots, following the lead of Meta , which debuted Muse in early September. Muse caught on so quickly that it topped the Apple App Store in less than two weeks . Well before that, AMD and Intel were already huge winners in the stock market this year due largely to surging demand for CPUs, but they've picked up steam in the past month, jumping 32% and 21%, respectively, beating all of tech's megacaps. AMD's growing strength in both CPUs and GPUs has pushed the company into the trillion-dollar market cap club. "As more agents are created and developed, and more people start to use them for more tasks, it's going to start to shift the workload away from GPUs and onto CPUs," said Ryan Shrout, president of Signal65, which consults on AI hardware and costs. Users learned about the power behind the new agents by asking them. Muse tells users that it runs on an AMD-powered computer, while Dots said it runs on a virtual computer powered by AMD's EPYC-branded CPU. A Meta spokesperson told CNBC that the company designed its system to use whatever kind of CPU is available. "We take a diverse approach to our hardware and are largely CPU-agnostic by design, which gives us the most flexibility in acquiring capacity," the Meta spokesperson said in a statement. OpenAI similarly uses multiple CPU providers, meaning AMD isn't the only game in town. Most servers at hyperscalers — Amazon , Google , Meta and Microsoft — use CPUs made by Intel or AMD. But nearly every major cloud provider is also developing custom chips of their own, typically based on Arm technology. Arm announced its own CPU for agents in March, with Meta as the debut customer, and its stock price has more than doubled since. Earlier this year, Nvidia released Vera — a fully redesigned central processor — along with an entire rack filled only with the CPUs . The chip giant says it built the new Vera CPUs specifically for agents and expects CPUs to be a $200 billion market by 2030. But it's one part of the chip industry where Nvidia isn't currently the favorite, analysts say. "It's just a new product and they're going to be competing against a lot of different players," Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview, adding that he believes AMD currently has the "best product." CPUs are driving a healthy portion of AMD's growth. Revenue in the company's data center business more than doubled to $6.7 billion in the quarter ended in June, accounting for almost 60% of total sales. " The conversation has changed quite a bit over the last eight to 10 months in terms of agentic usage," said Dan McNamara, AMD's senior vice president and general manager of compute and enterprise AI. McNamara added that CPU sales are going to "really ramp." Muse, Dots and even coding software like OpenAI's Codex use AI models to plan tasks that can run autonomously. The agents need their own computer that can run for hours or even days in the background, explained Futurum Group CEO Daniel Newman. GPUs are still needed for inference, or processing an AI model, but an agent also needs a CPU. "CPUs are actually performing the workflows while GPUs are doing the thinking," Newman said. Meta and OpenAI use virtual machines, which partition a server into several lighter virtual computers, so one server can support scores of users. Some AMD EPYC processors have up to 192 CPU cores. According to benchmarks and the agents themselves, Muse's virtual computer uses two cores and Dots uses nine. Benchmarks and queries show Dots using an AMD EPYC 9V74 CPU, which is available from resellers for under $3,000. The EPYC 9D25 reportedly used by Meta for Muse costs even less on the secondary market. Nvidia GPUs can cost more than 10 times that for a single chip, and they're usually sold in clusters of hundreds or thousands of chips.

events.title: Wall Street points toward gains, oil prices fall as markets await next week's earnings ramp up
events.summary: Wall Street is pointing higher ahead of opening bell after nearing record highs to open the week, while oil prices are down around the lowest level in more than a month Wall Street pointed slightly higher in premarket trading Tuesday after nearing a record close to open the week as oil prices retreat to the lowest level in more than a month. Futures for the S & P 500 rose 0.4% before the opening bell, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average climbed 0.6%, as did Nasdaq futures. Surging oil prices and bond yields have added to challenges for the broader stock market and companies in general, but expectations for strong company earnings have helped support stocks’ recent rallies. With little economic data coming this week, markets will continue to monitor geopolitical news as well as a handful of quarterly financial results from Levi's, PepsiCo and Delta Air Lines before earnings season kicks into high gear next week. Oil prices were down about 2% early Tuesday. Brent crude, the international standard, was down $1.99 to $98.33 per barrel, back to below the $100 mark, but still much higher than the roughly $72 a barrel level of late February. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up $1.83 to $87.60 per barrel. Analysts say upward pressures on oil prices have eased as larger volumes of oil have been crossing the Strait of Hormuz and oil flows through Saudi Arabia’s key East-West pipeline have been recovering, although tensions between the U.S. and Iran are still high. “While there are growing signs of a recovery in oil flows from the Persian Gulf, the market remains nervous about potential supply disruptions from the region. This is keeping prices well-supported for now,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a commentary on Tuesday. In the bond market, U.S. Treasury yields were near their multi-decade highs. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield eased to around 5.26%, after it briefly crossed the 5.35% mark, its highest level since 2002. Iran live updates: Trump says war will be over 'very soon,' but offers no details Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Investors are looking for higher returns to hold government bonds, as inflationary pressures have been rising, driven in part by the energy shock from the Iran war, while U.S. national debt has surpassed a record $40 trillion. The Federal Reserve releases minutes from its September meeting Wednesday, which is garnering heavy interest because the central bank decided to raise U.S. benchmark interest rates for the first time in three years. In midday European trading, Britain's FTSE 100 gained 0.4%, while France's CAC 40 and Germany's DAX each gained 0.6%. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rose 1.1% to 70,683.98. The benchmark has surged above the 70,000 level this week for the first time since early July. South Korea’s Kospi lost 0.9% to 6,941.39. Technology-related stocks in Japan and South Korea were volatile. events.title: Car buyers are stretching loans to afford payments — it's a 'potential warning light,' analyst says
events.summary: More than a quarter of new-car buyers who financed their purchase in the third quarter took out loans of 84 months or longer, according to car-shopping website Edmunds. Despite stretching out their loans, buyers faced a record-high average monthly payment of $787. The average amount financed also reached a record $44,664, up from $42,744 a year earlier. More car buyers are stretching out their loans in an effort to make the purchase affordable . Even so, monthly payments keep rising. A record 25.5% of financed new-vehicle purchases in the third quarter had loan terms of 84 months or longer, up from 21.8% a year earlier, according to a new report from Edmunds, a car-shopping website. The average monthly payment over that same period reached a record $787, up from $756 a year earlier, the data shows. "Monthly payments are rising because buyers are borrowing significantly more money overall," said Joseph Yoon, consumer insights analyst at Edmunds. Trump administration starts sending $500 Obamacare refund checks — who benefits SEC proposes investor exam to expand private-market access — how it could work Social Security claiming ages may soon get new names. What retirees need to know Trump Accounts have auto-enrolled more than 60 million children, Treasury says CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The average amount financed for a new vehicle reached a record $44,664 in the third quarter, up from $42,744 a year ago, according to Edmunds. The average transaction price of a new car was $50,089 in August, up 1.9% from a year earlier, according to the latest data available from auto-pricing company Kelley Blue Book. "If you need 84 months just to make the payment fit, that's a potential warning light that the vehicle is out of your budget," Yoon said. "Consider buying used, choosing a cheaper trim with more needs than wants, or saving longer for a higher down payment." Consumers are still getting squeezed The lengthening car loans come as consumers' budgets are being squeezed due to ongoing inflationary pressures. Additionally, consumer spending outpaced income in August, according to U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis data released Wednesday. "The gap has widened for months, funded in large part by growth in financial assets rather than paychecks," said Jeremy Robb, chief economist for Cox Automotive in a weekly auto update posted Monday. "But that gap could become harder to sustain if energy costs remain elevated and the conflict in the Middle East remains unresolved." High oil prices in the global market have driven U.S. gasoline prices up since the start of the Iran war in late February. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded gas is $4.36 as of Monday, according to AAA. While down from $4.47 a week prior, it's up from $3.13 a year ago. Financing costs have offered little if any relief. The average annual percentage rate on new-car loans was 7% in the third quarter, unchanged from both the previous quarter and a year earlier, according to Edmunds data. However, with bond yields remaining elevated, auto loan interest rates increased "across the board last week," Robb said in his post. The upward pressure on bond yields , which affect the rates that consumers pay on a variety of loans, comes amid persistent inflation and concerns about rising government debt . "Since most auto loans are pegged to the five-year or 10-year Treasury note, we expect that borrowing costs will increase" in the fourth quarter, said Patrick Manzi, chief economist for the National Automobile Dealers Association, a trade group that represents auto dealerships. About 1 in 5 have monthly payment of $1k or more Meanwhile, a record 21.2% of financed new-car purchases had monthly payments of $1,000 or more in the third quarter, up from 19.1% a year earlier, according to Edmunds. Among those buyers with four-figure payments , 69% financed their cars for 72 months or longer. Stretching out a loan also comes with an extra cost — borrowers generally will pay more in interest over time. The average amount of interest paid over the life of a loan reached a record $9,938 in the third quarter, up from $9,442 a year earlier, according to Edmunds. Longer loans also mean borrowers build equity more slowly, potentially increasing the risk that they will owe more than the car is worth if they sell it or trade it in before paying off the loan. "In the first few years of an 84-month loan, almost every dollar of your monthly payment goes toward interest rather than the car's principal balance," Yoon said. "Combine that with standard depreciation, and you're much more likely to stay in a negative-equity position for the vast majority of the loan term." That's become an increasingly common problem.

events.title: Why older lawmakers may wait too long to step aside
events.summary: U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa is 93. He hasn't said whether he's going to run again in 2028. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images U.S. Sen. Ed Markey is 80 and has served in Congress for half a century . His Democratic primary challenger in Massachusetts, U.S. Rep. Seth Moulton, is 47 and made generational change a centerpiece of his campaign. Markey won the Sept. 1, 2026, primary anyway by nearly 30 percentage points. He’s not the only octogenarian to prevail in a competitive primary in 2026. Eleven won their primaries and are on the ballot for the 2026 midterm elections . The oldest primary winner was Sen. Jim Risch of Idaho, an 83-year-old Republican. It seems to be an issue both major political parties agree on: For many candidates, age is just a number, even when it starts with an 8 or a 9. Letting go My colleagues and I study succession in family-run businesses and other occupations where leadership, identity and longevity can become deeply intertwined. Whether someone is in charge of a company or is a lawmaker, their work does not only keep them busy. It provides status, an identity and a sense of mission. Letting go means giving up more than a job. When business leaders or politicians linger for too long , it can be costly for their companies or constituents because potential successors may become frustrated by waiting and decide to move on. When any kind of leader remains in their role for decades, underlying reasons can range from a genuine love for what they do to not knowing what they will do – or who they will be – once they leave. However, waiting too long can mean they’ll have to hand off their responsibilities in crisis mode. In family businesses, my research team found, the people closest to their leaders – including relatives, employees and longtime supporters – may go quiet rather than press the issue . This dynamic is not limited to the business world. It also applies to many of the older members of Congress. A closer look at the large numbers of legislators who continue to serve during their golden years reflects two trends. First, many are elected for the first time when they’re middle-aged. New House members were about 50 years old and new senators around 55 in 2025. Second, although the median age of House lawmakers is now about 60 , and 66 in the Senate , there’s a small group of long-serving members who remain in office into and past their 80s and keep running for reelection. Seeing the advantages of ‘not yet’ Every lawmaker can have a reason to say “not yet.” So can their staff members, who may be loyal to them and their missions and professionally invested in the work they have built together. Political parties value the electoral advantages of incumbents, while constituents may value the seniority, relationships and influence that come with having spent decades serving in Congress . And incumbents can sincerely believe important work remains unfinished . However, unusually prolonged service in any position increases the possibility that illness, cognitive decline or death will lead to an unplanned and probably rocky transition. What’s more, when politicians serve into their late 70s, 80s or beyond, they are breaking with ordinary employment patterns. The typical American retires in their early 60s , with two-thirds of U.S. workers exiting the labor force before their 65th birthday. U.S. Sen. Dianne Feinstein of California arrives at the U.S. Capitol on May 10, 2023, after a more than two-month break tied to a hospitalization for shingles. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images Setting good and bad examples There are examples of long-serving politicians choosing to plan their exit closer to standard retirement age. One is Barbara Boxer. After more than three decades in Congress, the 74-year-old California Democrat announced in January 2015 that she would not seek reelection to the U.S. Senate the following year. “There is a time when you want the next generation to step in and step up,” she said. Boxer’s early decision gave prospective successors nearly two years to organize and voters the opportunity to choose among them. Kamala Harris won the seat but stepped away to serve as President Joe Biden’s vice president. This departure offers a striking contrast with that of Boxer’s longtime colleague, Sen. Dianne Feinstein, who remained in the Senate through a lengthy health-related absence in 2023. Feinstein, also a California Democrat, died in office that September. She was 90 years old. She served on the influential Senate Judiciary Committee , which considers federal judicial nominations, including Supreme Court nominees. During her nearly three-month absence, the committee was deadlocked on dozens of Biden nominations after Republicans refused to let the Democrats appoint a temporary replacement for her and she refused to step down. The tragic way Feinstein’s storied political career ended illustrated what can go wrong when lawmakers keep saying “not yet” until it’s too late . That turned out to be the case with Biden, who reluctantly ended his presidential reelection campaign in July 2024 . However, several books published since then include details about how his inner circle initially advised him to run again . A rushed attempt at succession followed Biden’s abrupt withdrawal from the race. Harris became the Democratic nominee without participating in any of the 2024 primaries. When change finally came, it arrived under duress rather than by design. And Harris lost the election to Donald Trump. U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, talks with an aide during a committee meeting in 2023. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Fearing what might follow U.S. Rep. Kay Granger, a Texas Republican, announced in 2023 that she would not seek reelection the following year. It soon became clear that severe health problems were preventing her from serving her constituents. The former House Appropriations Committee chair didn’t cast a vote in her final six months in office for a good reason: She had dementia and was staying in a Texas assisted-living facility that provided memory care services to some residents. Granger died in August 2026 at 83 . U.S. Sen. Mitch McConnell, a former Senate majority and minority leader, has announced that he will step down when his current term – the Kentucky Republican’s seventh – ends in January 2027. But a fall, hospitalization and subsequent stint in a rehabilitation center in mid-2026 prompted renewed public scrutiny of the 84-year-old’s health and ability to complete his term. U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, who turned 93 on Sept. 17, 2026 , and appears to be in good health, has not yet said whether he’s running for a ninth six-year term in 2028. events.title: Spain’s government approves new urgent housing measures after a night of unrest in Barcelona
events.summary: Spain's government has approved urgent measures on the country's housing crisis MADRID -- Spain’s government on Tuesday approved urgent measures on the country's housing crisis , after an outbreak of violence the night before in the coastal city of Barcelona saw tens of thousands taking to the streets. The Barcelona turmoil late on Monday followed protests across the country over the weekend that demanded measures to resolve a crisis sparked by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid , the country's capital. In Barcelona, Spain’s second-largest city, a severe weather alert over the weekend had forced organizers to reschedule the protest for Monday. What began as a massive peaceful march turned violent when groups of hundreds of hardcore activists clashed with police, throwing stones and setting fire to trash containers. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez 's government approved measures similar to those rejected by Parliament last Friday, which prompted his call for early elections on Nov. 29. The measures will be sent for ratification by an interim legislature, which remains active until the elections. The smaller, interim legislature — known as “permanent commission” — is composed of 69 members, compared to the 350 that sit in the regular Parliament. Iran live updates: Trump says war will be over 'very soon,' but offers no details Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' Alejandro Quiroga, professor of political science at Madrid’s Complutense University, told The Associated Press that the maneuver of having decrees approved by the interim legislature was constitutional but also a necessary politically move by Sánchez. “I don’t think Sánchez had an alternative,” Quiroga said. “If you are calling early elections so you can keep the public’s focus on housing, you can’t just sit back and do nothing about it. That wouldn’t have been smart." The new measures are to extend protection against evictions for vulnerable Spaniards until 2030, regulate room rentals, impose a new tax on seasonal rentals, ban speculative real estate purchases and give tax breaks to landlords, Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez told reporters last week. Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the housing market , despite strong economic growth in Europe’s fourth-largest economy. The protesters have been demanding stronger protections for tenants, measures to combat fraud and a ban on evictions when alternative housing is unavailable.
