events.title: My husband used ChatGPT to become a better husband. I hate to admit it, but it helped.
events.summary: The author's husband turned to ChatGPT for advice. Courtesy of the author I initially disliked that my husband had turned to AI after one of our arguments. The response connected his triggers with patterns I'd seen in our relationship. It also made me consider my own role in some of our conflicts. My husband is always trying to grow — as a husband, dad, entrepreneur, and overall good person. Our marriage is by no means perfect, but we're both always willing to hear each other out, work through challenges together, and troubleshoot solutions . But when he recently texted me following an argument with his "thoughts and plan" via a ChatGPT thread, I didn't know how to respond. His prompt was brief, but honest and straightforward — I'm sometimes short-tempered and end up saying something I shouldn't. I've recognized these six different scenarios as triggers... What are some tips and tricks I can use to not be so short? I've read tons of articles about the " ChatGPT doctor " and, through my PR work supporting both tech companies and behavioral health organizations, have discussed at length the concerns about using AI for things like medical advice or therapy. But that wasn't what triggered me — it was that he was being given an answer, cutting corners to avoid analyzing personal missteps or thinking about what comes next. Instead, he hit enter and received a 30-day "tone reset plan." It just irked me. The transcript changed my mind Then I read through the conversation and, once I got past the boosted ego fluff giving him "respect for even asking, as most men just justify it," I started to see things a bit differently. The author's husband asked ChatGPT for relationship advice. Courtesy of the author First was the psychological breakdown of why he reacts the way he does. Because my husband uses AI for all facets of his life — from personal branding to strategy help for his business to tracking calories— it knows him quite well on a personal level. It first responded by touching on the fact that because he has overcome heart surgeries , fights as a young adult, and chaos, his nervous system is "wired for intensity," so his body flips into threat mode, and when that happens, he goes from "thoughtful husband/father to protector/defender in 0.2 seconds." The feeling I had while reading that back was reminiscent of those triumphant 'aha' lightbulb moments I often get when our therapist goes deep and pulls something from the depths of our history, making a connection I would never have thought of. Those are the moments that make the $150/hour price tag so worth it. Simply put, I hadn't analyzed his reactions to that extent prior, but it all made sense to me. And then, ChatGPT told him what his brain hears in that moment—the translated versions of "I'm not being valued", "I'm losing control", or "Something bad is about to happen." When fear takes over, like the potential worry of our child being in danger, that naturally leads to fight or flight mode. That is all logistical, but my focus was particularly sharpened when I thought about the first part of the response about not feeling valued. Admittedly, that wasn't the first time the theme was rearing its ugly head, and whether his reaction was warranted or not, it was me who made him feel undermined or overlooked in some way. ChatGPT made me take a good, hard look in the mirror I wasn't ready for. The AI-crafted plan Then it went on to break down the six specific triggers he identified, offering ways to respond in each moment. For example, when feeling disrespected, a productive way to respond to get clarity and avoid escalating the situation could come by saying: "Hey, that came off a little sharp. What did you mean?" Following the specific examples and bigger picture view about building calm authority, ChatGPT offered to build him a 30-day plan, "something tactical you can run like you would your short-term rental business." That one made me chuckle and cringe at the same time — because he is so tactical and loves approaching scenarios as business challenges. It knew exactly how to provide guidance and advice in a way that resonated with him, and he did indeed request the plan. The "Tone Reset Protocol" was broken into four phases: awareness, replacement, nervous system control, and leadership. The guidance offered a combination of scripts, questions to ask himself, and specific actions to take. We actually talked through these when we sat down to discuss how to move forward. Giving credit where credit is due Most men love a solution to a problem. They are fixers. But, like all of us, sometimes it's hard to know where to start and how to move forward. What I appreciated is that there was an initiative to recognize the problem, look inward to identify root causes, and actually ask for help. That's a level of thoughtfulness that, whether learned or innate, is worth celebrating. So maybe it doesn't matter where growth starts. events.title: AI agents don't always understand how companies work. This startup raised $5.2 million to solve that.
events.summary: Zeroset's founders started the company earlier this year. Zeroset Zeroset raised $5.2 million from a Google VC arm to enhance AI for company operations. Zeroset's product integrates with enterprise applications to provide better context to AI agents. Check out the pitch deck the company used to secure the funding. AI agents are getting better at completing tasks. But one startup says the digital assistants don't actually understand how the companies they're working for operate. Now, Zeroset has come out of stealth and raised $5.2 million to build models that give AI agents a constantly updated picture of a company's operations. Zeroset's cofounder and CEO, Akshat Kannan, said today's AI models have little knowledge of the inner workings of an individual business because that information can be scattered across customer relationship management systems, ticketing, and internal docs. Nor are AI models typically trained on a company's proprietary data. "Models off the shelf have no understanding of the dynamics of how an enterprise actually works," Kannan told Business Insider. "They have no understanding of how the work gets done." Zeroset's first product, Nebula, connects to software a company already uses, including Microsoft 365, SharePoint, Outlook, Teams, GitHub, and workplace messaging tools. It then tracks how information and activity across those systems change over time. The idea is to give AI agents more than a pile of company documents to search through. Instead, it wants them to understand the sequence of events and decisions that make up a workflow so that it knows how similar cases were handled previously. It can then do that work autonomously. Zeroset was founded in January by Kannan, 18, who dropped out of Stanford this year, and William Zhang, 21, who dropped out of the University of Texas last year to work on the startup . The company is still in a closed research preview and will progressively expand access to customers rather than do a single broad launch. The company plans to combine a license component with usage-based pricing that scales with the amount of data and agent activity running through Nebula. Zeroset said its initial focus is on enterprises and AI-native companies that deploy long-running agents in industries like manufacturing, supply-chain operations, and financial research. It indirectly competes with companies like Mem0 and Zep, which are building memory infrastructure for AI agents. Its $5.2 million pre-seed round was co-led by Gradient and 2048 Ventures, with participation from Leblon Capital. Gradient is a venture capital fund founded by Google in 2017 that focuses on seed and early-stage AI and machine learning startups. Zeroset has five employees and plans to use its fresh funding to hire researchers and systems engineers, fund early enterprise deployments, and pay for model training. Kannan said that training is one of its highest costs, and in one peak training run, it spent about $100,000 in two weeks. events.title: Ray Dalio predicts a debt crisis within 3 years as we're 'approaching our limits'
events.summary: Ray Dalio is bracing for a debt crisis. Jemal Countess/Getty Images for TIME Ray Dalio expects the US to face a debt crisis "within the next three years." The hedge-fund billionaire said the cost of servicing the national debt is squeezing other spending. Dalio flagged the AI boom's growing reliance on debt and the danger of overinvestment. Ray Dalio says the US is careening toward a debt crisis before the end of this decade. The billionaire investor said in a Bloomberg Television interview on Tuesday that he anticipates a debt crisis "within the next three years," or by the fall of 2029. The author of "How Countries Go Broke" and founder of hedge-fund behemoth Bridgewater Associates said the scale of the national debt and the  rate at which it's growing  mean we're "approaching our limits." US debt breached the $40 trillion mark in August, representing an inflation-adjusted increase of more than $10 trillion, or over 33%, since 2019. Dalio said that this trajectory is unsustainable because of the soaring cost of servicing the debt. Those interest payments exceed $1 trillion a year or almost one-fifth of the federal budget, leaving less money for Social Security, healthcare, defense, education, and other priorities. "When debts accumulate faster than they're paid back, then debt service costs grow," he said. "That becomes a higher and higher percentage of one's cash flow. And when that happens, it starts to squeeze out spending . And so then you have a problem." Dalio also underscored that geopolitical tensions have tempered other countries' demand for US debt. Moreover, the AI boom has become " heavily debt-financed ," which threatens to tighten credit in riskier categories such as auto loans, he said. The Wall Street veteran warned that trend could feed tensions over the wealth gap, as "the people who have less get squeezed the most in that part of the cycle." Dalio said he's seeing even AI hyperscalers "begin to encounter issues " with accessing credit, and he's "starting to see those limits being hit." He suggested that AI companies are overinvesting to ensure they're competitive in an uncertain future market, potentially inflating a tech bubble. He added that bubbles burst when people need cash, for example, if they need to repay loans or pay a wealth tax , and that's a phenomenon to "keep an eye on." Dalio has been sounding the alarm on a debt crisis for years. He's described rising debt as an "aggressive cancer," and said it "accumulates like plaque" on a financial system and threatens to cause a "heart attack" for the US economy. He's also said the debt threat has combined with political division and foreign wars to form a " perfect storm ," and he feels like he's "on a boat headed to rocks." events.title: This robotics startup raised $75 million to automate drug manufacturing. See the pitch deck.
events.summary: Multiply Labs CEO Fred Parietti Multiply Labs Multiply Labs raised $75 million to automate drug manufacturing. Its robots make complex drugs like gene therapies and mRNA treatments. Its pitch deck shows how it pitched investors, including Founders Fund and AstraZeneca. AI can help discover new medicines , but making them is another story. Multiply Labs, a robotics startup based in San Francisco, wants to solve that. The company, which builds robots for manufacturing complex drugs, announced on Tuesday that it raised $75 million in a Series B funding round, bringing its total funding to more than $100 million since its founding in 2016. The round was led by NantWorks, a holding company founded by billionaire Patrick Soon-Shiong . Other investors include AstraZeneca , a Multiply customer, Lux Capital , and Founders Fund . "Someone has to make the drugs," Multiply CEO Fred Parietti told Business Insider. The company's office, which I visited this summer, is a large warehouse in the Dogpatch neighborhood of San Francisco. Its robot is a large, long box packed with test tubes and robotic arms. The round comes as investors pour money into "physical AI" — AI systems that act in the real world. Multiply has deployed its machines with a small group of customers. That means the company is still early, and its next test is whether it can turn a small number of expensive, highly specialized machines into a scalable manufacturing business. Today, each robot costs several million dollars to build and relies on a supply chain spread across Europe. Multiply automates the production of gene therapies and mRNA treatments, which are still largely made manually in laboratories. Production is slow, difficult to scale, and vulnerable to human error and contamination. Manufacturing some gene therapies can cost more than $1 million per dose, according to a 2025 research paper. "The only way to hit throughput, cost, and quality is with robotics," said Parietti. "It must cost not like a house, but like a car. So from millions [of dollars] to tens of thousands." Drugmakers such as AstraZeneca and Legend Biotech purchase Multiply's robots and operate them at their own facilities. Multiply also makes money from cartridges used in the machines and from service and support. Parietti wouldn't say exactly how many machines Multiply has deployed, but said it's a "high single-digit number." See the pitch deck Multiply used to raise $75 million below. events.title: Type One Energy raised $200M to build a fusion power plant by 2034
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Type One Energy , a Knoxville, Tennessee-based startup founded in 2019 to build fusion power plants, announced Tuesday morning that it has raised $200 million from investors. The funding helps the startup move up the ranks of the top-funded fusion power companies . But fusion is a costly field to work in. It sits at the cutting edge of plasma physics, materials science, and advanced computation, and even $200 million doesn’t always go far. Even so, the new Series B should get the company halfway to paying for a 400-megawatt commercial power plant, Type One CEO Christofer Mowry told TechCrunch. If Type One can bring it online by 2034, he added, the company could complete its first power plant using less capital than many of its competitors, even with one or more subsequent rounds of funding. The secret, Mowry said, is Type One’s business model. The company will design the power plant and many of its components, then turn to a “bespoke” network of suppliers chosen for the project to build them, he said. Most fusion startups rely on suppliers for some components, but Type One plans to go further. That approach keeps costs down. “The amount of capital that we need to raise to commercialize fusion at Type One is just a different order of magnitude than if you were going to be vertically integrated,” Mowry said, referring to companies that make most of their own parts in-house. “Why would I want to spend on bricks and mortar?” he added. “I used to run a big nuclear manufacturing company. That’s expensive.” The fusion startup has already started assembling a roster of partners. Type One will build its first two fusion devices on the Tennessee Valley Authority’s Bull Run site, and infrastructure consultant AECOM is working on engineering for Infinity Two, the initial commercial power plant. Competitor Commonwealth Fusion Systems has licensed its high-temperature superconducting magnet technology to Type One, and the technology will help form the backbone of Type One’s reactor design. By relying on outside suppliers, Type One becomes what’s known as an integrator, a company that assembles a product from parts made by others. That minimizes its own risk from activities like manufacturing, but it introduces a different kind of risk. The upside is access to partners that may have more expertise in certain areas, like AECOM, the infrastructure consultant working on Infinity Two. “They have 10,000 people, most of them are engineers of one kind. We’re never going to have 10,000 people,” Mowry said. The downside is that integrators have less control over their suppliers than an in-house team does. The most famous recent example might be Boeing, which relied on Spirit AeroSystems to supply fuselage sections for the 737 and 787 airliners. After a series of quality-control failures, including a door plug blowing out on an Alaska Airlines flight in 2024, Boeing bought Spirit, bringing it in-house to improve standards. Type One is betting that it can manage the integration risk, and that it will be lower than the risk of doing everything in house. “These business models are successful because they let companies focus on managing risk and developing a high level of competency in their slice of the value chain,” Mowry said. The round was led by repeat investor Breakthrough Energy Ventures and Clutterbuck Capital, with participation from Lowercarbon Capital, Siemens Energy Ventures, and SiteGround Capital. events.title: How Palestinian reporters defied Israel’s genocide to redefine journalism
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Western media have come under scrutiny for buying into the Israeli narrative rather than standing up for vulnerable journalists in Gaza and elsewhere. Israel has killed about 250 journalists since launching its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023. That is more than the number of journalists killed in all wars in the past 150 years combined. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) says Israel has engaged in “the deadliest and most deliberate effort to kill and silence journalists” that the media watchdog has ever documented. list 1 of 4 Gaza filmmakers slam BBC after shelved documentary wins Bafta list 2 of 4 How the media manufactured consent for genocide list 3 of 4 Echoicide: Who decides which truths survive in Gaza? list 4 of 4 The pro-Israel censors are starting to lose Jonathan Dagher, the head of Reporters Without Borders’ Middle East desk, called the targeting of journalists “a tragedy for journalism”, while the United Nations human rights chief, Volker Turk, called Gaza “a ‘death trap’ for journalists”. Yet, beyond the statements and condolences, Israel has never been held accountable for its killing of Palestinian journalists – a practice that long predates the genocidal war on Gaza, but that took on an industrial scale over the past three years. Instead, the silence of the international community and lack of solidarity from Western media professionals emboldened Israel as it pursued the genocidal war and normalised journalists’ killings. But despite trying to suppress the truth about its massacres and attempts at ethnic cleansing, Israel – historically an acknowledged master at propaganda – has largely failed in its efforts over the past three years, thanks to the bravery of the very voices it tried to silence. That too is the story of how journalism has changed since October 7, 2023. Western media outlets and their prominent faces often claimed to be “neutral” in their coverage of the genocidal war. But the very concept of neutrality in journalism has come under question amid the genocide. The Western media were rarely neutral when viewed according to the basic tenets of journalism and professional standards. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza so far. But Western outlets often framed headlines in the passive tense when reporting on these killings, conveniently shielding Israel from blame. Palestinians were killed by Israel, mostly in circumstances that violated rules of war. These details were not highlighted, and the Israeli narrative that Hamas was using Palestinian civilians as a “human shield” was amplified. When Al Jazeera journalist Anas al-Sharif was killed in a targeted attack in front of al-Shifa Hospital in August 2025, CNN carried the Israeli accusation that he worked for a Hamas cell in its second paragraph, an allegation Al Jazeera has rejected. Weeks before the killing, Irene Khan, the UN’s special rapporteur on freedom of opinion and expression, had warned against “repeated threats and accusations” against al-Sharif by the Israeli army. Israel killed 22 people , including five journalists – one of whom worked for Al Jazeera – in a “double-tap” strike in September 2025. It claimed that it had targeted a “Hamas camera.” Most media outlets ran the story. The Reuters news agency, whose journalist was also killed in the attack, confirmed that the camera belonged to it. Similarly, when Israel targeted media personnel in Lebanon early in the war, a Sky News post on X called it a hit on a “Hezbollah-linked” broadcaster. Israel has also been accused of jailing and torturing Palestinian journalists for doing their job. During the genocidal war, it has tried to control the narrative domestically too, cracking down on Haaretz for its critical coverage of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s failures on October 7, 2023, and the atrocities in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. The Netanyahu government imposed a ban on Al Jazeera, calling the network a security threat. Al Jazeera described the shutdown as a “criminal act” and warned that Israel’s suppression of the free press “stands in contravention of international and humanitarian law”. This was not the first time Al Jazeera has been targeted. In 2021, a Gaza building housing Al Jazeera’s office was destroyed in an Israeli missile strike. Israel has killed many Al Jazeera journalists even before October 2023. Shireen Abu Akleh, considered a voice of Palestine, was killed by an Israeli soldier while she was reporting in the occupied West Bank in 2022. Her killer was never charged for the murder. Assal Rad, an activist and Middle East historian, has accused the Western media of enabling attacks on journalists. “When you’re repeating what Israel says, you’re creating space to legitimise the targeting of their own colleagues,” she said in an interview with Columbia Journalism Review on September 30.

The CPR administration said in a statement [PDF] that it became aware on October 2 of irregular activity during September and established the scale of the breach over the weekend. In a TV interview last night, digitization minister Christina Egelund said it was too soon to say whether the country would issue all-new CPR numbers, one of the solutions proposed following the breach. Danish cybersecurity specialist Jan Kaastrup told TV 2 that treating CPR numbers as secrets was a "broken" approach and argued that a number alone should not be accepted as proof of identity. "We live in a digitalized society, and therefore we should have much better identification systems," he said. Egelund described the company whose access was abused as "small." Private businesses can obtain CPR data under section 38(1) of the Danish Civil Registration System Act, subject to restrictions set out in the ministry's access terms [PDF]. Eligible recipients include companies, foundations, other legal entities, and individuals conducting business. However, access concerns a defined group of people identified individually in advance, and recipients must be legally entitled to process the information under the GDPR and Danish data protection law. The Register asked the ministry why such broad access was given. CPR numbers underpin access to public services and many everyday transactions in Denmark, which has a population of aroun d 6 million people . The database includes the information of over 55,000 people living in Greenland who also use CPR numbers for healthcare, tax services, and banking. The ministry said the register contains approximately 11 million records, including people who have died or moved abroad, which explains why the affected total exceeds Denmark's current population. The ministry also noted that names and addresses of persons who chose to register with name and address protection were not exposed. The CPR administration blocked the unnamed company's access and said it was working with specialists and relevant authorities to establish what happened. It has notified the Danish Data Protection Agency, and police are investigating. ® Classic Outlook clings to stale search results as Microsoft works on a fix Moved messages linger and throw errors when clicked, leaving Windows Desktop Search as the workaround Zombie instructions on carefully constructed web pages could trick GitHub Copilot CLI into sharing secrets Run the CLI in autopilot mode and take your chances The VMware exit is a protection upgrade PARTNER CONTENT: VergeIO says an exit is also an opportunity Asos app delivers a data leak threat instead of fast fashion Rogue notification claims Snowflake instance compromised, but customer info theft remains unverified Brighter isn't better and more is less.

events.title: Current price of oil as of October 6, 2026
events.summary: As of 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $101.43 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $4.38 below yesterday morning’s level and about $35.50 higher than where it stood a year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $105.81 -4.13% Price of oil 1 month ago $97.87 +3.63% Price of oil 1 year ago $65.94 +53.82% Will oil prices go up? No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds. Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring. It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out: Brent crude oil is the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) is the main benchmark of North America. Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s delivered the first major oil shock when the Middle East slashed exports and placed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices fell in the mid-1980s due to lower demand and an influx of non-OPEC oil producers joining the market. Prices surged again in 2008 as global demand grew, but then crashed alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand plummeted like never before—pushing prices below $20 per barrel. To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: U.S. shale executives have no idea when the oil market will go off a cliff Putin admits weakness as Ukraine claims 51% hit to Russia’s oil refining capacity NVIDIA Head of Sustainability: how to accelerate America’s nuclear energy renaissance Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Russia’s drones are getting faster and deadlier. The West is racing to catch up.
events.summary: Ukrainian and Western defense firms are making their interceptor drones faster. Ints Kalnins/REUTERS Russia is increasingly using deadly jet-powered drones to attack Ukrainian cities. US and European defense firms are rushing to develop new interceptor drones to counter the threat. Business Insider spoke with manufacturers about their push to build a new class of interceptors. The Russian weapon looks kind of like a cheap cruise missile. It has a thin fuselage, outstretched wings, and a mini turbojet engine that propels it across the sky. But Russia's Geran-5 isn't a missile. It's the newest and fastest weapon in a family of jet-powered drones that Moscow is using in rising numbers against Ukraine. The unrelenting attacks have intensified since the start of the summer, further straining Kyiv's already stretched air defenses. Ukrainian interceptor drones , initially designed to counter Russia's slower, propeller-powered drones, are being rapidly upgraded to combat newer, faster models and have already downed several Geran-5s. The race is no longer just to build interceptor weapons. It's to build ones with the speed to catch Russia's latest weapons . American and European defense companies are rushing to develop similar capabilities to counter new Russian threats. Business Insider spoke with Western and Ukrainian military officers, officials, and defense companies about the push to develop next-generation interceptors . "The percentage of jet-powered threats is rising," said Lt. Col. Matt Keogh, who is tasked with procuring drone technology for the British Army. "And there is a commensurate level of interest being presented on the interceptors to defeat them." A worsening threat The Geran-5 is Russia's newest and fastest jet-powered drone. Wild Hornets/Screengrab via X Interceptor drones emerged in 2025 as one of Ukraine's top defense priorities. They quickly proved highly effective against nightly bombardments by armed Geran-2 drones, piston-powered aircraft with a maximum speed of about 115 mph. Russia responded by developing faster variants equipped with small turbojet engines. The Geran-3 exceeds 200 mph, while the Geran-4 can reach 310 mph. The Geran-5, the newest variant, can fly at speeds up to 375 mph. Unlike its delta-wing predecessors, it more closely resembles a cruise missile. These drones, which are faster, deadlier, and harder to stop, are playing a growing role in Russian strike tactics. Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 2,800 jet-powered drones in August, compared to 350 in June. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 26 that Kyiv shot down just 55% of the jet-powered drones that month, a significant drop from its interception rate for propeller-powered drones, which officials regularly said was above 90%. Russia is investing heavily in jet-powered drones. It has expanded the infrastructure at air bases to support their launch, and Zelenskyy said last month that Moscow plans to spend $12 billion on producing these drones and other strike weapons in 2027. The consequences have been deadly. Nine people were killed, and dozens more were injured, in a recent Russian attack involving nearly 100 jet-powered drones, Ukrainian authorities said. A Ukrainian soldier prepares an interceptor drone for air defense operations. Frédéric Pétry/Hans Lucas via Reuters Connect The rise in jet-powered drones has forced Ukrainian companies to adapt. Defense firms that built the first generation of interceptors are now developing faster models. Some, like Wild Hornets' Sting S or SkyFall's P1-SUN JetKiller , have already recorded combat kills. "In war, every new capability quickly generates a countermeasure," said Valerii Zarubin, the CEO of BlueBird Tech, a Ukrainian company developing a jet-powered interceptor. If we are talking specifically about jet propulsion and the higher speeds of these drones, interception systems have to evolve accordingly." Interceptors are getting faster The realization that interceptor drones must be faster has extended beyond Ukraine's borders. Western defense companies have, throughout the war, developed new weapons based on the tactics and innovations observed in Ukraine. Now, many see faster interceptors as the next major leap, driven both by lessons from Ukraine and a growing appetite for cheaper ways to defeat drones. Ukrainian Col. Volodymyr Gordiienko, the program design branch head at the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis Training and Education Centre , said that when jet-powered drones first began appearing in limited numbers last year, JATEC was working with French startup Alta Ares on defenses against older, slower threats. Ukrainian companies have already unveiled a new class of faster interceptor drones. Kay Nietfeld/dpa via Reuters Connect Recognizing the emerging risk, JATEC advised monitoring the new drones, noting that they could become a capability gap. Alta Ares acted and developed an interceptor capable of taking down jet-powered drones. Gordiienko said that early identification and quick reaction gave NATO "a promising solution under development." "Western defense innovation should be about anticipating future challenges," he said, "rather than spending several months developing solutions in reaction to an existing capability gap." Across Europe, defense tech companies are reaching the same conclusion and moving swiftly to adapt. Lithuania's Granta Autonomy is considering developing a jet-powered successor to its current interceptor, which has a top speed of roughly 200 mph. Czech firm LPP Holding is working to increase the speed of its existing counter-drone system, the JWI-4000, which can top 185 mph and operate in GPS-denied environments. And Germany's Tytan Technologies is developing a new jet-powered interceptor designed to engage targets at "greater distance and with greater speed." These efforts reflect a growing recognition that today's interceptor speeds won't be enough for tomorrow's threats. Jason Cornelius, the CEO of Perseus Defense, said it's not enough for an interceptor to fly as fast as its target — there must be a speed overmatch. The American firm developed a small, ground-launched missile that's powered by a solid-rocket motor and flies at high-subsonic speeds. After testing its current interceptor with the US military, Perseus is now designing a larger, more powerful model specifically for jet-powered drones. Cornelius said the goal is to test the new model as a prototype by the end of the year. An interceptor built by Perseus launches during a test. US military photo NATO militaries have, for decades, fielded air defenses designed to engage threats like drones, cruise missiles, and helicopters. But many now view interceptor drones as a crucial addition to their arsenal after watching them reshape the air war in Ukraine. events.title: SpaceX stock is taking off again, but with one key difference this time
events.summary: SpaceX is the star of the stock market again as the Nasdaq 100 Index makes all-time highs. With Monday's 8% rally to $171, shares of the rocket maker have jumped nearly 50% off its lows, reclaimed its IPO price and made CEO Elon Musk a trillionaire again. The run doesn't stop there. Morgan Stanley analyst Adam Jonas reiterated a $300 price target for the company Monday, and last Thursday, SpaceX's Falcon 9 rocket delivered four astronauts to the International Space Station in under eight hours — a record. With the stock building momentum, options volume was twice the 30-day average Monday as 1.7 million contracts worth a total $900 million exchanged hands, 1 million of them calls worth more than $640 million. The sentiment recalls the fervor with which SpaceX debuted in June, but there's one key difference this time around: after seven weeks of trading within a 10% price range, SpaceX implied volatility is significantly lower. That means that unless it keeps up the velocity of its moves the past two days, traders should expect a longer haul if they're looking for new highs. It took SpaceX less than three full sessions to go from $171 to its intraday high of over $225 after its June debut. At the time, implied volatility was over 110. Today it's at 55, up from an all-time low below 50 on Thursday. As a result, market-makers are assigning less than a 50% chance SpaceX touches $225 at any point between now and July, according to options pricing at the close of Monday's session. Looking at closer-dated expiries, there's a 54% chance the stock will touch $185 by the end of this month. Also of note is that market-makers are assigning equal or higher implied volatilities to puts as they are calls, Barchart data shows, suggesting downside swings are as great a possibility as an upside surge. It's common for puts to trade with richer options premium than calls in indexes like the S&P 500, but for stocks, skew can go either way. In Nvidia, by comparison, calls are more expensive in many expiries, meaning investors are more concerned with missing rallies than avoiding crashes. Still, options flows in SpaceX Monday were decidedly optimistic. Traders likely bought 456,000 calls, compared to under 240,00 puts, according to Cboe LiveVol. They likely sold 250,000 puts and 295,000 calls, the data show. "Starship has helped out but it seems like Wall Street is piling in starting Q4," said Charles Moon, a technical and momentum trader at Prosper Trading Academy in Chicago. "SpaceX and Tesla are feeding off each other. They're moving more in sync lately." The 30-day correlation between SpaceX and Tesla is currently 0.66, according to ThinkOrSwim data. "Adjusted for growth, SpaceX is one of the cheaper ways to play the strong optionality of the Space and Intelligence Economy," Morgan Stanley's Jonas wrote in a note to clients Sunday.

events.title: Saudi Arabia restores East-West pipeline flows to 5.8 million bpd, energy minister says
events.summary: Saudi Arabia had restored oil flows through its East-West pipeline, which had come under Houthi attacks, to 5.8 million barrels per day by Tuesday morning, its Energy Minister said. Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman told the Made in GCC Forum in Bahrain: “The East-West pipeline that was heavily attacked is operational now. Today around 5.8 million barrels of oil [flows] through the pipeline.” Operations were halted at the kingdom's main cross-country pipeline, which has a capacity of up to seven million bpd, after an attack last month. But engineers have managed to restore the flow to replenish global supplies disrupted by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz . Prince Abdulaziz stressed the importance of resilience, preparedness and developing the skills needed to support future industries. “Gulf countries have witnessed many issues since [the] Iraq-Iran war and the invasion of Kuwait until today. The most important lesson is the supply and logistics chains,” he said. He said one of the most important lessons was the need to rely on Gulf capabilities to meet energy, medicine and food demand. “The development of industries and the transformation of the raw materials available to us into products to meet our needs should go hand in hand with innovation,” he added. “Without it, we risk becoming consumers of technologies rather than producing it.” Prince Abdulaziz said 70 per cent of the workforce in the kingdom's vital sectors are Saudis. “Localisation gives us greater flexibility and ability to withstand disruptions. Having multiple logistical options was one of the key factors that enabled us to deal with the crisis.” Manufacturing push The Gulf states are seeking to turn the economic vulnerability exposed by the Iran war into a push for deeper industrial integration, with officials calling for enhanced production within the region and greater co-operation across supply chains. Also speaking at the inaugural Made in GCC Forum was Abdulla bin Fakhro, Bahrain's Minister of Industry and Commerce, who said the test for the Gulf was not simply to recover from the energy crisis but to use the experience to strengthen its economic base. “The GCC region has faced exceptional significant security challenges this year as our countries were subjected to a fierce Iranian aggression but we proved that we can protect our countries and overcome the challenges,” he said at the three-day event, being held at Exhibition World Bahrain from October 6 to 8. The Gulf now has an opportunity to capture a greater share of the goods it currently imports, he added. Gulf countries import more than $600 billion worth of goods a year, while the combined economy of the six states is worth about $2.4 trillion, he said. Intra-GCC merchandise trade, however, stands at only about $46 billion. “How many of the products, components and intermediate materials we import today can we manufacture here in the Gulf?” Mr Bin Fakhro said. A focus on domestic production would lead to new factories, investment and the creation of skilled jobs, while strengthening the region's ability to withstand future shocks. “We want to move from successful national industries towards an integrated Gulf industrial ecosystem,” Mr Bin Fakhro added. “We want it [Made in GCC] to become a Gulf economic and industrial identity representing quality, reliability and innovation.” Meanwhile, GCC Secretary General Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi said the bloc already has a substantial industrial base, with more than 22,000 factories employing about 1.7 million workers. Gulf industries contribute about 3 per cent of the region's GDP, he said, but called for the six member countries to move beyond separate national industrial strategies towards a more integrated manufacturing system. “When we integrate our industrial capabilities and align our policies, we can achieve greater prosperity for all our countries,” Mr Albudaiwi said. The GCC is developing 20 joint industrial investment opportunities, he added, with the first package already approved by its Industrial Co-operation Committee.

events.title: Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
events.summary: Plague is still endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak. Dozens of people have been quarantined in Russia’s Siberia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances. Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube and died. list 1 of 3 Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia; US monitoring case list 2 of 3 Trapped in occupied Oleshky: Ukrainians face hunger, drones and landmines list 3 of 3 Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters Plague is a severe, life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Between 1346 and 1353, the bubonic plague – one of three forms of the disease – was known as the Black Death. It caused one of the most fatal pandemics in the world across Eurasia and North Africa. Some 30-60 percent of the population of Europe is believed to have died in that outbreak. Pneumonic plague is less common than bubonic plague. It is a severe form of the infection that can spread from person to person. What happened in the Russian lab and should we be worried? On Monday, Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague last week. According to Russian media reports, Shipilova became ill while at work on September 30 and died two days later at a hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Several media reports suggest there may have been an accident at the lab, but this has not been officially confirmed. About 200 people who came into contact with the dead woman have since been quarantined, and parts of the hospital where she died have also been cordoned off. An aluminium plant nearby has instructed its workers to wear masks. Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk to meet with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials four days ago. In a statement quoted by the TASS news agency, Rospotrebnadzor said officials in the Irkutsk region had detected two cases ⁠of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with the researcher. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted. Later on Monday, Russian authorities said they found no evidence that the woman’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and said the situation was under control. Kobzev said in ⁠a statement that the woman had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.” He added that the situation was under control and that all known contacts with the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision. What is plague and what are its symptoms? The bacterium which causes plague, Yersinia pestis, is carried by small wild mammals and their fleas. In Siberia, where it is endemic, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with the plague, however. But cases occur every year in other parts of the world, notably in Africa. According to the Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in the US, plague has been detected in people of all ages, from babies to those aged in their 90s. Half of the cases occur in people aged 12 to 45. Men and women are susceptible, although it has been slightly more common among men. There are three main types of plague, affecting different parts of the body. These are bubonic, septicaemic and pneumonic . According to the World Health Organization (WHO), bubonic plague is the most common clinical form. Symptoms include painful swollen lymph nodes or “buboes”. Septicaemic plague infects the blood while pneumonic plague affects the lungs. The WHO describes septicaemic and pneumonic plague as “less common, but severe forms” of plague. A fourth type, pharyngeal plague, is rare. It can be contracted by eating infected meat. According to the US-based Cleveland Clinic, besides swollen lymph nodes in the case of bubonic plague, those infected with any of the forms of plague can display the following symptoms: Specific symptoms for Septicaemic plague, which can occur as a complication of bubonic plague, include abdominal pain and blackness in tissues, particularly on figures, toes and the nose, according to the CDC. Pneumonic plague, which occurs when bacteria from bubonic or septicaemic infections reach the lungs, is accompanied by shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing and sometimes bloody mucus. Other complications can also arise from plague if it is untreated, according to the Cleveland Clinic. These include: Meningitis – a severe infection that causes inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord. Tissue death and loss of limbs from gangrene. Bubonic plague has a death rate of 30 to 60 percent.

events.title: Why Sam Altman takes his hardest questions to Nikesh Arora
events.summary: Nikesh Arora has a knack for piercing directness.  I profiled the Palo Alto Networks CEO for our latest issue . A tech veteran leading the only pure-play cybersecurity company in the Fortune 500, Arora has a “tell it to you straight” posture that has made him a sought-after mentor. Case in point: When he needs advice, Sam Altman has for years turned to Arora.  “I think it’s hard to get direct, actionable advice,” Altman told me. “Most people aren’t sure, aren’t confident, are busy, or aren’t going to spend enough time. Maybe they don’t want to offend you.” Arora doesn’t mind. He’s been known for that hard-driving rigor since his days at Google (he joined months after the company’s IPO, rising to chief business officer under Eric Schmidt). As I write in the story:  At Google, Arora developed a reputation for tear-inducing toughness, and he doesn’t deny it. “If people show up in this room unprepared, they’ll leave the room knowing they were unprepared,” he says. “I say to the people who come into this room, ‘If you have a lot going on, give it to me, and I’ll deal with it—but don’t show up here looking dazed.’”  An exacting attitude is necessary, Arora says, when the work has such high stakes.  “Would you want to get on that rocket that was built by somebody who was hungover and decided to not tighten the screw?” he asks rhetorically. “Would you ever excuse the person who didn’t do all the checks on a plane before it took off with 200 lives at stake? You expect that from these people. You expect them not to screw up. So why is it tough that I expect my team to not screw up? In every business we work, there are life-threatening or life-ending things that can happen if people don’t pay attention.” It’s intense, yes. But that sort of intensity is perhaps warranted in the seat Arora occupies: AI has upended the cybersecurity landscape, with escalating stories of “agents gone rogue” and the looming prospect that there may be more cyberattacks than ever. Arora—also one of cybersecurity’s omnipresent acquirers—is right in the center of a generational moment, for cyber, for AI, and by extension for us all. events.title: I’ve spent a decade teaching AI to write. Here’s why your slop posts are ruining your LinkedIn
events.summary: We’ve all seen it. Bland, formulaic copy that reeks of a household-name LLM, all over your LinkedIn feed. The experience is familiar. You read a CEO’s LinkedIn post, only to scroll down and see three more posts that look just like it. The same turns of phrase, the same tone, even down to the same humorless “jokes”. If you can recognize this, well, you’re not alone. LinkedIn’s problem with AI slop became so bad, in fact, that the platform launched a “seems like AI slop” button on July 30th. It was used more than a million times in just the first two weeks.  And they had good reason: 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts from April to June 2026 were fully AI-generated, according to data from Pangram. Those who just took their posts from generic LLMs clearly thought they had the answer. Input a generic prompt, highlight whatever was spat out, copy and paste onto their account. But, and this will come as no surprise, it doesn’t work. Those using generic LLMs to write their LinkedIn posts are actually seeing around 40% fewer views than they did before.   Posts written by generic AI just aren’t working. If anything, they’re turning readers away from the pages and people they’re supposed to care about. So, what’s the solution? It’s not, as you might immediately think, to turn away from AI altogether. We can’t ignore the fact that AI now plays an important role in the content demands of today’s marketing landscape. Instead, the answer lies in tackling “slop”.  The demands on marketers, and anyone creating content for brands, exponentially increase year over year. More channels and more forms of content keep emerging, and algorithms consistently reward those who post regularly. Writing social posts went from something done occasionally to something mandatory. Business leaders became aware that to build a brand, they needed to post regularly on the company’s account and their own. In response, everyone reached for the same tools, which meant everyone ended up sounding exactly the same.  Think of it this way: if the CEO of an S&P 500 company uses the same basic ChatGPT tools as your local mom-and-pop, these two drastically different businesses are essentially sharing the exact same copywriter. Even 10 years ago that would have been inconceivable.  The appeal of tools like ChatGPT was that they rapidly produced serviceable copy in order to fulfill the demand for content. But in plugging that gap, they created several more. The fact is, those who opt for slop forget something fundamental: posts are meant to communicate something. Turning to a generic AI tool with a vague prompt to post for the sake of posting is, by design, ensuring that your final post will have nothing interesting to say.  Slop is obvious. There are tells that clue readers in to the fact that someone has just unthinkingly copy-pasted something from an LLM. I’m sure they’re familiar to anyone reading this: the liberal use of the em-dash; rhetorical question openers; short, declarative closing sentences; and endless lists of three. These linguistic devices are what we talk about when we’re discussing AI fatigue. Generic, predictable language that we see over, and over, and over. In 2023 you might have been able to get away with it. But in 2026, it’s recognizable instantly.  Finding what actually works is a balancing act. First, zero in on your voice. Find posts you have written that sound like you, with the right energy and tone. Look at which posts did particularly well and drove engagement; LinkedIn analytics can be an excellent tool for this. Once you’ve got a basic set of parameters, then you can move on to the most important part of all: making sure you’ve got something to say. LLMs, by design, pick out the most common phrases and takes. They’re built to generate mediocre, middle-of-the-road opinions and copy. So find the take that makes you stand out.  There’s nothing wrong with using an AI tool to write your LinkedIn posts; you just need to be sure that they sound like you, and that there’s some real substance in there. Look for data, stats, figures, stories, and anecdotes that only you own. Offer people something new.  I’ve spent a decade teaching AI to write marketing emails, push notifications and texts that drive conversions, not just engagement. It works because the messages focus on what customers actually care about, which in turn delivers what marketers care about. The same principle applies to LinkedIn. Likes and comments are the engagement, and the conversion comes from readers who remember and trust you. Slop only prioritizes the first part, and entirely forgets the second. Then, take a critical look at the finished product. This might feel like it’s taking up valuable time, but taking even five minutes to read the post out loud, cutting any sentence you wouldn’t say to a colleague, can make all the difference between a dozen eyes on your post and a thousand. The sheer amount of AI slop on sites like LinkedIn, which maintains steady user adoption year on year, means that a distinct voice is only becoming more valuable. In a sea of AI slop, it’s more important, and perhaps easier, than ever to stand out from the crowd.  The answer to AI slop isn’t in abandoning AI, nor is it as simple as vowing to never touch an em-dash again. It’s in abandoning slop: unthinking, generic slop that tells us nothing, and does nothing for us. You’re not writing to beat a detector, or to ensure that no one flags your post. You’re writing to communicate something. To inform, to entertain, to share, to connect. The truth is, there was always slop out there; LLMs just made it easier to post.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Fire-protection specialist Deluge launches SGX IPO to raise over $23 million for acquisitions
events.summary: Founder and chairman Vincent Cheo (centre), pictured with CEO Lee Wai Wah (left) and CFO Fredrik Tan. SINGAPORE - Homegrown fire protection company Deluge is looking to raise gross proceeds of $23.4 million for new infrastructure and acquisitions through an initial public offering (IPO) on the Mainboard of the Singapore Exchange. The company on Oct 6 lodged documents for the IPO comprising 15.6 million shares at 60 cents per share, with 14.8 million placement shares and 800,000 public offer shares. A separate cornerstone tranche will account for the remainder of the funds raised. SAC Capital is the issue manager for the IPO, and serves as the joint book-runner and underwriter with Maybank Securities. Deluge’s shares are expected to start trading on Oct 16. Founded in 1983, Deluge specialises in fire suppression systems, fire alarms and fire-fighting equipment, spanning the full fire protection lifecycle from design, prefabrication and installation through to maintenance and servicing. These include active fire systems such as fire alarms and water-based sprinkler systems, as well as passive fire systems like fire-resistant structural elements. The majority of Deluge’s business - around 92% - is primarily based in Singapore. The company recently began expanding into the data centre sector in Johor, and counts Singapore-based operator DayOne, as well as construction companies Sunway and Gamuda, as customers. As at March 31, Deluge had an order book of $410 million, of which 87% comprised of government contracts. These contracts helped Deluge secure the largest share of Singapore’s fire-protection market in 2025, at about 8.3 per cent, according to Frost & Sullivan. In addition, it is one of only eight contractors in Singapore to hold the highest L6 grade certification from the Building and Construction Authority, which allows it to bid for jobs of unlimited contract value. Chief investment officer John Paul Chen told analysts and the media on Oct 2 that Deluge’s 8.3 per cent share of a market comprising 775 fire-protection contractors pointed to a highly fragmented industry, presenting significant scope for growth through acquisitions and consolidation. A highly fragmented industry is one made up of many small competitors, with no company controlling a large share of the market. Chen noted that the current market is “very disorganised with low accountability”, which could pose a danger to residents and building tenants. “If your condo is being maintained by six different fire contractors over a 10-year period, I think you should be worried because everyone would not know what they are checking, and I think that’s a problem.” With consolidation, Deluge would be able to ensure that smaller contractors are accountable for their work, and “eliminate” those that are not compliant. Since its founding, it has secured projects totalling more than $1 billion across Singapore’s critical infrastructure, including a $109 million contract in relation to the ongoing construction of the North-South Corridor, and a $73.5 million contract from the Land Transport Authority for the Cross Island MRT line. Other major projects include the Changi East train depot, which will support the Cross Island Line, as well as offshore and marine projects like liquefied natural gas plants and offshore platforms. Chen said Deluge’s revenue streams are sufficiently diversified, reducing its dependence on large integrated projects. He sees significant growth potential in its lifecycle services segment, which provides recurring maintenance and servicing of fire-safety equipment throughout its useful life. He added that competition is not a threat to Deluge’s existing projects as the barriers to entry are very high, with most of its current maintenance contracts already signed on longer terms. At the same time, there are plenty of older buildings whose fire protection contracts will be up for renewal in the next few years. Many would possibly need a complete overhaul of their equipment, and Deluge sees this as a good opportunity to increase its market share. Citing the Cross Island Line project, for which Deluge was awarded a 20-year maintenance contract, he said: “Fire protection is a long-term business. You do not have a building that you build and then later change your fire contractor every few years. It doesn’t work that way. “If we installed it, we are probably the best people to also maintain it efficiently and productivity-wise.” Deluge also benefits from longstanding client relationships, having worked with most of the customers in its order book for between 10 and 20 years. For the 2026 financial year (FY) ended March 31, lifecycle services contributed close to half of the company’s gross profit of $38.8 million despite only making up one-third of its revenue, compared to integrated projects. Net profit was $11.8 million. Revenue in FY2026 was $116.7 million, lower than FY2025’s $140 million but 3.1% higher than FY2024.

events.title: Lao Huo Tang, Kenny Rogers companies clear CPF arrears
events.summary: The court heard that the CPF arrears for Kenny Rogers F&B and Kenny Rogers (Marina Square) were completely cleared as at Oct 5. PHOTO: SCREENGRAB FROM KENNY ROGERS ROASTERS SINGAPORE/FACEBOOK Two companies linked to Lao Huo Tang cleared all CPF arrears, resulting in charges against them being acquitted by the State Courts on Oct 6. Kenny Rogers-linked companies also settled their CPF arrears by Oct 5, with payments made personally by former director Thomas Hong, avoiding composition charges. Lao Huo Tang and Kenny Rogers restaurants are well-known in Singapore, with multiple outlets, and these resolutions prevent further legal actions over unpaid CPF contributions. SINGAPORE – Two companies linked to restaurant chain Lao Huo Tang have cleared their Central Provident Fund (CPF) arrears, with charges against them disposed of after the matters were compounded, the State Courts heard on Oct 6. Lao Huo Tang F&B received a discharge amounting to an acquittal (DATA) on all nine charges before the court. A DATA means the accused is acquitted of the charge, rather than merely receiving a discharge that leaves open the possibility of prosecution on the same charge later. The latest development comes after the State Courts on Sept 29 heard that Lao Huo Tang F&B owed $39,121 in CPF contributions for June, July and August. At that hearing, the prosecution said $25,986 remained outstanding for June and July alone. The court at the Oct 6 hearing heard that Lao Huo Tang Restaurant, which had also cleared its CPF arrears, is applying for DATA on a ll six char ges. According to the charge sheets seen by The Straits Times , the company previously owed CPF monies to six workers for December 2025. Lao Huo Tang is known for its herbal soups and Chinese dishes. Its website lists outlets at Causeway Point, Sun Plaza, Jurong Point, Marina Square, The Star Vista and NEX. CPF arrears cleared for Kenny Rogers F&B and Marina Square Separately, the court also heard on Oct 6 that CPF arrears involving Kenny Rogers-linked companies had been cleared. Thomas Hong, founder and CEO of Lao Huo Tang Group, told the court on Oct 6 that all arrears involving its companies Chickita F&B, Soup Empire Holdings, Kenny Rogers (Marina Square) and Kenny Rogers F&B had been cleared. The court heard that the CPF arrears for those companies were completely cleared as at Oct 5. Hong is currently the director of Chickita F&B, which is wholly owned by Lao Huo Tan g Investments where Hong is a director, according to company records. Kenny Rogers F&B’s current sole shareholder is Soup E mpire Ho ldings. The prosecution sought time to confirm that all the payments were in order. The matters were adjourned to Nov 3. Payments made in personal capacity, no composition charges When the judge asked about composition, the prosecution said the payments had been made by Hong in his personal capacity and there would therefore be no composition charges against him. Kenny Rogers F&B had owed $2 5,294 i n CPF contributions for June, July and August when it appeared in court on Sept 29. It had paid a $3,000 composition amount but failed to meet an earlier direction to pay $13,000 towards the arrears. At the same hearing, Kenny Rogers (Marina Square) had $2,236 in CPF contributions outstanding for August after paying $7,156 towards arrears for June to August. Kenny Rogers Roasters is listed as one of Lao Huo Tang Group’s brands on its website, which lists three Singapore outlets, at Downtown East, Marina Square and The Clementi Mall. Vihanya Rakshika is a business correspondent at The Straits Times, with a focus on business operations and corporate credit issues.

Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the Congress party, was among the lawmakers detained in the Indian capital on Tuesday, but was released soon after, the AFP news agency and local media reported. list 1 of 4 India’s Ujjain tense as mosque partially demolished for Hindu pilgrimage list 2 of 4 Can India’s ‘cockroach’ movement oust Modi’s election chief? list 3 of 4 Pakistan, India summon diplomats after two people killed in border incident list 4 of 4 Mass protests demanding poll chief resignation shake India for third day The march is the latest in a series of near-daily protests beginning last week led by student groups, opposition parties and India’s “Cockroach” youth movement. The protesters are demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, accusing the polling body he oversees of manipulating voter registrations to benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. “The election commission is a puppet in the ‌hands of the government,” Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge told reporters as the march began. “After failing multiple times, Congress leaders have decided to establish anarchy in ⁠the country and attack institutions,” BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra told reporters before Tuesday’s protest. Lawmakers carried placards, waved the national flag, and shouted slogans against Kumar during the march, roughly 1km (0.6 miles) long, to the Election Commission headquarters from parliament, through the centre of New Delhi. India began its Special Intensive Revision of voter lists in Bihar last year before state elections. The exercise has since expanded to most states and federally administered territories. Critics say the process requires documents that are confusing and difficult to obtain, risking the exclusion of millions of eligible voters. Election Commission data shows voter rolls could shrink by as much as 30 percent in some regions. The Election Commission says the voter-roll revision is designed to remove duplicate, deceased or ineligible entries and maintain electoral integrity. On Friday, it directed its officials to register eligible voters inadvertently omitted from electoral rolls.

events.title: BlackRock steps up Gulf investment
events.summary: The News BlackRock is ramping up its commitments to the Gulf as the world’s largest asset manager seeks to boost exposure to a region that it expects to use more of its vast state wealth to invest domestically in the wake of the Iran war. Despite no resolution to the conflict, now in its eighth month and keeping the Gulf in a state of suspended uncertainty, the firm is “undiminished in our focus” on the region, said Ben Powell, chief investment strategist for the Middle East and Asia-Pacific at the BlackRock Investment Institute. Counterintuitively, the bullishness stems from the region’s relative stability: “In terms of the rules of the game, the positive attitude towards business, not to mention human capital, financial capital, energy … I feel very confident that this is a story that is true and real and going to play out over the next five, 10 years,” he said. Stability “in a world of great moderation, that’s not that interesting,” Powell said. “But in a world of excitement, that becomes much rarer … it is worth 10 times what it was in a world where everything’s okay.” And increasingly, everything is not okay. Powell’s broader outlook is that persistent inflation, fragmentation, and higher capital costs will make investors more selective. “We’re all going to be incorrect more often … Where you can find confidence, grab it with both hands because it’s in short supply,” he said. Know More BlackRock, which manages more than $15 trillion, has offices in Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Riyadh, Doha, and Kuwait City. Powell said the Gulf will “continue to be a significant exporter of capital,” but that “at the margin, maybe some portion of that money that was going to flow out is going to stay at home.” He put the amount at $50 billion to $100 billion, and cautioned that the estimate has wide error bands. Powell tied that shift to the $2.1 trillion in strategic capital spending the institute estimates the Gulf states will make in its diversification push through 2030. The bigger change, he said, is a focus on “societal and economic resilience” across energy, infrastructure, and the region’s build-out for AI, including “some projects where we hope utilization rates will be very low.” Some of that spending is “almost an insurance policy,” Powell said: “We’re going to build pipelines we hope we never use.” Through “a solely economic lens, that would not make much sense,” he said, but the need for redundancy as global geopolitical tensions rise means it makes “all the sense in the world.” Powell also expects more spending where AI, energy, and defense overlap. “They’re all kind of the same thing now,” he said. Step Back BlackRock’s Global Infrastructure Partners is part of a $30 billion infrastructure partnership with Abu Dhabi sovereign wealth fund L’IMAD, national oil company ADNOC, and Singapore’s Temasek, announced in May. The asset manager is among a growing number of global firms in Abu Dhabi’s financial center, ADGM, drawn by proximity to sovereign wealth funds like ADIA and Mubadala, family offices, and the region’s expanding appetite for private credit. Gulf capital is still flowing out at a record pace: the region’s sovereign wealth funds invested $53.9 billion across 108 transactions in the first half of 2026, an all-time high , according to Global SWF. Notable Singapore’s Temasek will open its first offices in the Gulf early next year, joining a growing list of global investors expanding into the region despite ongoing conflict. OpenAI is in talks with BlackRock and UAE funds, including Abu Dhabi’s MGX, to raise as much as $30 billion , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Pro-Palestine Greens challenge Labour’s grip on Starmer’s former seat
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Green Party leader Zack Polanski hopes to shake Labour, which has held Holborn since the seat was created in 1983. London, United Kingdom – At a meeting organised by a Muslim group in London ahead of a closely watched by-election, candidates from the Green and Liberal Democrat parties made their cases to residents beside empty seats. Their Labour and Conservative peers did not turn up. Labour candidate Sagal Abdi Wali, a Somali-Muslim woman, told The Guardian she did not attend because she had a prior obligation and the invite had come too late. But the organiser, the Camden Muslim Network, pushed back, saying that she was invited earlier. list 1 of 3 Israeli fans direct monkey chants and military slogans at Ireland’s players list 2 of 3 Morocco’s pro-Palestine protests challenge Rabat’s deepening Israel ties list 3 of 3 The Burnham bounce: Is Labour gaining ground against Reform? Fifteen candidates are in the race for former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s old seat, including Green Party leader, Zack Polanski, who hopes to become a member of parliament. Since the seat was created in Holborn and St Pancras in 1983, the Labour Party has held it. Starmer was first elected in 2015 and held it until his resignation, which triggered the by-election due to take place on Thursday. At the meeting, the conversation ranged from local issues such as housing to Israel and Palestine. Lib Dem candidate Patrick Stillman said his party had long called for Palestinian statehood but would not support a full boycott. But Polanski had a different opinion. “I think the Labour government’s position is deeply cynical to apologise over Gaza, to recognise that mistakes have been made but to continue to sell arms to Israel, a country that’s committing a genocide,” he said to applause, adding that his party, which recently voted to describe Zionism as racism, supports a full boycott. In leaflets sent to constituency residents, the Green Party focused on Abdi-Wali’s time as a Labour councillor and, more recently, as leader of Camden council – a role she secured in May. One reads: “Bring change, Replace Labour, Vote Green”. On its reverse: “Every single Camden Labour councillor refused to sign the Palestine solidarity pledge or support pension fund divestment . Only Greens continue to stand firm on Palestine.” Last month, Abdi-Wali spoke to the Camden New Journal, a local newspaper, about Gaza and the Green Party’s leaflets. It was “obviously inaccurate” to say the Labour council did not feel strongly about the issue, she told the paper. “I want to focus on making sure that we’re able to put the message of what [Foreign Secretary] Ed Miliband is now doing with the government and on Palestine and Israel and Gaza and the West Bank.” In January, Camden Friends of Palestine (CFOP), a local group that formed in response to Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, presented a petition to the local council with 4,000 signatures calling for the council to divest its pension fund from companies involved in Israel’s actions in the occupied Palestinian territories. Abdi-Wali, then a Labour councillor, did not support the motion. Rather than committing to divestment, most councillors voted to refer the question to the pension board for review. “My impression of her and her politics is that she’s just really incredibly silent on everything, if there isn’t a career motive for her, and that’s kind of disappointing,” said 38-year-old Shadin, a resident and CFOP organiser, who plans to vote for Polanski. “Watching a livestreamed genocide has made a lot of people that I know … disengage from mainstream politics or parliamentary politics”. Like many London constituencies, a key issue is housing. According to a “2026 state of the borough” report by Camden council, 8,380 households were on the waiting list for social housing at the end of March 2025, “an increase of 9.5 percent on the year before.” On Friday, in the constituency’s more affluent area of Primrose Hill, one resident said they would vote for Labour in the upcoming election, while another believed that regardless of who wins, life will not change. In Camden, another resident told Al Jazeera that while they live in the area, they were not aware of the election, as Labour canvassers buzzed to gain entry into a nearby estate in the background. As both parties make their final efforts to secure victory, recent polls predict a close race. In the 2024 general election, Starmer won the seat with 49 percent. Andrew Feinstein , a pro-Palestine independent candidate came second, with 19 percent. The British gambling firm Ladbrokes and Stats for Lefties, which examines polling, both predict Labour will win.
