events.title: Bird flu adds to fears for threatened species at proposed wind farm site
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bird flu and wind farm spark fears for threatened species at Ramsar-listed wetlands The endangered Australasian bittern inhabits the Glenelg Estuary and Discovery Bay Wetlands. ( Supplied: Simone Carmichael/DPE ) The combined impact of bird flu and a proposed wind farm in Victoria's south-west poses risks to threatened bird and bat species, ecologists say. Developer HMC Capital says the project has undertaken extensive measures to mitigate the risks. A decision is expected on the future of the Kentbruck wind farm next month. Expertly camouflaged amid reed beds and sedgeland, the elusive Australasian bittern is a highly revered sight among birdwatchers. Across Australia, fewer than 1,500 birds are estimated to remain in the wild. In south-west Victoria, a small population of the endangered birds inhabit the Glenelg Estuary and Discovery Bay Wetlands all year round. Mark Bachmann is worried about the threatened bird and bat species inhabiting the wetlands. ( Supplied: Mark Bachmann/Nature Glenelg Trust ) In winter, the population at the Ramsar-listed site grows when more birds fly hundreds of kilometres south after breeding on the inland rice fields of the New South Wales Riverina. The Ramsar Convention was a treaty signed in 1971 in the city of Ramsar, in Iran, to conserve the world's most important wetlands. In Australia, nominations for Ramsar sites to the federal government must come from the relevant state or territory government and must meet at least one of nine criteria for possible listing. It is illegal to damage a Ramsar site's ecological character without ministerial approval. The bittern, along with the endangered fairy tern, hooded plover and the brolga, which is also at risk from habitat loss in Victoria, are among the species ecologist and managing director of the Nature Glenelg Trust Mark Bachmann holds concerns for amid nearby mass bird flu mortality events and a proposed 105-turbine wind farm. Brolga inhabit the Ramsar-listed Discovery Bay Wetlands. ( Supplied: Mark Bachmann/Nature Glenelg Trust ) In August, hundreds of dead and dying birds were found to have contracted H5N1 avian influenza at Portland and the Glenelg River Estuary at Nelson. Mr Bachmann said the "compounding threat" associated with bird flu "presents too much risk for the wind farm project to go ahead". Decision on nation's tallest turbines looms Seven years ago, renewable energy developer HMC Capital put forward plans for the wind farm — including turbines up to 270 metres tall — in commercial pine plantation land between Nelson and Portland. A final decision on the 600-megawatt Kentbruck Green Power Hub project is expected on November 10. A spokesperson for the developer said the project's approach was "highly sensitive to the impact on birds" and had undertaken "extensive research" and independent expert investigations to mitigate the risk to birdlife and bat species inhabiting the nearby wetlands. An image produced by Neoen showing how its Kentbruck Green Power Hub wind turbines could look among pine plantations near Nelson. ( Supplied: Neoen ) Among measures taken to placate dissent from community members and environment groups, the developer reduced the number of wind turbines by 33 per cent and agreed to set up a $30 million ecology fund to sponsor ecological studies, protection activities and species recovery projects. The spokesperson added that the wind farm project was "critical for the transition to clean energy and will power hundreds of thousands of homes, as well as provide power to the nearby Port of Portland and Portland Aluminium Smelter". A 'litmus test' for renewables projects Back in Nelson, Mr Bachmann said the federal government's looming decision on the wind farm would be "critical" to the intersection of environment, community and future renewables development. A map of the Kentbruck Green Energy Hub from its public consultation documents. ( Supplied: Neoen Australia ) He said the project would see turbines situated about 300 metres from the Ramsar site boundary and 500 metres from the edge of the wetland, "potentially disrupting flight paths of birds and bats". Mr Bachmann argued the additional proximity to coastal areas experiencing "more frequent" bird flu cases heightened uncertainty. He said the impending decision on the wind farm would set a national precedent. "It could either deter development in inappropriate locations, or it could signal that you can pretty much put a wind farm anywhere.

events.title: ASX rises for third straight day, Nasdaq hits new record high — as it happened
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts ASX rises for third straight day, tech rally drives Nasdaq to record high — as it happened The Australian share market ended its day higher, driven by gains across banks, miners and real estate stocks. The Nasdaq hit a record high after Wall Street's tech stocks surged, while the euro has fallen to a 22-month low against the Australian dollar. Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog. Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice. Australian dollar: flat at 69.7 US cents, +0.1% to 62.1 euro cents Wall Street: Dow (+0.2%), S & P 500 (+0.7%), Nasdaq Composite (+1.1%) Europe: DAX (+0.1%), FTSE (+0.3%), Stoxx 600 (+0.4%) Asia : Nikkei (+1.1%), Hang Seng (+0.7%), KOSPI (-1%) Oil (Brent futures): +0.4% at $US100.68/barrel 10-year bonds: US 5.32%, Australia 5.41% Prices current at around 4:50pm AEDT Choose what information you see below by using filters And that's all we've got for you today. We'll be back with you tomorrow morning for another exciting day on the markets. ASX finishes higher with real estate in the lead The Australian share market's benchmark ASX 200 index has closed 0.6% higher at 8,736 points . The real estate sub-index led the way, up 1.2% . Utilities (+0.9%), industrials (+0.7%), financials (+0.7%) and miners (+0.7%) also posted strong rises. However, the Australian tech sector was dumped (-1.1%) , despite New York's tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing to a fresh record high overnight. Surging US interest rates 'a bigger problem for others' The usual optimism from Rabobank global strategist Michael Every in his daily note. "Monday saw Treasuries slump again, 10s up to 5.31% and 30s to 5.67% , the highest since early 2002," he observes. "If we keep going like we have since February, we'll soon have 20th century yields again, a shock for the generation who weren't born in it and for elders who kept telling themselves "lower for longer" would hold after the geopolitical consensus couldn't. "That's obviously a huge problem for the US but, as usual, it's proving a bigger problem for others." Every cites civil unrest over the potential for austerity in France, but we can see the local dissatisfaction brewing over the RBA's string of rate rises, the latest of which had a strong flavour of response to rising US rates. "Meanwhile, the US Nasdaq just hit a new record high, again taking us back to the turn of the century and its dotcom bubble ," Every continues. "That's another reason we can't expect yields to fall back easily — at least not until the miraculous deflationary impact of AI and SI (also referred to as AGI). "Either way, SI is now the national security equivalent of the 20th century Manhattan Project and the 19th century investment surge into railways and steel. It won't stop easily. "Neither will national security spending in general as wars rage on." So, inflation is back and, in his view, not going away for a fair while, therefore meaning we'll have higher interest rates for longer and all the fallout that comes with that. Euro sinks, largely due to France's record debt and political uncertainty The euro has dropped to a 17-month low against the US dollar. It's also near a 22-month low against the Australian dollar. Essentially, concerns about France's ability to rein in its budget deficit and a sharp bond market sell-off last week stirred fears of a return of sovereign debt crisis dynamics in the euro zone. French government bonds have been sold off as expectations of higher policy rates and rising political uncertainty cast doubt on the ability of the euro area's second-largest economy to put its public finances on a more sustainable footing. “Latest bond market dynamics are increasingly concerning and somewhat reminiscent of a sovereign debt crisis," Hauke Siemssen, strategist at Commerzbank, said. The French government is seeking to enact an unpopular 2027 budget to lower its deficit and contain its record-high debt load, a tall order in a deeply divided ‌parliament as political factions position ahead of next year's presidential election. "We're pretty pessimistic about the euro. We think it's going to go down to under $US1.10," said Joseph Capurso, a currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank. "We're not surprised that we've seen this weakness... For the euro to rise, you'd need a big decrease in oil prices... a big increase in expectations for European monetary policy tightening. "Another one would be them starting to get their act together on reining in the budget deficit, though I think there's no chance of that happening anytime soon.

events.title: OpenAI will start watermarking ChatGPT’s text in the EU
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. OpenAI will start adding an invisible watermark to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union to comply with the EU AI Act, the company said Monday in a blog post . The EU AI Act’s transparency rules , which took effect on August 2, require AI companies to mark AI-generated content in a way other systems can identify. OpenAI said the watermark will roll out over the coming weeks to eligible ChatGPT and Codex users on all plans, but only in the EU. Developers using OpenAI’s API anywhere in the world can turn it on for select models starting today; it’s off by default. OpenAI said it is not making text watermarking a global default at launch. The watermark is not an actual symbol, but works by subtly shaping the model’s word choices, leaving a pattern readers can’t see, but a detector can pick up. Because it lives in the words themselves, it travels with the text when it’s copied and pasted. OpenAI said the watermark doesn’t identify the user, and that it saw no meaningful change in its models’ performance with it switched on. OpenAI also published a technical report for its method, called textGrain, alongside the announcement. Co-written with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it walks through an example of using a secret key to sort next-word predictions to finish the sentence. Add hundreds of these nudges together, and the detector can spot AI-generated content using only the text and the key. Can the watermark be removed by editing? OpenAI’s tests suggest yes. In one test, replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%. The company also said short passages, math answers, and translated text are harder to detect. “These limitations contribute to our decision to provide initial detector access only to approved researchers and expert organizations, who can help us evaluate reliability and responsible uses,” said the company. OpenAI also cautioned that a missing watermark “does not prove human authorship.” The text could be too short or too heavily edited, or it could come from another company’s AI. “[Watermarks] can indicate that an OpenAI system generated or processed part of a passage, but not how much human judgment, editing, or creativity went into it,” the company said. The announcement comes two months after Anthropic said it would watermark text generated by Claude, a move it’s applying worldwide. That decision drew backlash from some Claude users , who argued they had supplied “the instructions, context, decisions” while Claude was just “the tool.” OpenAI had built a text watermark before but held off on releasing it, partly over concerns that users would switch to rivals that didn’t watermark, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. Anthropic, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and OpenAI are among the companies that have committed to following the EU’s code of practice on AI-generated content. events.title: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
events.summary: President Trump said Monday that the United States will help Russia amid a potential case of pneumonic plague , though he hasn't spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Why it matters: International concern spiked over the weekend over the news that a Russian lab worker had died from a possible case of pneumonic plague, reminding some of how the COVID-19 epidemic began. Trump's comments came after a question about the reported death of Darya Shipilova, who was potentially exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia. There has been no official confirmation that Shipilova's death was due to pneumonic plague, but five hospitals in the area and dozens of institute workers have been quarantined out of precaution. Russian health authorities say Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing showed no pathogen tied to her work. No additional deaths or sicknesses tied to the incident have been reported. What they're saying: "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday. "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can." Trump said the disease used to be more controllable, but "microbes and the germs have gotten stronger." The president appeared to be referring to antimicrobial resistance , but pneumonic plague itself remains treatable with antibiotics when diagnosed early Between the lines: The White House is monitoring the outbreak, Axios scooped, with the Department of Health and Human Services and State Department also on alert. The European Commission is also "very closely" monitoring the suspected outbreak. Go deeper: How pneumonic plague spreads, and how it is and isn't like COVID

events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Although it’s only been a couple of months since Etched raised $700 million at a $21 billion valuation , the AI chip startup is already being plied with investment offers at double or more its value, according to people familiar with the company. Etched is reviewing incoming bids that range from $40 billion from top-tier investors to $50 billion from lesser-known backers, one person said. These fundraising talks are early, so terms of any deal, should one happen, may change. Etched declined to comment. While this may seem like a fast timetable to raise another mega round, Etched is pursuing a particularly expensive segment of the AI industry: building full AI hardware systems powered by its own proprietary chips. The person familiar with these offers said that if it raises as much as its last round, this could give Etched a cushion of as much as 3.5 years of runway. There are reasons why VCs are hot to own a piece of Etched. The four-year-old startup shows promise of challenging Nvidia. Not only did quant trading firm Jane Street lead the last $700 million round, it is also a customer that took delivery of an early system. Etched said in July that it had already secured $1 billion in customer orders, including the one from Jane Street, after manufacturing its test chip at a TSMC factory this summer. Co-founder and COO Robert Wachen previously told TechCrunch that investors are so enthusiastic because Etched has designed two new components from scratch to speed up inference — the computing process that happens after a user submits a prompt. The company claims its chips can process more tokens faster and at a lower cost than Nvidia’s. That’s the reason its processors have been so attractive to Jane Street, for whom a microscopic advantage in speed can yield massive profits. The startup has also impressed investors with its ability to attract engineers from Nvidia, with roughly 15% of Etched’s 400-person workforce having previously worked at the chip giant, according to The Wall Street Journal. Etched also operates a new 10-megawatt data center in Silicon Valley and established a facility in Taiwan to coordinate production near TSMC. Co-founders Gavin Uberti and Chris Zhu famously met in an advanced math course at Harvard, while Wachen was Uberti’s roommate and they dropped out to pursue the company. In terms of fast rounds at big leaps in valuations, Etched already has a history of them. The startup announced a $300 million round at a $10.3 billion valuation led by Sequoia in July. It announced the $700 million round at a $21 billion valuation in September. Back-to-back funding rounds, which essentially act as a single financing split into two tranches with separate valuations, are increasingly common among the buzziest startups. events.title: Private-credit worries spur Fed review
events.summary: The Scoop The Federal Reserve Bank of New York has been visiting big banks to review their loans to private credit firms and understand their exposure to a financial industry that has unnerved investors and global policymakers. Fed officials have gone into JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Barclays, and Morgan Stanley since the spring with questions about overall exposure, risk-management, and collateral quality, people familiar with the matter said. The Fed, JPMorgan, Barclays, Wells Fargo and Morgan Stanley declined to comment. The review was prompted in part by JPMorgan’s move in March to mark down large swaths of loans in private credit portfolios, particularly those to software companies threatened by AI, the people said. The Fed has concluded its review of some of the banks, including JPM, said the people. It’s not uncommon for the Fed to go into banks to review their holdings, particularly when there are frequent headlines about potential risks. The Fed also does regular on-site evaluations and continually surveys for banks’ risks. Know More Private-credit firms are one of the fastest-growing borrower sets for banks, which were chased out of risky lending after the 2008 crisis but have since found their way back into the trade by lending to the firms that replaced them. Loans to nonbank institutions have risen from $300 billion in 2016 to more than $1.5 trillion according to FDIC data, and now account for 11% of all bank loans outstanding. Those loans are backed by private-credit firms’ own loans, a debt pile that has unnerved regulators. The European Central Bank also recently expanded a probe into private credit, looking at banks with exposures to the market. Last week, the Securities and Exchange Commission released a rare statement about fair value in private assets, serving as a reminder to lenders that they should be rigorous in their valuations and disclosures. The Bank of England, during its September Financial Policy Committee meeting, said that private credit could be vulnerable to worsening financial conditions after testing the resilience of private markets. The private credit market got slammed earlier this year when investors panicked about funds’ exposures to software companies, which suddenly seemed obsolete amid developments in AI. The concerns caused investors in certain types of funds to pull out their money at record rates — sometimes requesting nearly 40% of a single fund in a quarter, but most funds have capped at 5%. Private credit lenders have long been criticized for the way they value their loans, or mark them, in particular when there is disparity between where different lenders value the same loan and when a company’s underperformance fails to translate to their marks. But lenders utilize third-party evaluators to create the marks and say they are making careful investments. Redemption rates have declined at many of the private-credit firms and some investors have warmed to software deals again , as more of them find avenues to finance themselves both in and out of the private credit market. Notable JPMorgan was early to reassess its valuations for loans to private credit companies.

events.title: How states are tackling midterm pump pain
events.summary: States are taking on the stubbornly high fuel prices squeezing Americans ahead of the midterm elections , pushing through tax holidays and other tactics to offer relief while federal efforts have stalled. Why it matters: With November 3 less than 30 days away, the political stakes of those price-lowering levers — even if the relief is only modest — are surging amid sky-high costs. While several lawmakers have introduced legislation aimed at or pressed for suspending the federal gas tax, which is 18.4 cents per gallon for gas and 24.4 for diesel, Washington hasn't coalesced around a solution. Driving the news: That's left states seeking ways to give their residents relief. Case in point: Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine (R) signed a bill last week that suspends Ohio's gas tax for 90 days, an effort that earned bipartisan backing. There's an underlying election story: The state's Democratic gubernatorial candidate, Amy Acton, had called for a gas tax holiday, followed by her rival, Vivek Ramaswamy, announcing a plan with GOP leaders. Flashback: Georgia was the first state to suspend its fuel taxes amid the war in Iran, with Republican Gov. Brian Kemp approving a 60-day pause back in March. Since then, at least five other states (including Ohio), have suspended, lowered or stopped increases in their fuel taxes. Kemp declared a state of emergency in late September and suspended the excise tax again for 30 days. Utah cut its gas tax by some 15% through the end of the year. Gov. Andy Beshear (D-Ky.) froze an expected increase in the gas and diesel taxes in May. Illinois suspended its set increase this summer for six months. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun (R) also suspended Indiana's gas tax in April. He renewed the suspension in late September and lifted restrictions on dyed diesel for farmers and timber harvesters. Friction point: The Trump administration signaled openness to a gas tax holiday this spring, but Congress must suspend the levy. While the idea has been floated before, lawmakers have never done so. Suspending the taxes can bring some relief to consumers, but it wouldn't offset the spikes they've felt at the pump since the start of the war. Plus, critics note doing so could increase the deficit and hurt the Highway Trust Fund it fuels. But as Axios' Ben Geman noted back in May, political winds aren't always predictable — especially with drivers and truckers still feeling the strain months later, and as political messages cluster around cost-of-living concerns. Zoom out: Other states have taken a similar approach to Braun by waiving seasonal and traditional restrictions for strained industries. For example, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey (R) directed state law enforcement to stop enforcing rules against dyed diesel, usually reserved for off-road machinery and exempt from taxes, "to relieve the state's agricultural and timber communities." Louisiana , Nebraska , North Carolina , Oklahoma and Texas took similar action. Still, other states pursued different avenues for relief: California recently took action to permit cheaper, winter-blend gas to be sold earlier than usual, while Michigan allowed gas stations to sell lower-cost gasoline earlier this spring. The bottom line: Even if a federal gas tax holiday remains unlikely, pump pain — and perhaps, the possibility of future political pain — is fueling state action. On Monday, the company said it revamped its North agent harness, which launched early last year, to improve collaboration, access control, token spend, and overall security of the platform. As you'd expect from an enterprise focused agent framework, Cohere's North 2 is designed to tie into existing knowledge bases and SaaS apps in order to automate various business processes. North 2 introduces a variety of features and functions that should be familiar to anyone who's used Claude Code or OpenClaw. Among them is the concept of skills, libraries, and automations. Skills are arguably the simplest, and are essentially standard operating procedures documenting how the agent harness should complete tasks. The skills are often generated by working with the agent to complete a task and then documenting which steps achieved the best results. With North 2, Cohere says that it has made it easier for these skills to be shared so that users aren't wasting time reinventing the wheel. Presumably, this should improve consistency by avoiding having the agent take different routes to achieving its goal, something that might miss key information or nuance. To facilitate the creation of new skills, North 2 also introduces the concept of automations, generic templates that can be customized using a drag-and-drop graphical interface, not unlike LangFlow, which we looked at earlier this year. Alongside skills and automations, Cohere's North 2 does something similar for shared knowledge and assets, which it calls libraries, to ensure that agents are working off of the same datasets. Finally, North 2 adds memory, a core feature of most modern agent harnesses, to ensure that agents can maintain context across multiple sessions. In some sense, these features are a bit like self-generating macros, but rather than being limited to Excel, they work across multiple applications and data sources. Sovereign AI remains a major talking point for Cohere, which says enterprises can deploy North 2 where they like and use their preferred models. If enterprises want to deploy the harness on-prem in an air-gapped environment, they can. If they prefer to run it in the cloud, that's also an option. Along with new features aimed at collaboration and automation, North 2 implements new guardrails designed to help enterprises get a handle on their token spend and access controls. Flow control functionality, meanwhile, promises greater visibility into which departments are hogging all the tokens, while access control functionality offers admins the ability to assign access control lists to various libraries and skills so that interns can't get their hands on proprietary data just because they asked for it. North 2 is only the latest in a slew of enterprise focused agentic AI platforms which have been rolled out over the last year. Essentially every major and minor cloud provider has introduced some kind of agent harness tailored to enterprise needs. The competition has only gotten hotter over the last few weeks as OpenAI , Meta and others have set their sights on the enterprise.

events.title: How Greg Jackson runs Octopus Energy with no HR, no bonuses, and no succession plan
events.summary: The Signal Interview In a little more than a decade, Octopus Energy has grown from an outlandish idea into Britain’s largest energy provider. It now powers 12 million homes in eight countries, manages wind and solar farms from Scotland to South Korea, manufactures heat pumps, installs smart meters, leases out 50,000 electric vehicles, and supplies technology to utilities around the world. The tentacles of this “Octoverse” all lead back to Greg Jackson, a founder-CEO who has built his 13,000-person company without bonuses, HR or IT teams, or a succession plan. Beyond the walls of the company’s London headquarters, which is filled with thousands of its plushy pink octopus mascots, Jackson’s empire may look like an unwieldy one. It is not, he insists: “The thing that’s connecting it all is the underlying insight: that the technologies of electrification can deliver tremendous cost savings, but only if you build a new system.” And building that new system requires using every tool at his disposal. “There’s a scene in the movie where the astronauts are stranded and they’re going to die unless the solution is found. And on the ground, Mission Control assembles … everything there is on the space station, like duct tape and bits of piping, and they say, this is all we’ve got to save their lives,” he explains. “In any business, you choose your constraints, and then how you assemble the stuff you have to create the outcome you want.” Octopus’ job is “to take all these ingredients and say, how can we outcompete the old world of energy with better products and services with better value?” Jackson says, before reaching back to the beginning of that old world for another analogy. “When [Thomas] Edison first started building electricity businesses, he didn’t just have to innovate, fund, and build centralized electricity generation, which he did. He also had to invent the grid and distribution model. He also had to invent or sell the products that use electricity, from lightbulbs to music players. And if I look at what we’re doing, it’s almost trivial in comparison.” How to run a 13,000-person company with no HR department The growth of Octopus, which had revenues of £13.7 billion last year and a valuation of $9 billion at its last fundraising, poses a challenge for its irrepressible founder: how to transmit to thousands of employees the energy that has powered him since he dropped out of school at 16 to write video games. Jackson no longer knows each staff member by name, but he still runs his company by the same rhythms with which he started it. Each Monday starts with a gathering of senior executives to review performance data from the previous week. That helps maintain “pace and alignment,” Jackson says. Each week ends with “family dinner,” a Friday afternoon all-hands event at which the company recaps its latest innovations, achievements, and challenges. The Friday sessions began over beers with a small founding team, and Jackson “discovered that it was the best way of reminding you how great your colleagues were, and re-energizing you on the big picture.” Livestreams have since replaced in-person drinks. But the gatherings help Octopus “start the week left-brain, end it right-brain,” Jackson says, and help him explain to staff what they need to do next “and maintain the energy to feel great about it.” The company has no intranet or staff newsletters, he adds, so if people don’t tune in to “family dinner,” they won’t know what’s happening. Less is more in internal communications, he says: “The more information you put out there, the less it gets read. What you want to do is make sure the stuff that goes out there is canonical and consumed.” Octopus also has no central human resources department, devolving people management responsibilities to individual teams unless legal staff need to step in. Still a private company, it gives equity to every employee, but it pays no bonuses outside a few sales roles. Jackson says this is because he’s determined to focus people on the company’s success, rather than their own individual advancement. Similarly, Octopus sets no divisional performance targets, to keep each division from promoting whatever will make them look best at the expense of others, he adds. “The most important thing for us is to build trust among our team, so they wake up every morning thinking, ‘How do I drive the company’s mission?’ Not, ‘How do I get myself promoted?’” Hands-on leadership, from the cockpit to the customers Even as Octopus has grown to span industries as diverse as renewable power generation and software licensing, Jackson says his job has barely changed. The CEO’s role is still to understand customers and industry economics; set the vision for where the company needs to go; and build a team with the expertise and innovative impulses to get it there. For a pilot, the view from the cockpit window of a small Cessna is not that different from that of an Airbus A380, he says: “The difference comes when you look back.” If Octopus became a more complex organization, “then I’d get drawn more into wandering down the aisle of the plane than looking forward out the window,” he reasons. “The bit that really matters for me is being in the cockpit, looking forward, however many people we’ve got behind us.” So Jackson is constantly checking that his headcount is not growing faster than Octopus is adding new customers, as he looks to avoid diseconomies of scale and guards against the spread of bureaucracy. Yet he is equally anxious about ensuring that he is not losing touch with customers as their numbers run into the millions. Octopus was built on a proprietary technology platform called Kraken, which it spun off as a standalone company after a fundraising that valued the former subsidiary at $8.7 billion. Kraken gives Jackson and every member of his staff a “single view” of everything that is happening in the company, from customer service to pricing, energy trading to finance. Despite that tech-driven transparency, Jackson has maintained a habit of regularly meeting customers face-to-face. In the two weeks before our interview, he met roughly 1,000 customers at three different events, he estimates. “I stand on stage and talk to them, and then I get off the stage and have beers with them and understand their real experiences. They tell me not what our reports say, but what their real experience of dealing with our team is.” Everyone who signs up for an Octopus service is given Jackson’s email address. He used to answer each message himself, until Octopus reached 1.2 million customers and he found himself falling asleep at his keyboard at 2 am. Now his chief of staff and a team of five people farm out customers’ complaints and observations to the relevant executives, but he thinks the system still builds a “magic connectivity” with customers. “We’re not crazy hippies,” he says. “If we genuinely love our customers, they reciprocate.” How a CEO replaces themself when ther

events.title: After Factory’s public spat with Khosla, Menlo proudly invests
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy and his team announced Monday in a blog post that the firm has invested in AI coding startup Factory. Menlo declined to comment on how much it invested but said the deal was part of Factory’s latest funding round announced last month at a $5 billion valuation. A source familiar with the deal told us the investment was significant to Menlo — not a token gesture — and that Menlo would have invested more had there been room on the cap table. Ordinarily, something like this wouldn’t necessarily be news; startups often extend previous rounds to add new investors. But last week, Factory co-founder and CEO Matan Grinberg was embroiled in a very public airing of dirty laundry when he alleged that he had fired investor Chris Degnan of firm RPT Partners from his role as board advisor. Grinberg said he feared Degnan may have shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition. The accusation followed Degnan’s move to Cognition as its chief revenue officer. A who’s who of the tech industry came out of the woodwork either to support Degnan and condemn Factory, or vice versa, but none was more surprising than Vinod Khosla. Khosla’s firm is an investor in both Factory and Cognition. But that didn’t stop the venerable VC from calling Factory a desperate “struggling second tier competitor,” and accusing Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan and impugning his character. Degnan disputed Grinberg’s story, saying he resigned and that he’d rebuffed a competing job offer from Grinberg. So Menlo’s full-throated endorsement of Factory, which praised its founders, its tech, and its relationship with its customers, is more than a feather in Factory’s cap. It’s a statement that Factory is not in the state that Khosla implied it was. Murphy famously bet his firm on Anthropic back when it appeared to be an also-ran to OpenAI and has been on a hot streak ever since, landing deals with Lovable and Legora, for instance. So now some VCs are calling Factory “the next Anthropic. “ Sequoia’s Shaun Maguire, also a Factory backer who came out on X in support of Grinberg last week, appears thrilled with Menlo’s endorsement, saying the firm is “on a tear.” Notably, Menlo is not an investor in competitor Cognition. events.title: Reflection debuts Beam, an open-weight AI model to rival Chinese models at lower compute cost
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Reflection AI is officially unveiling Beam, its first frontier, open-weight AI model. The two-year-old, Brooklyn-based startup claims Beam matches the performance of leading Chinese open models on advanced reasoning benchmarks at dramatically lower costs, a claim that could heat up the race to build a Western answer to DeepSeek, Qwen, and Z.ai. Reflection’s announcement confirms reporting from Axios over the weekend that the startup was close to a launch. The company shared new details in a lengthy blog post Monday , which described Beam as a text-only mixture-of-experts model trained on high-compute reinforcement learning to be effective at reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks at “a fraction of the token cost and inference time compute” of rivals. Beam is a 501-billion-parameter model with 23 billion active parameters. It was pretrained on 23.8 trillion tokens and has a 1 million token context window. To compare, Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 has roughly 744 billion total parameters with 40 billion active. Reflection’s performance claims haven’t been independently verified, but on advanced reasoning benchmarks, the company says Beam scores on par with Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 and outperforms today’s leading Western open models while using “3-4x less inference compute.” Reflection calls it a “workhorse model” for enterprises, the public sector, and developers. Reflection is positioning itself against closed labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, against popular open models from Chinese developers, and against Western players like Mistral, Meta, and Cohere. Its most direct U.S. rival might be Inkling , the open model from Mira Murati’s Thinking Machines Lab released in July. Reflection’s own benchmarks show that Beam outscores Inkling on four coding tests where both report results, but Inkling is a multimodal model and Beam is text-only. Reflection was founded in 2024 by two former Google DeepMind researchers and has raised roughly $4.7 billion from backers, including Nvidia, Sequoia Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners, per PitchBook. Its last round valued the company at a $25 billion pre-money valuation . The startup has also been locking up compute — a key ingredient needed to train frontier models capable of luring customers away from Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s closed models, as well as the cheaper open-weight models from Chinese labs. This summer, Reflection signed deals collectively worth more than $7 billion with SpaceX and Nebius to secure access to Nvidia’s GB300 chips through 2029. Reflection is aiming Beam and future models at enterprises and sovereign nations. The pitch is to build “AI factories,” a product that would let institutions build their own customized, local AI system by training Reflection’s AI models on their own proprietary data. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose company backs Reflection, has long championed the “AI factory” idea and pushed to strengthen the open AI ecosystem — a vision that would also benefit Nvidia, whose GPUs would power those systems. Axios reported that hedge funds and trading firms are among those eager to build such systems. Reflection has already begun testing the concept of a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea . Reflection says it will release Beam’s weights and full technical details this month, with distribution through hyperscalers and neoclouds and integrations across open source libraries at launch. Reflection did not respond in time to TechCrunch’s requests for more information. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Water facility to drought-proof Sydney's west could supply data centres
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney Water confirms new $1.2 billion recycling plant could supply data centres A new water recovery facility in Sydney's west is set to service data centres, as well as homes and businesses. ( ABC News: Timothy Ailwood ) Concerns are being raised about a $1.2 billion water facility meant to bolster drought resistance being directed to service data centres. The new Kemps Creek facility treats 14 Olympic-sized swimming pools of wastewater a day, but there are plans to double it as the city grows. One expert told the ABC there were questions surrounding how the extra supply needed from data centre usage would be replaced. Concerns have been raised about recycled water from a new $1.2 billion facility built to bolster Western Sydney's drought resilience being used by data centres. The Kemps Creek facility opened last month to treat 35 million litres, or roughly 14 Olympic-sized swimming pools, of wastewater daily. There are plans to double this to 70 million litres as the city grows. The Badu Yarragul Water Resource Recovery Facility opened last month. ( ABC News: Timothy Ailwood ) Stuart Khan, who has published more than 200 peer-reviewed journal articles on issues relating to water quality and treatment, said demand from data centres was not accounted for in the Greater Sydney Water Strategy plan, which was created in 2022. "We have identified that we can get up to 140 gigalitres per year … from recycled water schemes into the future over the next couple of decades," Professor Khan said. "If we take that away from customers, we give it to a new industry that wasn't accounted for in the strategy, then we need to think about where we are going to replace that future water supply from." Stuart Khan says there is a lack of "big picture perspective". ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) The strategy was designed to address the increasing pressure on water supplies due to a growing population and unpredictable climate cycles. While the new Badu Yarragul Water Resource Recovery Facility at Kemps Creek's environmental impact statement nor its environment protection licence mentioned data centres explicitly, it does reference "industrial and business use". Professor Khan said while data centres provided opportunity for Sydney, there needed to be consideration for how recycled water was prioritised. The facility has capacity to connect 140,000 new homes and businesses across Western Sydney, including the new airport. Sydney Water said the facility would produce high-quality treated water suitable for non-drinking purposes in homes, industrial and business use, agriculture, and for greening public spaces. "There's a real opportunity for this to be used for data centres," Sydney Water managing director Darren Cleary said. Darren Cleary says there is opportunity for the facility to be used for data centres. ( ABC News: Timothy Ailwood ) Mr Cleary told ABC News the water utility was investing $14 billion in capital over the next five years to ensure demand was met. "The infrastructure that will be delivered for them [data centres] will have to be done in a way that doesn't affect the services we provide to the broader customer base," Mr Cleary said. "So fundamentally they'll pay their way." Sydney Water has confirmed a new wastewater treatment plant at Camellia-Rosehill , due to open by 2032, would also supply recycled water to data centres. Sanaa Shah says there is a lot of uncertainty around data centre proposals. ( ABC News: Floss Adams ) Sanaa Shah, a senior campaigner for Sweltering Cities, which advocates for community-driven solutions to urban heat in Western Sydney, said water use had not been adequately considered in data centre proposals and local residents were concerned they would be caught short. "They remember the drought period, they remember water restrictions and they don't know if these rules are going to be equally applied to data centres," she said. "What we're witnessing right now is a frantic, reckless data centre boom … there's a lot of uncertainty around these proposals." Ms Shah called for a moratorium on data centre proposals until there were clear safeguards in place "to ensure that these big data centres don't suck up our energy resources and don't result in higher energy bills". There are more than 60 operational data centres across NSW, according to the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure. "The current SSD [state significant development] planning pipeline contains 18 data centre projects valued at $61.22 billion in capital investment," a spokesperson said. Mr Cleary says where the recycled water goes will be prioritised.

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters OpenAI to flood your eyeballs with visual ads 22 hours ago Anthropic says its IPO could herald the end of the world as we know it 1 day ago arXiv imposes rate limit on paper submissions to stem the AI slop tide 3 days ago Cloudflare tries to outplay Jev with open-weight Clef models 4 days ago AWS offers local, open source leash for agent harnesses 4 days ago Apple’s attempt to integrate AI into its various operating systems hasn’t been entirely well received, nor has the decision to make Apple Intelligence increasingly difficult to disable completely. Thankfully, the open source community has come to the rescue. A recently released open source tool called RemoveMacAI does pretty much exactly what it says on the GitHub-hosted tin : Aggressively rips Apple Intelligence out of macOS, disabling most of its AI features and removing downloaded models following the launch of macOS 27 last month. Siri AI? Gone. ChatGPT and other AI extensions? Eliminated. Genmoji, random boxes offering to jazz up your writing, summaries of notifications and app content, and automatic photo clean-up? Never to be seen again. More importantly, RemoveMacAI can claw back the storage occupied by Apple’s AI models - potentially over 12 GB , depending on the Mac. You might just get confused and think it’s 2025 again. The impetus for RemoveMacAI, its creator Om Lahorey said in a LinkedIn post , is the fact that Apple made it practically impossible to remove Apple Intelligence features in macOS 27. “The settings are spread across about a dozen places, some of them only under Screen Time,” Lahorey wrote over the weekend. “Even with every one turned off, the models stay on disk. I wanted it gone in one step, so I wrote RemoveMacAI.” Unsurprisingly, Lahorey’s tool blew up on Hacker News, with plenty of people happy for an easy way to get rid of Apple AI tools. As of writing, the repo has over 1,500 stars, so it's clearly struck a nerve with frustrated macOS users. It’s simple to run, as its GitHub page explains: install it via a curl command to its GitHub repo, or with Homebrew, and then fire it up in the terminal. Selected features can be left enabled, or Apple Intelligence can be disabled completely, while a single command can revert the changes and restore the previous settings. RemoveMacAI works by installing a configuration profile, which the user has to approve, that applies Apple’s own restriction keys for Apple Intelligence features. Models are then removed via Apple’s asset service. Lahorey credits another open source tool called pared , and its developer, with mapping the asset service, model sets, and settings keys needed to remove Apple Intelligence. Pared functions similarly to RemoveMacAI – you can consider RemoveMacAI to be a more user-friendly wrapper for the other tool. As for whether it will persist, Lahorey explains that the config profile RemoveMacAI installs redirects the download for Apple Intelligence models to a closed local port, so updates to macOS shouldn’t result in the models being reinstalled. Also worth mentioning, Apple System Integrity Protection remains enabled with the models disabled and uninstalled, as no files under System are directly modified by the tool. Dictation should still work as well, as speech models aren’t removed by RemoveMacAI. That said, it’s certainly possible a future macOS update will break RemoveMacAI’s functionality. So if you’re interested in giving the tool a shot, there’s no guarantee this particular escape hatch will remain open forever.

events.title: The next chapter for Singapore equities
events.summary: All local stock sectors are expected to record positive earnings-per-share growth in the next financial year Singapore equities are entering a new phase, supported by stronger economic growth, broader earnings momentum and rising investor participation. Over the past five decades, Singapore’s stock market has developed alongside the country’s rise as a global business and financial centre, while The Business Times has helped investors follow the companies, industries and market developments behind that progress. The paper’s golden jubilee comes at a time when Singapore equities are entering a new phase, supported by stronger economic growth, broader earnings momentum, rising investor participation and measures aimed at strengthening capital formation, liquidity and research coverage. The timing is significant. Singapore’s 2026 gross domestic product growth forecast has been raised to 5 per cent from 3.5 per cent in June, reflecting stronger expectations for manufacturing, non-oil domestic exports, bank lending, and finance and insurance. The improvement is also showing up in company earnings. All local stock sectors are currently expected to record positive earnings-per-share growth in the following financial year, with technology, financial services and industrials among the stronger performers, while around 25 listed companies returned to profit in the latest reporting season. With the Straits Times Index’s (STI) discount to analysts’ weighted target prices now much narrower than the average since end-2021, the market’s next gains will depend less on valuation catch-up and more on earnings, cash flow, capital returns and execution. The STI tells only part of the story. Investors ultimately commit capital to companies, assessing their earnings, cash flow, balance sheets and ability to create value over time. As listed companies report results, raise fresh capital, expand operations, pursue acquisitions and return cash to shareholders, clear reporting helps investors separate short-term market moves from longer-term business performance. That is where BT has remained relevant over the past five decades, following the companies behind the headlines and helping investors understand what is changing and why it matters. One measure of a market’s relevance is whether companies continue to use it to support their growth. Since 2017, about S$90 billion has been raised through Singapore’s equity market, with secondary fundraisings accounting for about four-fifths of the total. For five decades, BT has helped investors follow the developments shaping Singapore’s listed companies and capital markets. Most are undertaken with a specific purpose, whether to fund acquisitions, increase capacity, enter new markets or support new growth initiatives. Investors are rarely focused on fundraising alone. They want to understand what management intends to do with the capital and whether those plans can deliver stronger business performance over time. That places greater importance on investor engagement, company communication and guidance. A fundraising may be completed in a matter of days, but investors often spend months and years assessing how the proceeds are deployed and whether the expected benefits are realised. As companies provide updates on strategy, execution and performance, investors are better able to judge whether management is delivering on the objectives presented at the time capital was raised. As more market activity becomes linked to business expansion, acquisitions, capacity investment and corporate transformation, the value of clear reporting and analysis will only increase. The steady flow of results, disclosures and corporate developments creates a greater need for investors to understand not just what has happened, but also why it matters. For five decades, BT has helped investors follow the developments shaping Singapore’s listed companies and capital markets. That role remains just as relevant today as investors assess not only what companies have done, but what they intend to do next. The market itself is also becoming easier to follow. The steady flow of results, disclosures and corporate development creates a greater need for investors to understand what has happened and why it matters. Research coverage has expanded significantly in recent years, bringing more listed companies into the news and into investor discussion. More initiations are being published, and more investors are gaining access to detailed analysis on business performance, industry developments and company strategy. This is particularly relevant for small and mid-cap companies. Many operate in industries that have benefited from Singapore’s economic development and regional growth, yet often receive less attention than the market’s largest names.

events.title: Beyond paper tigers: Evolving SGX’s regulations to match Asia’s needs
events.summary: New rules will have to be pioneered and original best practices must be established Like many other young Asian exchanges, Singapore has borrowed from older exchanges in establishing its regulatory regime. In 1976, the same year that The Business Times was launched, another very important event took place on the other side of the world. That year, the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) requested that the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) amend its listing requirements to include an audit committee composed of independent directors (IDs). Thus, the role of the ID was born as we know it today. The SEC’s request followed the 1970 bankruptcy of Penn Central, a major railway operator, due to financial troubles that took the company’s directors entirely by surprise – as well as revelations in 1973 that hundreds of companies had made illegal campaign contributions to then president Richard Nixon’s re-election campaign. These two major scandals, coming in close succession, lent strength to an emerging idea that boards needed to be truly independent to effectively monitor management . Since then, support for the independent board has grown steadily. Today, it is upheld as a best practice for corporate governance around the world. The SGX Rulebook requires IDs to constitute at least a third of a listed issuer’s board. This requirement rises to half if the chairman is not independent, is part of management or also holds the role of CEO. Yet, Singapore – along with many other Asian jurisdictions that have endorsed the need for director independence – continues to grapple with paper tigers: IDs who either cannot or do not effectively challenge controlling shareholders. This challenge of independence is just one of several that Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) faces in the development of its regulatory framework – particularly the portions that relate to transparency and governance. As Singapore’s equities market goes through a period of reflection and rejuvenation, it has become clear that we need to relook many of the assumptions that form the foundation of our rules. We have had a long enough runway to realise that some concepts that work in Western developed markets, such as relying on IDs, who are a better check on management than on controlling shareholders, may not work as well here – at least not without some adaptation. The Stock Exchange of Singapore, one of the precursor companies that was combined to form SGX, was founded in 1973, only a few years before BT . In the grand scheme of things, we are a very young exchange. The world’s oldest, the Amsterdam stock exchange, was founded in 1602. NYSE dates back to 1792 and the London Stock Exchange had its start in 1801. The Stock Exchange of Singapore was founded in 1973. Like many other relatively young Asian exchanges, Singapore has borrowed heavily from older exchanges in establishing its regulatory regime. This was necessary, partly because not doing so would make it tough to attract international investors and partly because established regimes had proven track records. So far, many of these transplanted systems have worked well. As a member of the International Organization of Securities Commissions, SGX’s listing and trading rules align with various international benchmarks – such as those for accounting standards and market surveillance. It has become clear, however, that some systems are working better than others. The reliance on board independence as a check is one element that clearly needs improvement. Another is the very close alignment of our corporate governance code with that of the UK, which is a market where institutional investors actively monitor corporate disclosures and punish poor transparency or bad behaviour by selling down a stock or voting down a resolution. Other elements of the Singapore regulatory regime that have been singled out for improvement are rules governing how shareholders vote, what issuers disclose , levels of acceptable free floats and the avenues for minority redress. None of this is to say that Singapore should abandon its existing regulatory principles. We have seen in our market evidence of IDs performing their roles effectively and improving outcomes for shareholders. We have also seen evidence that motivated shareholders can and do agitate for change with success. As we find our feet as a truly Asian exchange, however, it is necessary for our regulation to be fit for our environment. The high proportion of individual-controlled and family-controlled companies in our market makes it clear that the conflict of interest between majority and minority shareholders needs to be better addressed. The low proportion of institutional shareholders focused on our market, meanwhile, makes it clear that market discipline alone may not produce certain desired outcomes.

events.title: Reflection AI unveils an open-source Western answer to Chinese labs
events.summary: The News Reflection AI, the startup billing itself as America’s answer to open-source Chinese AI, is releasing its first model, called Beam. The company, founded in 2024 by former DeepMind researchers, is positioning Beam as a “workhorse” that performs better than other Western open models. The model is particularly strong at coding and agentic tasks, cofounder and CEO Misha Laskin told Semafor. It also needs three to four times less computing power to reason through a problem than comparable open models, he said, making it faster and cheaper to run. The model’s capabilities are comparable to one of China’s Z.ai’s recent models, GLM-5.2, which was released in June; Beam is “approaching” the performance of Alibaba’s most advanced model, Qwen 3.8-Max, which trails the top closed American models from OpenAI and Anthropic. China’s startups and tech giants have led the world in open-source AI. Several large Western companies have recently embraced Chinese models as a way to reduce costs for certain repetitive tasks like customer service and writing routine code. Beijing has also promoted open source as a diplomatic tool to help other countries in their tech development. But because open models can be downloaded and run with fewer safeguards, their rise has also raised security concerns: US and UK government evaluators found that recent Chinese models could help hackers exploit code vulnerabilities. New York-based Reflection sees a large market in businesses, governments, and other entities building sovereign AI systems that don’t or can’t use Chinese models, but still want to “own” and control how they use AI, Laskin said. “They don’t really have very good options today,” he said. Reflection is already training its next model, which Laskin said would be “much more” powerful and performant than Beam. Know More The startup, which has investments from Nvidia, Sequoia, and Citigroup, in June confirmed it closed its latest funding round at a $25 billion pre-money valuation. With Beam’s release, Reflection joins a slate of other Western startups, including Thinking Machines Lab and Mistral, that also offer open-weight AI models. Its release comes as calls for AI regulation reach a fever pitch in the US, after a slate of alarming security incidents. The leading US AI labs and tech companies signed what US President Donald Trump called a “morally binding” agreement on safety principles following a White House meeting. Trump has pushed for companies to regulate themselves, rather than subject them to federal oversight, but the political calculus could shift quickly should the Democrats take over Congress in November. Reflection says it wants to enable “builders of open models to be able to contribute to the discourse that is happening in DC on regulation,” Laskin said. “You want multiple voices around the table, both open and closed, and they should be working collaboratively on helping the government regulate AI,” he said. “We see this entrance as something that enables more open model perspectives to be part of the discourse in DC.” Laskin said Reflection is working with both the US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence and the UK’s AI Safety Institute to assess the model’s capabilities.

events.title: Tories unite behind Badenoch, but road to recovery remains long
events.summary: Farage’s woes have given some a reason to hope, but insiders say focus on economy over culture wars is needed to win back centrist voters During a quick-fire Q&A at the Conservative party conference this weekend, Kemi Badenoch was asked who she would pick between Robert Jenrick or Suella Braverman. “Why do you keep offering me these? It’s like asking if I’d rather be shot or drowned,” the Tory leader responded with her trademark directness. The Tories appear more united than they have done in years. Part of that is because they have a common enemy to unite against: Tory defectors to Reform. It is not lost on Badenoch’s team that this time last year, it was a matter of when, not if, Jenrick, her erstwhile leadership rival, would try to oust her. Mutinous Tory MPs were privately predicting her demise. But after a successful conference, Badenoch limped on – and Jenrick emerged a diminished figure who weeks later would be kicked out of the party. His presence, however, lives on, with shadow ministers openly sharing their relief that he is no longer among their number. “Nobody knew how much we hated Robert until he left,” said one shadow cabinet member. Others were less polite. “Rob going was like pulling out a splinter,” one said. “I miss him like I miss an abscess in my molar,” another added. But while the unity comes, in part, from a mutual dislike, there are of course other factors: Badenoch’s strength as a leader; the country’s yearning for stability; the constant threat of Reform UK to the party’s right. Badenoch has been running the show for almost two years – the longest serving Tory leader since Boris Johnson – and has begun to set out her principles, writing a 30,000 word pamphlet titled The Right Way before the conference. Tory MPs also seem to have finally realised that voters take a dim view of the party cycling through leaders at such breakneck speed, with five in the past eight years. Nigel Farage’s woes have also given them reason for hope: while the Reform leader believes his party will recover from a difficult summer, some Tory MPs are confident that his party has peaked. Other party insiders – possibly more plugged into what is going on in their constituencies – concede that Farage still represents a huge threat. They are among those concerned about Badenoch pitching to the right. Instead, they say that she needs to do more to win over centrist voters for the party to stand a chance of winning another election. Part of that is by focusing more on the economy and less on culture wars. “There’s no point telling Kemi not to do anything. But we do have to be careful with our language,” one MP said. Another added: “That’s not Kemi’s instinct. But she does finally seem to understand it all has to be about the economy. That’s where we win.” Badenoch believes she can “shrug off” the Liz Truss anchor and beat Reform and Labour on the economy, MPs say. Andrew Griffith, her shadow chancellor who has previously worked in business, helps the party’s credibility, they add, and Badenoch will speak more about the topic this week. The Tory leader also polls ahead of her party, which insulates her from much internal criticism. One adviser said the Tories do better when their leader is in that position – citing David Cameron and Boris Johnson – but worse when they’re behind, as Rishi Sunak was. Badenoch has told her top team that they have to work “day by day” to restore the party’s fortunes. Yet there is no escaping that almost two years after she was elected as leader, the Tories are still polling lower than they did in 2024 with their catastrophic general election defeat. “You won’t hear much from us on that,” one senior aide said. “The qualitative stuff is good but it’s not backed up yet by the numbers. We need to put on three or four points in the polls. If we do that and gain momentum we’re back.” Others are hopeful that the exposure of their conference week can give them enough of a lift in the polls to help them maintain the narrative that they’re on the march. The spectre hanging over the whole affair, however, is the prospect of a snap general election. Andy Burnham’s political away day at Chequers on Monday has got many Tories spooked, even though the prime minister has ruled out calling an early election. Perhaps more in hope than expectation, shadow cabinet ministers said they did not believe Burnham would call an election. “He said it would be irresponsible and it’s hard to walk that back,” said one. However, Badenoch told a bash for Tory MPs on Sunday night the party was getting ready for an election regardless. But while she sounded bullish, her closest lieutenants are anything but. “If there is one, we’re all fucked,” they said.

Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Instinct, the AI agent now valued at $10 billion as of its latest funding round, is expanding into group chats. The startup announced on Monday that users will be able to add the agent to chats with friends, which could be helpful in certain scenarios like travel planning, snagging event tickets, running fantasy leagues, organizing carpools, or managing who’s bringing what to Thanksgiving. Notably, the group chats with the AI agent will work even if a user’s friends haven’t joined Instinct, the company said. With the launch, Instinct moves ahead in its battle with top competitors in the space, like Meta’s Muse. The latter doesn’t yet offer the group chat functionality, though Meta’s older app, Meta AI, can be added to group chats on WhatsApp, Messenger, Instagram, and Facebook. Instinct in group chats Starting today, early access users can add Instinct to group chats. A new Instinct joins and works for the whole group. Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can… pic.twitter.com/pqJX7ieC7B — Noah Shinn (@noahrshinn) October 5, 2026 Instinct and Muse have been running neck and neck recently, with both of them adding the ability to make phone calls over the past couple of weeks, as their agents try to win more of the consumer AI market. Last week, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Dots, personal AI agents that can also be used in ChatGPT Spaces, collaborative workspaces where the Dots and humans work together. On X, Instinct founder Noah Shinn explained how Instinct handles users’ privacy and security in group chats. He said a user’s personal Instinct agent will ask permission before connecting with the group’s Instinct agent, and that users can also choose which groups they trust and can remove that trust at any time. Shinn also said the group’s Instinct is siloed from the users’ personal accounts, which it cannot access. The personal agent will always ask the user’s permission before sharing information or taking any action. If new members join the group chat, any pending replies from a user’s personal Instinct agent are held before those are shared with the group, too. “Making plans with friends usually turns into a frustrating back-and-forth over times and places. With Instinct in the group, you can explore options together, agree on a plan and get it done, all in one thread,” Shinn wrote. The feature is rolling out initially to Instinct’s early access users but will expand to all users “soon.” To gain access to the new feature (or other recent additions), users can ask their Instinct agent to put them on the list to try it out. events.title: Gatorade maker recalls 122,000 cases of popular sports drink across 37 US states
events.summary: PepsiCo initiated class II recall of 28oz bottles last month over ‘undeclared’ yellow dyes, FDA notice says About 122,000 cases of the popular sports drink Gatorade have been voluntarily recalled across 37 US states due to their having “undeclared” food dye, according to an official federal notice . The varieties of the drink involved in the notice include 28oz bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Lime Zero, Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero, the notice said. Gatorade’s manufacturer – the soda giant PepsiCo – initiated its recall on 25 September, said the advisory, which was posted on the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)’s website. The notice said the recall was considered class II, implying “a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote”, according to the FDA. “Undeclared Yellow No 6 and/or Yellow No 5” dyes were listed in the FDA notice as the “reason for recall” for people who are potentially sensitive to them. PepsiCo did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. The states listed for the recall are: Alaska, Alabama, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin. CBS News reported that it was not known whether refunds were available for people who purchased the recalled Gatorade drinks. The FDA has come under fire during Donald Trump ’s second presidency, including after the agency implemented layoffs , slashing its staff by almost 20%.

events.title: Imposter recruiters taking over the job market
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Jobseekers exploited by recruitment scammers on LinkedIn Job seekers are noticing an increase in recruitment scams on LinkedIn. ( REUTERS/Robert Galbraith ) Tony Young is one of many Australians who have applied for work using websites like LinkedIn, only to realise afterwards it was a scam. The former tech executive has sent out applications for more than 400 jobs over the past three years. While responding to a job advertisement on LinkedIn, Tony was contacted by someone claiming to be a consultant who could help improve his resume. When he refused, the "consultant" quickly lowered their offer and asked Tony whether he would "do it for $50". The ABC has observed an uptick in fraud targeting jobseekers as soon as they update their online status to indicate they are looking for work. Sophisticated employment fraudsters target jobseekers as soon as they announce their unemployment. ( ABC News ) It includes fake job ads, fraudsters posing as recruiters with "cloned" profiles and people taking advantage of desperate jobseekers by offering to help with CV writing for significant sums of money. Australian jobseekers are being warned about this pervasive, sophisticated employment fraud as recruiters voiced concerns to the ABC and in online forums about fake advertisements flooding recruitment websites. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said in just two months, July and August 2026, it received 138 scam reports relating to LinkedIn with reported losses of up to $254,449. Tony said he often received emails or comments on his online posts that seemed to be from companies purporting to be "hiring" on LinkedIn. In June, he received an email from a so-called "career and talent leader" at engineering consultancy Aurecon who wanted to have a "senior leadership discussion" with him. Tony says he often receives targeted emails and comments. ( ABC News ) The ABC can confirm that no-one from Aurecon actually contacted Tony. In addition, the person who emailed Tony had cloned a LinkedIn profile belonging to a real employee from the engineering firm. Aurecon said it was aware that fraudsters sometimes misused its brand name to deceive jobseekers through fake job emails, fraudulent websites or unsolicited job offers. The company stressed that it conducts formal virtual or in-person interviews before making offers and would never ask candidates to make any up-front payments. LinkedIn's latest Job Search Safety Pulse report has found Australians are more vulnerable to recruitment scams than ever. Nearly half of the people surveyed for that report said they would take risks when applying for jobs due to ongoing cost-of-living pressures. More than a third said they would be more likely to let their guard down. Questioning whether a job is "actually real" has also become a routine part of the job search, according to the LinkedIn report. The same report found 61 per cent of Australians had seen a job ad that they suspected was fraudulent and 27 per cent have come close to falling for one. Around 16 per cent of the respondents said they had fallen victim to job scams. For younger gen Z jobseekers, born between 1997 and 2012, employment scam victim percentages rose to 25 per cent. Do you know more about job scams on LinkedIn? We would like to hear from you! Contact our journalist confidentially on li.yiying@abc.net.au or li.yiying@proton.me . "Recruitment scammers often pretend to represent large companies or recruitment firms and will contact people either directly through LinkedIn or via email with a job opportunity that is tailored to the information on their LinkedIn profile," an ACCC spokesperson said. They said "job scams may ask people to pay money to start a job" or participate in a "course or training". Trevor Churchley says scam activities on LinkedIn have become more noticeable in the past two years. ( LinkedIn: Trevor Churchley ) Tech recruiter Trevor Churchley said scam activities on LinkedIn had become more noticeable in the past two years. Mr Churchley said he was personally aware of several real profiles being "taken over or cloned". He said the fake profiles were then used to target jobseekers who publicly disclosed they were unemployed. "They're the perfect target to approach because … all of a sudden, they gain the attention of recruiters … hopefully leading to jobs," Mr Churchley said. Many applicants place the #opentowork banner on their LinkedIn profiles, hoping to become more visible to recruiters. Jobseekers attract attention from recruiters and scammers once they put an #opentowork banner on.
