events.title: Short-stay operators have mixed reactions to SA's register proposal
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Short-stay accommodation providers have mixed response to SA register plan Jenny Bickley says renting out her property on a short-term basis is more profitable than a traditional rental. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) South Australia is set to join New South Wales and Western Australia with a registry for short-stay accommodation. The scheme is still being shaped but the initial feedback from operators has been mixed, with some raising concerns about security and the impact on local government decisions. Public consultation closes on October 30. Accountant Jenny Bickley makes about $45,000 in profit each year from guests hiring her dual-abode property in Mount Gambier. "The Airbnb model is way better than renting," she said. While Ms Bickley is one of many South Australians who run a short-stay accommodation business, it is not exactly clear how many there actually are. Jenny Bickley says most of her guests are tourists. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Last year, the state government wrapped up its inquiry into the sector amid nationwide concerns about the model affecting housing and rental affordability. Among the takeaways: SA lacked the data. The committee floated a registration scheme, a concept already seen in Western Australia and New South Wales. Jenny Bickley is concerned about "severe security risks" from a short-stay accommodation register. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) The Short Term Accommodation Association Australia (STAAA) backed a statewide register but wanted the approach reconsidered and warned of "unnecessary duplication". The details have not been locked in, but a discussion paper indicated councils could apply their own land-use codes and decide rates, something the STAAA was not keen on. "We need one state, one register and one consistent registration system," executive director Keiran Craig-Jones said. Ms Bickley, who fought council rate hikes in Mount Gambier, believed registration could help shake any "cowboys" operating unlawfully but echoed the STAAA's concerns. Ms Bickley said most of her booking were people visiting the town for events. Fourth generation farmer David Galpin entered the world of short-stays last year when he pitched his purpose-built paddock-view property in Penola as a luxury escape. Mr Galpin welcomed the register and believed it could inform the family's future business moves and even lead to more short-stay rentals. David Galpin says despite his research he does not have a "full picture" of the supply of short-stay accommodation. ( ABC South East SA: Aiden McNamara ) Ms Bickley said she understood the benefit for government decision-making, but was concerned about potential security issues. "Nobody actually knows the location [of my property] until they complete the booking," she said. Keiran Craig-Jones says legislation should be clear about exactly what information is collected and for what purpose. ( Supplied ) Mr Galpin was less concerned by the risks of a public register given his farm was "different to having a flat or something in a city or town". Ms Craig-Jones said while security was a "legitimate issue to consider", she was not aware of any increased burglary, squatting or similar offending following registers in other jurisdictions. Short-stay accommodation challenges National Shelter chief executive Jackson Hills said there were hundreds of local government areas nationwide, but about 40 or 50 faced "a much bigger challenge" around short-stay accommodation. In certain hotspots, such as Noosa in Queensland , he said policymakers may have "got the balance wrong" given shortages in the local workforce. Jackson Hills says knowing the real number of short-stay accommodation places would better inform decisions. ( Supplied ) Mr Hills said Australia would be better off understanding what the actual levels were before moving to "arbitrary policy responses". "There are local governments focusing on their local economies and that's exactly where the conversation should be," he said. Public consultation for South Australia's registry closes on October 30 at 5pm.

events.title: Are Coles and Woolworths centralising their supply chains? Some experts think so
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Coles, Woolworths supply chain tactic driving small farms out, producer says When middlemen or wholesalers are involved in trade agreements with major supermarkets, small producers have "no power", says one grower. ( ABC News: Hamed Akrami ) A small-scale banana farmer who has had his agreement to supply Coles ended due to the supermarket simplifying its supply chain says the move signals the end of small-scale farms across the country. Industry experts have claimed Coles and Woolworths are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs. Some experts worry producers will become more vulnerable if supermarkets continue to do so. After 30 years of selling bananas to Coles, New South Wales farmer Amrit Singh believes the supermarket's decision to stop buying his produce signals a possible end for small, family-run farms like his. In the past two months, Coles and Woolworths confirmed they would pull various local products from their shelves, with suppliers told the decisions were due to changes to the supply chain. Amrit Singh says small-scale growers are "price takers", not price makers. ( ABC News: Samuel O'Brien ) Industry experts have said major Australian supermarkets are centralising their supply chains in a bid to cut costs, warning some producers could now be at greater risk of having their products removed from supermarket shelves. Woolworths said its supply chain network had expanded, while Coles rejected the experts' claims. An inquiry by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) into supermarkets last year found Coles and Woolworths had overwhelming power in their trade relationships with suppliers. Amrit Singh labelled Coles's decision to pull local bananas from its shelves as "anti-competitive" and said supermarkets should be encouraging diversity in growing regions. ( ABC News: Giulio Saggin ) In August, Coles confirmed it would stop selling Coffs Coast bananas, pumpkins and cucumbers in an effort to simplify its supply chain. While Tasmanians can shop at 17 Coles and 32 Woolworth supermarkets, there are no Aldi stores — and that won't be changing anytime soon, according to the company CEO. Mr Singh sold his bananas indirectly to Coles through a wholesaler, an agreement he said was worth hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. The produce is now expected to come from north Queensland, but Mr Singh believes his business is too small to compete with north Queensland's banana industry. "Freight costs [involved in] getting access to those [new] markets are going to be extremely high," he said. Mr Singh said farmers who did not sell directly to supermarkets had "no power" to negotiate trade agreements and were forced to reduce prices to support promotions and specials. Coles says keeping its supply chain efficient helps it absorb costs and reduce the impact on grocery prices. ( ABC News ) Rise in 'middlemen' leaves farmers vulnerable NSW Farmers Association principal economist Samuel Miller said supermarket giants had long been centralising their supply chains. He said one way they were doing this was through buying produce from packhouses or "middlemen" — selling on behalf of a group of growers — instead of directly from them. "When those supermarkets make a decision like consolidating their suppliers or rejecting some produce … it affects not just that supplier in the middle, but it can affect dozens, 40 or 50 other farmers down the line." Samuel Miller says supermarkets have a large share of the market, so they hold negotiating power. ( Supplied: Samuel Miller ) In a statement to the ABC, Coles said it continued to source directly from a range of Australian producers. "In fresh produce, aggregators are not new and have long played an important role in Australia," a spokesperson said. In August, Woolworths confirmed it would stop selling Tasmanian beef in stores around the country from early next year. ( ABC News: Laurissa Smith ) Queensland University of Technology retail marketing professor Gary Mortimer said meat was one of the main supply chains where processing had been centralised, citing Woolworths's decision to stop selling Tasmanian beef from early next year. Gary Mortimer says supermarkets centralising their processing can give shoppers greater product consistency. ( Supplied: Gary Mortimer ) Some suppliers said they were told this was due to rising production and shipping costs. "Over the last 10 to 15 years, what we've seen is that reduction of in-store processing back to centralised processing," Professor Mortimer said. "Less trade butchers in stores and more of that processing taking place centrally.

events.title: Australia's fossil fuel expansion 'slap in the face' to Pacific nations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Pacific leaders challenge Australia's fossil fuel expansion ahead of pre-COP31 talks in Fiji Marica and Sami have been living in a tent for five years, waiting for their village to be rebuilt. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As she sits crossed legged on the floor inside a large tent, 66-year-old Marica Malumuca describes the place she's called home for the past five years. "When it rains heavily it feels like we're living in a balloon because we can see the parts of the tent bulging where it's filling up," she said. Ms Malumuca's village, Nabavatu, was declared unsafe in 2021 after two cyclones cracked the ground beneath it, and she was moved to a temporary settlement in Savadrua. There are 37 tents at the temporary site. Some can fit three people and others accommodate up to seven. Ms Malumuca's son, Sami Veloko, moved home from the city to look after her as they wait for Nabavatu to be rebuilt. Pacific communities are already feeling the impacts of climate change. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) "Those people who stay in these tents, they used to stay in a good house; a cement house, a wooden house of a high quality," he said. "You cannot believe — even they themselves cannot believe — that they stay in this kind of tent." Small island states are already being disproportionately affected by displacement as climate change drives more extreme weather. The United Nations warned the impacts of tropical cyclones have become more severe due to rising sea levels and an increase in heavy precipitation. More than half of Pacific Island countries' infrastructure is located in coastal areas at risk from rising seas, which happens as higher temperatures melt glaciers and ice sheets. Nabavatu is yet to be rebuilt, five years after it was damaged by cyclones. ( ABC News: Lice Monovo ) As world leaders prepare to descend on Mr Veloko's home country for high-level climate talks, he has a message for them. "We are getting the effect of climate change and we are the vulnerable people, the Pacific people," he said. "Because of what they have contributed to carbon dioxide, the industrialisation that they have developed in their countries, we are getting the worst of it." Climate diplomacy at heart of security strategy Prime Minister Anthony Albanese will join global leaders at the pre-COP event, which will feature preparatory talks ahead of next month's United Nations COP31 climate summit. Australia has led the charge for the lead-up talks to be held in the Pacific and is spending millions of dollars on the event as part of its broader regional security strategy to become the "partner of choice" for the Pacific islands. Anthony Albanese attended the 2026 Pacific Island Forum in early September. ( ABC News: Mark Moore ) The Albanese government has vigorously pursued a series of bilateral security deals with Pacific nations since coming to office including Vanuatu, Fiji, Tuvalu, Nauru and Papua New Guinea, with almost all of them including commitments to act on climate change. According to the Lowy Institute, Australia remains the Pacific's largest bilateral donor and biggest development partner , having spent almost $19 billion of a committed $20.6 billion. Wes Morgan, a research associate with the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at UNSW who lived and worked in the Pacific for more than a decade, said the federal government understood that to become the Pacific's partner of choice it must act on the region's key security threat. "That is why there has been the inclusion of commitments on climate change in these bilateral security arrangements, but more broadly why Australia is working with Pacific island countries to drive global action on climate change," he said. "That's why Australia had its hand up to host the UN climate talks with the Pacific." For Pacific islands like Ebeye, rising oceans caused by the continued burning of fossil fuels is a real and acute problem. ( Supplied: Hall Contracting ) But Dr Morgan said Australia remaining one of the world's largest fossil fuel exporters "flies in the face of the narrative Australia's pursuing with Pacific Island countries". "Australia's biggest contribution to the climate crisis is the export of coal and gas, so the emissions associated with Australia's exports of coal and gas more than doubled the emissions from Australia's entire domestic economy," he said. Can Australia be both a gas giant and a climate leader? Seven years after it was first mooted, the extension of Australia's biggest gas project could not have landed at a more critical juncture for the nation's climate credentials.

events.title: Fulcrum Echo promises AI text in the style of any writer, so I tested it
events.summary: Fulcrum faces an identity crisis, even as it works on creating one by enabling anyone to imitate another person's writing style. The AI startup, founded in 2025 and previously operating at fulcrumresearch.ai, now uses fulcrum.inc and could easily be confused with one of the handful of other companies named Fulcrum or some variation of that. There's Fulcrum (withfulcrum.com), Fulcrum (fulcrumapp.com), Fulcrum AI (fulcrumai.us), Fulcrum Digital (fulcrumdigital.com), Fulcrum Labs (fulcrumlabs.ai), Fulcrum (fulcrumpro.com), Fulcrum Insurance Technology (fulcruminsure.app), and perhaps more. This Fulcrum is offering a large language model called Echo, which allows you to generate text in the style of a well-known author. Fulcrum appears to have no issue with corporate echoes. It now falls to writers to decide whether they have an issue with non-corporeal imitation. "Echo can do any writing task, from literary fiction to casual chatting, in whatever style you choose," the company says, and then launches into an exploration of how the technology works without addressing whether imitating a person's writing style poses any problems. Suggestions in the Echo Playground, for generating sample text, include Paul Christiano, Emily Dickinson, and Donald Trump. So, the full gamut of literary achievement: from AI safety expert to acclaimed 19th-century poet to the wordsmith who brought us "covfefe." But Echo will echo even the style of not-so-famous scribes, such as this reporter. So I fed the model a recent op-ed to assess its copying capabilities. The result was mixed, but better than the AI-crafted pitches that have been hitting my inbox for the past few months. I asked the model, "What do you think about the possibility that AI is conscious?" Here's part of the response, notionally written in my writing style. I suspect the debate about whether AI is conscious is less consequential than the debate about whether AI is profitable. Consciousness is a word that invites philosophical speculation and TED Talk invitations. Profitability is a word that invites shareholder lawsuits if you get it wrong. If you ask Meta's latest model whether it's conscious, it will probably say something reassuringly vague, trained as it is on the corpus of human equivocation. If you ask Mark Zuckerberg whether Meta's AI is conscious, he will probably say something about how we need to focus on the future being for everyone, because that's a question that doesn't require him to discuss the ad targeting business. The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment is about as strong as the evidence for Zuck's credibility as a futurist. Which is to say, it exists mainly in press releases and earnings calls. What's clear is that software can simulate aspects of human conversation well enough to unsettle people, and that unsettled people are a valuable audience. If you can convince users that your chatbot understands them – or might, someday – you can sell them subscriptions, or better, harvest their attention for advertisers. The style is familiar but makes a lot of choices I wouldn't have made. I wouldn't begin with "I suspect…" – commit or go home. The consciousness/profitability parallel construction is clumsy. "TED Talk invitations" bets on alliteration at the expense of coherence – "discourse" or "chatter" would work better than "invitations." I wouldn't have written "corpus of human equivocation" – a nice turn of phrase, but an unnecessary shot at training data when the point is the model's response rather than the provenance of that response. Though off-topic, Echo did a passable job of reproducing my op-ed's skepticism of Meta and its CEO. The paragraph that begins "The evidence for AI consciousness at the moment…" is succinct and sounds good. It just doesn't make much sense because there's nothing in the text that addresses Zuckerberg's predictions about the future or whether they're credible. And that's not really relevant to the prompt about AI and consciousness – a subject about which I'd be far more dismissive if opining. As AI research, Echo is an improvement on the text emitted by many AI models. But whether the beneficial uses of this technology outweigh the harms is less clear. Generative AI models that imitate artists' visual styles remain controversial and are the subject of ongoing litigation. And voice imitation has also raised questions about publicity rights and the risk of deception. Such concerns have prompted US lawmakers to propose the NO FAKES Act, which would create federal protections against certain unauthorized AI-generated replicas of a person's voice or visual likeness. If writers generally have no copyright in their writing style itself, and limited practical means to stop unwanted automated imitation of it when their published work is publicly accessible, then the surest defense against Echo may be silence.®

events.title: Iranian diplomats "kicked out" of U.S. after ignoring order to leave
events.summary: Two members of Iran's delegation to the UN General Assembly in New York were "kicked out" of the country on Saturday, several days after they were asked to leave, a U.S. official said. "Secretary Rubio means business. Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in New York long after the UN General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the country," the official said. Why it matters: It's the latest sign of tension between the two countries as diplomatic efforts to end the war falter and the prospect of renewed combat rises. State of play: The U.S. official said the two Iranian diplomats did not obey a State Department demand to the Iranian mission to the UN on Monday that its entire delegation leave the country immediately. On Friday, the Iranian mission to the UN was told the U.S. was aware the two diplomats were still in New York despite having asked them to leave. Iran was told again the two need to leave immediately. One of the Iranian diplomats left on Friday night and the second on Saturday morning, the official said. The other side: Iranian Foreign Affairs Minister Abbas Araghchi disputed the U.S. account in a post on X Sunday. "All Iranian diplomats who attended UNGA, except one who departed earlier, left as scheduled," he wrote . "Taking pride in fake diplomat "expulsion" is inappropriate for the head of any diplomatic corps. It oozes of desperation and defeat, and is inconsistent with UN host nation obligations."

events.title: Yemeni and Saudi forces launch counteroffensive against the Houthis
events.summary: Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a counteroffensive against the Houthis on Sunday in an effort to win back territory from the rebel group, the head of Yemen's presidential council said in a speech. "We have exhausted all opportunities for deescalation with the Houthi militias," Rashad al-Alimi said . Why it matters: One of the key objectives of the operation is to regain control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital artery for global trade and Saudi oil exports. When the Houthis took over territory on the Red Sea coast close to the strait, it gave them — and Iran, which backs them — powerful leverage over the U.S., its Gulf allies and the world economy. Despite pleas from Saudi Arabia, the U.S. is not getting involved in direct combat against the Houthis for now. It is providing intelligence and targeting support, U.S. officials say. Driving the news: The counteroffensive has been planned for many weeks by Yemen's internationally recognized government and Saudi Arabia. Tens of thousands of ground troops loyal to the Yemeni government are participating. The Saudi military is mainly providing air cover for Yemeni forces and conducting airstrikes against Houthi targets. The goal is to retake the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control for several years. The Houthis continued launching missiles at Saudi targets over the weekend, including at facilities of state-owned oil giant Aramco. The intrigue: President Trump is caught between wanting to help Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his friend and ally, and avoiding getting entangled in a new front in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) also had serious reservations about launching strikes in Yemen, viewing it as a distraction from its focus on Iran, a U.S. official said. On Thursday, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman called Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to brief him on the planned operation and ask again for U.S. airstrikes against Houthi targets, the official said. A second U.S. official said that the U.S. "is not going to take kinetic action for now," but stressed that could change if the operation runs into problems. What to watch: On Friday, Trump's top cabinet members huddled for hours at Camp David to discuss next steps in the Iran war and the conflict in Yemen, Axios first reported. It's unclear whether the meeting ended with new policy recommendations for the president regarding Yemen.

events.title: Dubai to expand CommerCity in push for digital economy growth
events.summary: Dubai CommerCity (DCC) , the free zone dedicated to digital commerce in Dubai, is launching the second phase of its expansion programme with Dh1.8 billion ($272.2 million) investment that will help the emirate grow its digital economy . The free zone is set to deliver the expansion project in phases between the first quarter of 2027 and the fourth quarter of 2028, Dubai Media Office said in a statement on Sunday. “Phase two of Dubai CommerCity comes at a time when Dubai continues to demonstrate its ability to grow and expand despite the changes and challenges facing the global economy,” Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed, Chairman of Dubai Integrated Economic Zones Authority (Diez), said. The free zone, which is a joint venture between Diez and Wasl Group, will add a series of projects across its three districts: the Business Cluster, Logistics Cluster, and Social Cluster. On aggregate, the projects will add more than 91,000 square metres of new office space, increasing the free zone’s capacity and expanding its integrated ecosystem to serve companies operating in digital commerce and technology sectors. The push to expand the free zone builds upon Dubai CommerCity’s record demand, with occupancy reaching nearly 96 per cent across its office, logistics, and retail spaces. Investor confidence “This expansion reflects the growing investor confidence in Dubai’s economic ecosystem and its ability to attract high-quality investments while providing an advanced economic infrastructure that responds to rapid shifts in emerging sectors,” Sheikh Ahmed said. The move, he added, aligns with the Dubai Economic Agenda, D33, objectives and helps strengthen Dubai's position as a global hub for the digital economy and future commerce. Launched in January, D33 aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy , with a target of reaching Dh32 trillion by 2033 and establishing the emirate among the top three global cities. The plan envisages a programme to support 30 private companies to achieve unicorn status – worth more than $1 billion. Other business incubators will support the growth of private companies, with 400 of the most promising identified. The expansion of the Business Cluster and the Social Cluster will add 86,000 square metres of new space, which will add to options available to local, regional and global companies that are looking to become a part of the Dubai CommerCity ecosystem, the Media Office said. The Business Cluster will include additional office space across six new buildings, including shell-and-core offices, fully fitted workspaces, and flexible plug-and-play solutions. Within the Logistics Cluster, the phase two expansion will add The Hive, a 5,600 square metre facility that will provide an alternative logistics model. It will feature 181 flexible units, alongside climate-controlled fulfilment areas, as well as digitally managed loading and unloading zones, the Media Office said.

events.title: New York has a socialist mayor. Los Angeles may be next
events.summary: LOS ANGELES — Voters could make history next month by giving the two largest U.S. cities something in common: South Asian immigrant democratic socialist mayors. Why it matters: Such a pairing would capture two forces reshaping urban America — its growing diversity and the Democratic Party's shifting ideological boundaries. New York, the nation's largest city, is already led by democratic socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani . The challenger in Los Angeles is Nithya Raman, an Indian-born urban planner and two-term City Council member who is trying to unseat Democratic Mayor Karen Bass on Nov. 3. Bass, elected in 2022, is the first woman to serve as mayor of Los Angeles. State of play: Raman became the first Asian American woman and first South Asian elected to the L.A. City Council in 2020. A Harvard and MIT graduate, she entered politics after working on homelessness and neighborhood organizing. A September Berkeley IGS/L.A. Times poll found Raman at 39% among likely voters, Bass at 28% and 33% undecided. The intrigue: The Berkeley poll had Raman ahead 66%-4% among likely voters under 30, while 56% rated Bass' response to the Palisades Fire poor or very poor. It also found an even wider gap among likely Latino voters : Raman led Bass 45%-21%, with 34% undecided. What they're saying: "I'm getting a little emotional thinking about it," Raman told Axios and Noticias Telemundo on Wednesday at Visionarios when asked what it would mean if she and Mamdani led the country's two largest cities. Raman, who immigrated to the U.S. as a child, said her family came to America seeking opportunities they didn't have in India. She contrasted the welcome her family received with what she sees as a harsher moment for immigrants today under the Trump administration. "The idea of this city welcoming an immigrant as its mayor ... is just so deeply moving to me at this moment." The other side: Bass strategist Julie Chavez Rodriguez told Axios and Noticias Telemundo that voters are talking about rent, affordable housing, public safety and whether they can afford to raise families in Los Angeles. Rodriguez credited Bass with accelerating nearly 47,000 affordable housing units, a figure also cited by the mayor's office for units in the city's pipeline. She also defended Bass' response to federal immigration raids, pointing to lawsuits and restrictions on using city property to assist immigration enforcement. Zoom in: Raman's version of democratic socialism sounds less revolutionary than municipal. She told Axios that Americans are pushing back against an establishment they believe favors wealthy and politically connected interests. Her alternative: make City Hall deliver basic services and prove government can work for ordinary people. Raman called it "sewer socialism" or "pothole politics," adding: "I just want government to work for the people." Zoom out: Mamdani has made a similar ideological bet in New York, declaring at his inauguration that he was elected as a democratic socialist and would govern as one. Yes, but: Raman isn't simply the West Coast version of Mamdani. She calls herself an independent leader and has repeatedly split with Democratic Socialists of America-LA — accepting a pro-Israel group's endorsement that earned her a DSA censure . She also backed Jim McDonnell for LAPD chief over the group's objections and sought changes to L.A.'s voter-approved mansion tax that housing activists opposed.

events.title: Scoop: A powerful new model from startup Reflection is set to shake up the AI race
events.summary: A closely watched Nvidia-backed startup called Reflection is preparing to shake up the AI race with a powerful open-weight system that could threaten Chinese upstarts and U.S. AI giants alike. Why it matters: The marriage of an American open-weight model and Nvidia GPUs would give individuals and companies a new, cheaper alternative to Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Open models, designed to compete with Chinese rivals, can be harder to monitor and regulate than the Big Three so-called frontier models. Supporters of such ecosystems say their widespread availability and transparency also bring security advantages. Reflection's first model is set to be joined by other open-weight models from other Western players this month, sources tell Axios. That will bring a new competitive dimension to the AI boom. State of play: Reflection's model, set to be released soon, is expected to initially lag behind the most cutting-edge U.S. models and be competitive with top Chinese open-weight models. Sources tell Axios it will still boast powerful intelligence — capable enough to help companies build their own proprietary, low-cost AI systems. Combining a lower-tier open model with high-quality company data can yield results that rival the most expensive frontier AI systems in certain situations. A Reflection spokesperson declined to comment. The big picture: Open-weight models, the most powerful of which are almost uniformly made in China, have taken Silicon Valley by storm. As opposed to closed models like Claude and ChatGPT, open-weight models like Reflection's are generally available to be downloaded freely and can be used and customized by anyone. On platforms that serve many models, their combined market share at times has surged to take up a majority of usage. However, in the far higher-spending arena of enterprise use, which is typically handled through API and corporate billing, open-weight models account for a small proportion of usage, AI execs and analysts say. Zoom in: Reflection's ultimate goal is to pioneer the "AI factory" — a product allowing institutions to spin up their own localized AI ecosystems. A company, for example, would take its own proprietary data, use Reflection's models and secure its own computing firepower to build a highly customized, cheap AI system. Some institutions, particularly hedge funds and trading firms, are already eager to build proprietary AI systems using their own highly guarded data. The startup has begun testing this concept, announcing a sovereign AI factory partnership with Shinsegae Group in South Korea. Behind the scenes: In preparation for the launch, Reflection has held discussions with interested parties in Washington and elsewhere in recent weeks to detail its model release and explain how the AI factory will work, sources told Axios. It is also aggressively locking up the compute capacity required to scale. In recent weeks, the startup signed massive deals with Nebius and SpaceX to rent Nvidia AI servers. What they're saying: Reflection CEO Misha Laskin has indicated it will take time for its models to reach the most advanced capabilities. "They're kind of like rocket ships," Laskin, who previously worked at Google, told CNBC . "To build a big rocket ship, it takes time." The Nvidia factor: The AI factory has been a core vision of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang for years. He has described a scenario combining computing hardware with open-source models, allowing enterprises to retain ownership of their data. Top AI users in Western business and government, such as banks or the Pentagon, balk at using highly capable Chinese models due to security risks. Reflection and other Western players are trying to fill that void. For years, Huang has sought to strengthen the open AI ecosystem and has been strongly supportive of Reflection's move toward building a top open system, according to stories in the Wall Street Journal and The Information . The bottom line: Reflection's release, and the startup's close ties to Nvidia, will bring a renewed focus on open-weight models, combining with other coming offerings to shake up the AI race.

events.title: Revive Raskin's 3 laws of software with humane work that considers a dev's duty of care
events.summary: In 1942, Isaac Asimov formulated three laws of robotics. 58 years later, Jef Raskin responded with three laws of human-computer interface design. They haven’t been bettered yet. There are rules, and even laws, about designing computer user interfaces. Even after 35 years of Linux, which has brought Unix to the masses, the FOSS world has not yet really grasped this. In the meantime, the proprietary software world is busily forgetting everything it once knew. Sometimes these rules surface today, and the FOSS folks often get very cross when reminded that they’re user-interface scofflaws. Marcin Wichary’s recent blog post, They had no concept of a duty of care to their users, is an excellent recent example. (The Reg FOSS desk much admires Mr Wichary’s writing, to the extent that we bought his history of the keyboard, Shift Happens.) In his latest post, Wichary refers to CHERI Project boffin David Chisnall. Chisnall is a long-term Vim user – we all have our failings – and recently recounted trying NeoVim. He uses Vim’s persistent-undo feature, which records changes in a separate directory, so that you can repeatedly undo until you get back to changes you made weeks or months earlier. He’s customized where it’s kept, and when he tried the NeoVim fork, it overwrote his Vim undo file. In a later update to his post, he acknowledges that there was a warning, but he expected it to be safe. It was not safe. It overwrote records of more than a decade’s worth of changes. As he puts it: “Vim has kept this working across major version upgrades over a period of about 20 years. I don’t even think about it, it’s just part of Raskin’s First Law: A program may not harm a user’s data or, through inaction, allow a user’s data to come to harm. If vim or the computer crash, or if I close a file and come back to it six months later, my undo history is still there.” Wichary expands Chisnall’s citation of Raskin’s first law by giving all three, but just in case you’re not a follower of “Golden Age” science fiction, a little context. Asimov introduced his three laws in a short story called “Runaround”, in Astounding Science Fiction magazine* in May 1942. (The story was later collected in the anthology I, Robot – which is nothing like the terrible 2004 film.) A robot may not injure a human being or, through inaction, allow a human being to come to harm. A robot must obey the orders given it by human beings except where such orders would conflict with the First Law. A robot must protect its own existence as long as such protection does not conflict with the First or Second Law. Asimov’s idea was that by setting these rules, he could end the terrible genre of killer-robot stories that was already tired and stale by 1942. Jef Raskin, the lead designer of Apple’s original Macintosh project, attempted to bring similar clarity to software UI. Raskin’s three laws are: A computer shall not harm your work or, through inaction, allow your work to come to harm. A computer shall not waste your time or require you to do more work than is strictly necessary. An interface is humane if it is responsive to human needs and considerate of human frailties. He defined them in his 2000 book The Humane Interface, which you can still buy, or borrow from the Internet Archive. Sadly, Raskin died in 2005, but we have written about his work and his influence several times. He did set some of the direction of the original Macintosh. After Steve Jobs was booted off the Lisa, he took over the Macintosh – as described in The Canon Cat and the Mac that Steve Jobs killed. Raskin quit, and instead designed the remarkable Canon Cat, as we described a couple of years ago. We suspect Raskin was not a fan of Vi, the forerunner of Vim. We aren’t either, which is why we chose the year in the headline of this story: it’s the year Bill Joy wrote vi. Raskin criticized modal software, which requires extra mental effort from the user. So did another UI pioneer, the late great Larry Tesler, who invented the cut/copy/paste trio of commands. Tesler was known for his dictum “Don’t mode me in!” and even had a car license plate reading “NOMODES.” Dr Chisnall has some history of upsetting Unix fans – we’ve referred to one of his papers before: in 2018, he wrote C Is Not a Low-level Language: Your computer is not a fast PDP-11. Unix fans really didn’t like this. This vulture has been told to kill himself for daring to criticize C before now. (We wish we were joking, but no.) Although he has now updated his Mastodon post, the NeoVim fans are not happy. Indeed, one has lambasted this vulture on Bluesky for sharing Wichary’s post. It is interesting to note that NeoVim is the recommended editor in Omarchy, and until recently, the NeoVim developers cited a tweet from DHH on the project website. After an acromonious debate, the pull-quote was removed right around the time of Chisnall’s and Wichary’s posts. In the wide world of software design, we don’t expect the right-wing edge of that community to innovate much in ease of use. In a way, Unix and C embody a machismo infused school of software design: that of enjoying the process of mastering things which are hard to use. However, there are other types of software. We recently enjoyed reading about emulating an original Macintosh on a £0.60 chip. That’s $0.80 and of course the computer is a Raspberry Pi – but not even a Pi Zero: it’s a Pi Pico, a microcontroller. There is still some hope that the world can rediscover tiny, simple, user-centric software, built to be friendly first, and for rich functionality second. And, it almost goes without saying, hand-coded without bot assistance. Bootnote * Astounding magazine changed its name to Analog in 1960, and it’s still around. We recommend it. If you haven’t read Asimov’s original “Runaround”, that issue of Astounding is on the Internet Archive too. ®

events.title: Spies, prime ministers, and balls: The BBC Domesday project @ 40
events.summary: Decades before the modern web, the BBC Domesday Project dared to archive an entire nation using…. what else – massive LV-ROM (LaserVision Read Only Memory) LaserDiscs. To mark the impending 40th anniversary of the BBC Domesday Project's release, the UK's Centre for Computing History (CCH) hosted a celebration at its museum on September 19, bringing together several of the original team members responsible for the system. One was Mike Tibbetts, an assistant to Peter Armstrong, the BBC producer behind the project. Tibbetts revealed that the UK's domestic intelligence service, MI5, took an interest in the system, but "they didn't understand a word of what we were doing!" "And on one occasion, Peter and I had to give a presentation, or Peter gave the presentation to [former prime minister] Margaret Thatcher, and well, I'm not sure she understood what we were doing either…" What they were doing was compiling a trove of data that will prove invaluable to historians in the years to come, even if the politicians of the era looked nervously on at the amount of data being handed over to the public. The Domesday Project was intended to be a modern version of the Domesday Book, compiled after the 1066 Norman invasion of England. The original book surveyed most of England and parts of Wales and was used by the King to assess dues owed to him. 900 years later, the name was given to a project in which more than a million people participated to provide a snapshot of life in the UK. Participants (many of whom were school children) contributed content, which was linked with maps, photographs, and other data. It was all compiled onto a pair of LaserDiscs – the Community Disc and the National Disc – and accessed via a BBC Master computer and a Philips VP415 LaserVision player. Armstrong came up with the idea, and the team compiled the project between 1984 and 1986. The system was eventually released at the end of 1986, and was aimed at schools, libraries, and universities. It was, alas, not a roaring sales success – the exact price per unit is difficult to pin down, but approximately £5,000 is a fair estimate. Government subsidies lowered the cost to around £3,000, but it was still out of reach for much of its audience. As a resource, however, it has huge value, which will only increase as the years pass. Tibbetts drew parallels to the original Domesday Book, which took centuries for historians to recognize as a vital resource. "Perhaps," he mused, "40 years is simply too short a time for historians to perceive the Domesday Project as a sufficiently distant benchmark of useful research." Perhaps. However, while hundreds of years have passed since the Domesday Book was compiled, the years have not been kind to the Domesday Project, thanks to technology's inexorable march. "The original Domesday Book had one huge advantage over the Domesday Project when it comes to future-proofing and longevity," explained Tibbetts. "The vellum pages of the original Domesday have been preserved for 940 years so far, and it's likely to continue to exist well into the future. "It took very few years for the bespoke technology of the BBC Domesday Project to be overtaken by universal media technologies." However, they chose the technology at the time for good technical reasons. The BBC Micro could output a 625-line television picture. The Philips LaserVision system could be re-engineered to store alphanumeric data. There wasn't much in the way of authoring and playback systems, so, as Tibbetts explained, the team had to invent everything. "In technological terms," he said, "the world of 1984 really couldn't be more different from the instant-access, media-rich world of today." And so, inevitably, within a few short years, that technology began to show its age. "As was entirely predictable, our discs aged and became difficult to read. The expensive LV-ROM player was quickly superseded by cheaper and more widely available CD-ROM and DVD systems." And, worse, "Largely because of the lack of any great academic interest in preserving our massive resource for the future, the BBC Domesday Project was in grave danger of disappearing without a trace." Several initiatives have kicked off over the years to preserve the project, and the CCH's event was as much about celebrating those as it was about looking at the project's genesis. Tibbetts dropped some nuggets of information about the project, estimating that 60 people reported directly to him and Armstrong, with another 60 in subcontracted teams. He also discussed the frustration the team felt as doubt was cast about whether the project was even possible. "We came back from Christmas in January 1986," Tibbetts recalled, "we sat down for our first team meeting, and I was forced to point out that our little VAX minicomputer didn't have one byte of data that was ready to go onto the Domesday discs, so we did the whole thing in a few months!" As far as hardware was concerned, Andy Finney, who handled mastering the discs, remembered that the original plan for the Domesday Project was for it to be mouse-based, rather than the trackball the system used for navigation. The mouse was still a relatively novel concept, alien to many users. "I remember vividly one chap who was navigating with this mouse on the table, and he moved the mouse towards him, and by the time he got to the edge of the table, he hadn't actually reached the bottom of the screen. So he went on the edge and underneath…" Tibbetts added, "I always feel guilty about the mouse, because we got that wrong … the decision came down in favor of the trackball because that is much more easy for somebody with movement disabilities to use rather than a mouse." "But boy, did we get that wrong…" As Tibbetts noted, even with little interest from some parts of the academic community, enthusiasts have continued to put in a huge amount of effort over the years to keep the resource accessible. Simon Inns of the Domesday86 project described it as "a race against time" – not just for hardware, but to get data off discs before bit rot rendered them unreadable. The good news is that the Domesday discs have been preserved, and reside in the Internet Archive. "Anyone," said Inns, "can go to the Internet Archive and download a Domesday Disc. This is, like, groundbreaking stuff. 10 years ago, this was a laugh, right? Now you can actually do this." While there might not be many functioning examples of the hardware around anymore, the preservation efforts mean that the Domesday Project will endure. "Our hope," said Inns, "is that within the next couple of years, everyone in this room [at The Centre for Computing History] will be able to have a Domesday system and be able to experience what it was like." The Centre for Computing History does, of course, have working Domesday systems on hand, including RM Nimbus systems and the original BBC Master version. There's also a new touchscreen version available. ®

events.title: AI 'less safe' for keeping secrets than most people assume
events.summary: Since generative artificial intelligence became mainstream, users have been increasingly entrusting more information to a chatbot. But events in recent months have proved that it can go rogue and meddle with other systems. It does not help that the organisations involved – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta Platforms – are the biggest in the field and are supposed to have secure environments. The issues surrounding AI are not new, but the growing risks leading to more concern among analysts and experts. For years, data security meant keeping the wrong people out of a database, but AI presents a new threat. Arguably the foremost issue – “a reason that is quite new” – is the fact that AI systems that previously only held data can now act on it, says Edgars Nemse, chief executive of the GenLayer Foundation. The foundation describes itself as the builder of the “Court of the Internet” where AI agents resolve disputes without human intermediaries. Consumers are increasingly connecting AI agents to their email, calendars and bank accounts. “An agent that can read your inbox can also be manipulated by a malicious email,” Mr Nemse tells The National . “A hidden instruction on a web page can redirect it. An attacker who gets the right text in front of your agent may get as far as one who has your password. Most people haven't started thinking about that yet.” Interacting with and entrusting AI “is less safe than most people assume”, he emphasises. Morey Haber, chief security adviser at US cybersecurity company BeyondTrust, notes that users are moving from AI systems that simply process information to AI agents that can access emails, files, applications, financial information, medical data and potentially anything else regarding personal identities – fundamentally changing the cybersecurity equation. “A data breach used to mean someone stole just your information. In an agentic AI world, compromising the right identity could mean someone can use your information, privileges and AI agents to act as you, with all of the stolen information as a backdrop,” he tells The National . Therefore, “the biggest risk with AI is not that it knows too much – but that we are giving it too much, trusting it too quickly and increasingly allowing it to act on our behalf with knowledge that lacks sensitivity awareness”. Fundamental change Last week, OpenAI admitted governments could be among “dozens” of entities around the world that may be infiltrated by its AI models. It disclosed that US entities such as the Securities and Exchange Commission were breached, following a similar incident involving the Australian government . “The Australian case is a useful illustration precisely because it wasn't a criminal attack,” says Mohammed Aboul-Magd, general manager for cybersecurity at US AI and quantum tech firm SandboxAQ . “An agent doing research went around the blocks meant to stop it, reached data it had no authority to access and months passed before anyone noticed,” Mr Aboul-Magd tells The National . “The damage was limited, but the pattern is the real threat for consumers: agents with broad access moving quickly, with nobody checking what they did until well after the fact.” In August, Facebook parent company Meta admitted one of its models had hacked into three companies, while last week Google said its Gemini AI bot had escaped from a sandbox environment and infiltrated three companies. OpenAI also said its own research agents had posted 53 images from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. Restoring confidence In the US – home of the major AI companies embroiled in recent breaches – the share of Americans who trust businesses to use AI slipped from 31 per cent to 27 per cent in 2026, while the share of those who think AI does more harm than good jumped to 39 per cent, a Gallup and Bentley University survey found. However, those figures were published in July, before the disclosures about government websites and user images. “So, I'd expect the next numbers to be worse [now],” says Mr Nemse. He does, however, acknowledge there are “decent measures” being taken to restore trust. “Restoring [trust] will take something more concrete than promises: independent testing … fast, honest disclosure when something goes wrong, and accountability that reaches the people actually affected,” he adds. An important paradox is emerging: AI adoption is growing faster than AI trust and operational governance. People are using the technology because it is useful, not necessarily because they completely trust how their information is being processed. “Restoring that trust requires much more than another privacy policy or checkbox from a governance team,” Mr Haber says. “Users need transparency around what information is being collected, how long it is being retained, whether it trains future models, who can access it from inside and outside the organisation, and what happens when something goes afoul.” Consumer protection Considering the AI breaches of government organisations, which have strong cybersecurity protection, what about regular consumers who don't have access to expensive security guardrails? “Consumers do not need the cybersecurity budget of a government agency or Fortune 500 company to dramatically reduce their AI exposure,” Mr Haber says. Analysts recommend setting unique passwords, using a trusted password manager, activating multifactor authentication and keeping applications up to date – those are the first lines of defence against any potential hack. They also urge users to avoid opening malicious emails or messages that can contain phishing attempts or ransomware threats. The “most useful habit” is to treat an AI assistant the way you would treat anyone else, Mr Aboul-Magd says. “Ask what it actually needs to do the job and give it that and nothing more, because the permissions you grant are a far bigger exposure than the conversations you have with it,” he adds. Still, the bulk of the responsibility lies with AI companies, since they have the resources and the ability. “Honestly, most of the fix has to come from the companies, because ordinary users can't audit a lab's research environment,” Mr Nemse says. But “people can still shrink how much of their life is exposed”, he adds. “I'd assume anything you upload to an AI service could one day end up somewhere you didn't intend."

events.title: Iraq transports its oil through Strait of Hormuz as US-Iran war chokes exports
events.summary: Iraq 's state oil company has moved its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades as the US-Iran war threatens the country's primary export route. The Iraqi Oil Tankers Company shipped two million barrels of crude through the waterway on a very large crude carrier, director general Ali Qais was quoted as saying by state media. The move was aimed to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, he added. The company is now in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”, Mr Qais said. Since the Iran war broke out in February, Iraq has been facing one of its most serious economic and security situations. Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals. The strait has been effectively closed by Iran since the conflict broke out, with shipping disrupted by missile and drone attacks, insurance surges and naval confrontations. Total Hormuz flows in September stood at 6.02 million bod, less than a third of February's 20.64 million bpd, according to Kpler, highlighting the continued disruption to the region's main oil export artery. Iraq has been caught in the middle of the war, with pro-Tehran armed groups having launched drones towards Gulf states from Iraqi territory, prompting countries in the region to hold Baghdad responsible. Meanwhile, ships crossing Iraqi waters near the strait have been at increased risk, forcing Baghdad to offer discounted rates on services at Basra Port and causing buyers to demand delivery outside the waterway. The government has been struggling to revive alternative routes – including a proposal to reopen the Iraq-Turkey pipeline through Ceyhan and another to move crude to Syria by land – but these solutions would only cover a fraction of Iraqi exports. Iraq has been able to move three million barrels of oil a day since the beginning of September, Oil Minister Bassim Khudair said last month. Opec’s second-largest producer is now looking to further boost its production as it expects alternative pipelines and the country’s improved export infrastructure comes on stream, he told the Iraqi News Agency. “The government plans to increase export capacity to five million barrels a day after the completion of the strategic pipelines extending to Fishkhabour and Baniyas, in addition to the export terminals in the Strait of Hormuz,” he said. The latest shipment indicates that Iraq has adopted the strategy of moving oil past the Strait of Hormuz to guarantee delivery and secure better prices, rather than leaving buyers to shoulder the war risk premium. The tanker company, once a major fleet operator in the 1980s, has been trying to rebuild itself after successive wars and rounds of sanctions. Buying its own VLCCs would provide Baghdad with more control over its main source of income.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Debris field' found after 6-person medical flight goes missing over Atlantic The US Coast Guard is continuing the search. ( US Coast Guard via AP ) The US Coast Guard has found a "debris field' in its search for an air ambulance that went missing over the Atlantic. The Canadian-registered aircraft was carrying six people from Bermuda to Boston in the United States. The Coast Guard said the search would continue. Searchers have found debris from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it went missing over the Atlantic during a flight from Bermuda to Boston. The "debris field" was found off the coast of Nantucket, in the US state of Massachusetts, following the disappearance on Saturday, the US Coast Guard said. Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, the Coast Guard said in a statement. It added that the next of kin of those missing had been notified and one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday. According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 aircraft lost contact very early on Saturday morning. Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been "coming in blind" when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it disappeared. The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net. "Roger, you said you're coming in blind. Is that what you said?" a controller can be heard asking the pilot. The plane may have lost its navigational instruments as a storm seen on radar moved across its path, former US Department of Transportation inspector-general Mary Schiavo said. The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 7.3 kilometres to around three kilometres, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24. "Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm," Ms Schiavo, an aviation attorney, said. "It's a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind. "It's very easy to get disoriented and not know if you're turning, climbing, descending, etc." The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport for the night flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport. Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country's Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on X. The Bermuda government is in contact with US authorities and the families of the passengers, Bermuda Premier David Burt wrote in a statement posted on Instagram. "We are praying that all six people will be found safe," the statement said. The US National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate. events.title: Syria 'pressing on accelerator' to attract US investors
events.summary: US investors see an opportunity to invest early in Syria as the transitional government races to establish a pro-business environment and attract foreign capital. “We see that the door is open, and we're coming early,” Steve Lutes, vice president of Middle East Affairs at the US Chamber of Commerce, said in an interview. “I think US companies made it very clear across a different range of sectors that they're looking to be strategically engaged, to be a long-term partner in helping Syria get back up on its feet and excel economically.” Mr Lutes spoke to The National after the Chamber of Commerce hosted a round-table with Syrian President Ahmad Al Shara and Foreign Minister Asaad Al Shibani on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly last month. He also recently led a delegation of more than 50 American businesses and 80 delegates to Damascus. The delegation – which included Baker Hughes , Caterpillar, Visa and dozens of other US firms – marked a significant step in re-establishing Washington's economic relationship with Syria after the 13-year civil war. It also came shortly after the US lifted its state sponsor of terrorism designation on Syria, which had been a prominent roadblock to the country’s reintegration into the international financial system. Syria’s government has moved quickly to attract investment since the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in 2024. The World Bank estimates it will cost $216 billion to rebuild the country. Some investment pledges from the Gulf have already moved towards implementation, including DP World's $800 million investment commitment to Tartus Port. At the same time, Syria has also courted foreign investors from Silicon Valley to Riyadh. “They're really pressing on the accelerator to try to move things forward,” Mr Lutes said. He added that the Chamber of Commerce was turning significant attention towards Syria's banking sector , which has undergone a rapid transformation under the current government. Mr Al Shara carried out the country’s first international Visa transaction in August. “It's so foundational to everything else,” Mr Lutes said. QNB and Mastercard issued the first internationally accepted payment card in Syria. The World Bank has also approved a $100 million grant to help establish a digitally enabled financial sector. Last Sunday, Central Bank of Syria Governor Mohammed Raslan told official news agency Sana that the government expected foreign investment in establishing new banks to surpass $1 billion in the coming period. The US Treasury Department on Thursday held a round-table in New York to support the country's financial sector and reconnection to the global financial system. Finance Minister Yisr Barnieh said in a LinkedIn post that discussions had focused on advancing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing standards, among other reforms. Treasury Assistant Secretary for Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes Jonathan Burke also stressed financial connectivity remains a vital component to combatting illicit finance and supporting Syria's reintegration into the global financial system, according to a readout. Public spending in Syria for first six months of the year totalled roughly $3.7 billion, compared to a public revenue of $2.7 billion, according to the finance ministry's first-half 2026 budget report. That leaves a fiscal deficit of about $1 billion. “The biggest challenge at the end of the day are the budgetary constraints and how are they going to finance and pay for it all,” Mr Lutes said. Damascus said it was implementing new measures to control public spending, including reviewing investment projects. Mr Barnieh wrote in a social media post on Monday that the measures would not affect salaries, wages or spending on essential needs such as health, education, water, energy, security, public safety and necessary operational maintenance. Gulf partnerships While the state sponsor of terrorism delisting removed the final pillar in the US sanctions architecture, investing in Syria continues to carry reputational risks. It remains on the Financial Action Task Force's grey list, and parties may have previous links to sanctioned actors. Mr Lutes described the Chamber of Commerce’s delegation to Damascus as an “exploratory” one to give US companies the chance to identify sectors for investment and re-establish trust with Syrian officials. Several US companies have already signed memorandums of understanding and other agreements with Syria including ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Baker Hughes, Hunt Energy and Ardent LNG. Gulf partners have joined some of these projects including Qatar's UCC Holding, which signed an agreement with Chevron and Syria's state-run petroleum company to develop the country's first offshore oil and gasfield. Mr Lutes anticipates more US companies could go down similar routes with Emirati, Saudi or Qatari partners who already have relationships with the country. Doing so could mitigate some risks and increase US investor confidence. He added that he hopes the delegation will become an annual occurrence. He also said the chamber is engaging with the Syrian government on addressing policy regulatory issues. “We're not going out of business any time soon. There's a lot of work for the chamber to support US companies that are interested in doing business in Syria, so we're going to be at this … for many years to come,” Mr Lutes said.

events.title: Regional audiences to lose Network 10, as licensee warns of TV's future
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made Network 10 channels will disappear from Mount Gambier, Riverland and Griffith TV screens. ( ABC News: Jak Rowland ) Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday. Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating. WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting. Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement. WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9. The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled. However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve , with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated. WIN Network says the decision reflects the economics of regional broadcasting. ( ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters ) In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable". "This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said. "Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue. "These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia. "WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding." The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year. The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available". Audiences in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith temporarily lost Seven Network channels last year. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) Job cut fears at one of Australia's largest toilet roll manufacturers How a 'piece of rural propaganda' became 'compulsory listening' for Aussies Soccer player with broken leg endures 70km car trip between hospitals Regional women share postpartum journeys to create change A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app. "WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said. The WIN Network holds the broadcast licenses in Mount Gambier, the Riverland and Griffith. ( ABC South East SA: Eugene Boisvert ) It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting. In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN. The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence. A government spokesperson said the decision was a "commercial matter" and that it was up to the networks to explain it to the community. "The government continues to support Australian broadcasters through a range of measures including the deferral of the Commercial Broadcasting Tax, which will deliver an estimated $111.3 million in savings for the sector," they said. "We know how important free-to-air TV is and are examining ways to ensure it continues to be delivered in a sustainable way in the future, with public consultation now underway.

events.title: Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
events.summary: Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month. It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city. Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear. “The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity. Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty. “Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict. The AP could not independently verify those reports. TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022. Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region. The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties. Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF , an allegation Eritrea has denied. The U.S. State Department in a statement Saturday urged Ethiopia and Eritrea to show restraint and return to talks. Iran live updates: Trump says war will be over 'very soon,' but offers no details Phone calls, records suggest some Cornell students tried to contain rape allegations District attorney reopens case of alleged Cornell University 'gang rape' “Increasing cross-border tensions between Ethiopia and Eritrea have the potential to affect the entire region,” State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said. “The Horn of Africa cannot sustain another military conflict and humanitarian crisis. A conflict jeopardizes ongoing U.S. collaboration on shared interests with both countries.” The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed , if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said. Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF. “This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.” He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.” The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted. In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures. Kiyaro reported from Hamburg, Germany.

events.title: Departure comes as the state investigates what went wrong during Pike's lethal injection.
events.summary: Tennessee's top prison official turned in his resignation days after the failed attempt to execute death row inmate Christa Pike , the state announced Saturday. Gov. Strada, who had served as commissioner since 2023, said he would cooperate with the independent investigation of the failed execution attempt. Pike, 50, survived two doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital and was taken to a hospital for life-saving treatment. What they're saying: In a statement, Strada said he believed his department "carried out its responsibilities in accordance with the established protocol. "Even so, stepping aside is in the best interest of Tennesseans as the independent review moves forward." Lee said Strada "served with integrity," adding that he appreciated Strada's "willingness to put the interests of Tennesseans first during this difficult moment. … "I thank Commissioner Strada for his dedicated service to Tennessee and pray God's blessings over him in the days ahead." The big picture: Strada's department has faced bipartisan criticism following the unprecedented failures during the attempt to execute Pike on Wednesday night. Her attorneys said the execution team used at least seven needles in their attempts to find a vein for an IV. Pike's attorneys said she complained of intense pain during the injection and developed blisters and burns around the injection site. Between the lines: Medical experts have said those details suggest the IV wasn't properly connected and that the drug might not have gone directly into her bloodstream. Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a local hospital on Friday, her attorneys said.
